1005-divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-he:
Dante Alighieri wrote the Divine Comedy, and the Rev. H. F. Cary translated its first part, Hell, or the Inferno, into English verse. Dante, lost in a dark wood, is guided by Virgil through nine circles of Hell, from limbo to the frozen pit, meeting sinners great and small in thirty-four cantos.

Cary's translation, in blank verse, keeps Dante's terror and pity, as each canto adds a new torment and a new moral. The Inferno is the most famous part of the Comedy, and Cary's version long served English readers as its standard. The book remains the doorway into Dante, for readers new to the medieval vision of judgement.
10690-a-desperate-chance-or-the-wizard-t:
Old Sleuth, a popular dime-novel pen name, published A Desperate Chance in 1897 as a thrilling narrative of the Rocky Mountains. Desmond Dare, son of a New York widow whose farm faces foreclosure, takes a desperate chance in a narrow gulch far from civilization. A campfire meeting with strangers, including a wizard tramp, sets the adventure in motion.

The tale runs through alarms, pursuits, and revelations in the high country, with a brave lad at its heart. Old Sleuth writes in the breathless style of cheap weekly fiction. Readers get a fast, old-fashioned Western adventure, typical of the dime novels boys once devoured.
10862-the-white-waterfall:
James Francis Dwyer wrote The White Waterfall as an adventure story in the International Adventure Library. Its chapters run from the song of the Maori and the professor's daughters through a knife from the dark, a storm, the Isle of Tears, and the pit. The ledge of death, the valley of echoes, devil dancers, and tombs of silence follow, toward the white waterfall itself.

A quoted song points the way to heaven out of Black Fernando's hell, setting the tale's tone of peril and escape. Dwyer writes brisk, exotic adventure for boys and general readers. The book offers islands, chases, and strange rites, in the popular adventure style of its day.
10973-the-late-mrs-null:
Frank R. Stockton wrote this 1886 comic novel about a Virginia plantation called Midbranch, with nine hundred and fifty acres, a lawn never crossed by carriages. The old family mansion, its persimmon tree, and its tobacco and wheat fields set the scene for a story of mistaken identity and stubborn old ladies.

Mrs. Null, late in the title's teasing sense, drives the comedy, and one memorable scene has an old lady seizing a double-barrelled gun on the porch steps. Stockton mixes Southern local colour with farce, letting misunderstandings pile up before they clear. Readers who enjoy gentle, character-driven comedy will find the novel's humour still fresh.
11130-greek-in-a-nutshell:
James Strong, professor of exegetical theology at Drew Theological Seminary, wrote this 1876 outline of Greek grammar with brief reading lessons for beginners in the New Testament. Strong prepared the manual for a normal class and for the Sunday-school assembly at Chautauqua, in twelve series of two pages each, later expanded with fuller reading lessons.

Lesson one gives the alphabet, with forms, names, and sounds, from alpha, a in man, to omega, o in no, with notes on pronunciation and accents. Later lessons parse verbs, nouns, and particles, with numbered notes explaining roots, augments, and moods. Strong promises that mastering this small book conquers the real difficulties of New Testament Greek, a good beginning being half the battle.
1125-all-s-well-that-ends-well:
Helena, a doctor's daughter, cures the King of France and claims as her reward the hand of Bertram, a young count who scorns her low birth and flees to war. William Shakespeare's problem comedy follows her pursuit of him through trickery, a bed trick, and a final reckoning at court.

Bertram's vows and Helena's patience divide audiences: is this a happy ending or a forced one? The play's wit and its dark view of rank and desire set it apart from the sunny comedies. It rewards readers who like Shakespeare at his most questioning.
11373-through-the-wall:
Cleveland Moffett's 1909 detective novel Through the Wall, written at his Paris home in the Villa Montmorency and illustrated by H. Heyer, follows French detective Coquenil through a blood-red sky, a private room number six, footprints, a weapon, and a passage through a wall. Chapters include Coquenil's greatest case, Gibelin's points, the towers of Notre-Dame, Lloyd and Alice, Pussy Wilmott's confession, a third pair of boots, a yellow tooth, a dog's memory, and a lost dolly.

Moffett, author of The Battle, writes a Paris mystery in the French manner, with a brilliant, theatrical detective. The novel's clues accumulate like stage properties, each chapter adding a twist. Detective-fiction readers will find it a lively example of pre-war transatlantic mystery writing.
11626-the-dawn-of-all:
Printed in Great Britain at the Mayflower Press, Plymouth, this novel opens in Rome in Lent 1911 with a man waking slowly in bed. Memory returns by steps: a sheet below his chin, a red coverlet like a blood-coloured landscape, and a ceiling remote as heaven's vault.

Roaring in his ears sinks to a murmur like a tide at high cliffs. Later he hides the purple at his throat under a thin cloak, slips out into Ambrosden Avenue, and walks west down Victoria Street, weary of a silent, well-ordered ecclesiastical house. The story follows a priest's inner life in a changed Catholic world.
11913-mr-meeson-s-will:
H. Rider Haggard's Mr. Meeson's Will follows Augusta, a young woman dealing with a publisher, and Eustace, disinherited in the second chapter. Later chapters move from Augusta's little sister and her decision to the Royal Mail Steamer Kangaroo, a catastrophe at sea. Kerguelen Land, a remote island in the southern ocean.

Augusta's rescue and the fate of Mr. Meeson turn on a will, and Haggard mixes publishing satire with shipwreck adventure, a combination his readers knew from his African romances. Passages on voyages compare sailing ships and steamers. They note how a seed roots and flowers on a sailing ship, then withers as the voyage drags, in a metaphor for love tested by long separation.
12093-the-song-of-the-stone-wall:
Helen Keller's Song of the Stone Wall, published in October 1910 with copyright in 1909 and 1910, began as a poem Keller intended to dedicate to Dr. Edward Everett Hale, who loved old walls and the traditions clinging to them. Hale died before publication, and the dedication became a memorial instead.

Keller writes of fearless journeyings and old forgotten things, of ancestors whose blood warms the fingers tracing their story, and of embossed books unobliterated by time. Later passages climb a hill past tumbled rocks, scattered like sheep or great birds at rest, to aged pines where a maiden's moccasins tread. There, stone walls become a figure for endurance, memory, and the struggle with darkness.
12181-the-story-of-bessie-costrell:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote The Story of Bessie Costrell as a short village drama, published with Fenwick Career in 1910. Ward, a leading late Victorian novelist, sets the tale in an English country parish, told in scenes rather than chapters.

Bessie, a laborer wife, wrestles with guilt, drink, and small thefts, while her husband Isaac promises to do better and brings news of a son return. The story follows temptation in a household where half-crowns and public-house talk carry real weight. Ward moral is stern: poverty and drink corrode character, and repentance comes late. The tale is brief, bleak, and carefully observed, a minor Ward work with a sharp village eye.
12343-the-art-of-iugling-or-legerdemaine:
S. R. published The Art of Jugling or Legerdemaine in 1612, a book that exposes conjuring tricks, card and dice cheating, alchemy frauds, and foolish charming. The author writes for gentlemen who desire insight and private practice of mirth and recreation.

Chapters decipher conveyances of legerdemain: how to tell what card a man sees at the bottom of the pack, how to shuffle a marked card undermost, and how to spot false dice. Cautions warn against cheats at cards and dice, the beggarly art of alchemy, and the foppery of cousening charms. The book is both a manual and an exposure, teaching tricks while warning readers not to be tricked. It is an early classic of magic literature.
1264-the-wheels-of-chance-a-bicycling-id:
H. G. Wells sends Hoopdriver, a draper's assistant on his first cycling holiday, pedaling through southern England, where he meets Jessie, a young woman fleeing a dull life, and resolves to rescue her. The idyll follows their ride, their mishaps, and the older man who pursues them.

Wells writes the comedy with warmth and a reformer's eye: the bicycle, new and cheap, gives clerks and girls a taste of freedom. The tale is light, funny, and kind. It captures the 1890s cycling craze and the small hopes of ordinary folk, and it still charms.
12654-the-roll-call:
Arnold Bennett's Roll-Call, third edition, follows a young artist through London and the Five Towns. Its opening pages list Bennett's many works, from Clayhanger and Hilda Lessways to The Card and The Regent, with fantasias, short stories and books on writing and life.

The novel itself, a study of ambition, art and love, centres on a painter who seeks fame in London while ties to home pull him back. Bennett writes with his usual clarity about work, money and marriage. The Roll-Call offers a serious, readable portrait of an artist's career, in the tradition of Clayhanger and Hilda Lessways.
12691-the-high-school-left-end-or-dick-c:
H. Irving Hancock's High School Left End, or Dick and Co. Grilling on the Football Gridiron, follows Dick Prescott's football season. Chapters run from sulking in the football camp and the start of the Dodge mystery through soreheads in conclave. A football notice, Dick firing both barrels, advice for Bayliss and two girls turning the laugh follow.

Does football teach real nerve, Dick refusing the crown like Caesar, and Bert Dodge starting something? A school traitor's strategy, a fear for the plotter, a cattle car, a school cut and a Thanksgiving Day game follow. Hancock writes schoolboy football with moral energy, where sulker and real man are distinguished on the field. The book is a spirited sports tale for boy readers.
12793-cobwebs-from-an-empty-skull:
Dod Grile, pen name of Ambrose Bierce, gathered these fables and tales in 1874 from the comic paper Fun, illustrated by the Dalziel brothers. Fables of Zambri the Parsee open the book, followed by brief seasons of intellectual dissipation and divers tales, from The Grateful Bear to Dr. Deadwood, I Presume. Satire, not sense, rules.

A poodle arguing with a giraffe about a foot, and a dog chasing a dragged deer, show the book's absurd, biting humour. Bierce aims his wit at folly in all ranks. The collection suits readers who enjoy dark, clever fables in the Victorian comic vein.
12803-headlong-hall:
Thomas Love Peacock wrote Headlong Hall in 1815 as a comic novel of ideas, set at a Welsh country house party. The squire gathers philosophers, poets, clergymen, and cranks, each bent on forcing nature to fit a pet system. Dinners, walks, a tower visit, and a ball give them room to argue.

Peacock lets each guest talk himself into folly, from the moral novelist to the landscape gardener, while romance quietly pairs off the younger guests. The book's wit lies in talk, not plot, and its short chapters move fast. Readers who enjoy satire of grand theories will find it still fresh and funny.
12827-the-rising-of-the-red-man-a-romanc:
John Mackie's romance of the 1885 Riel Rebellion opens on March 16, 1885, as Louis Riel addresses Métis and Native people near Batoche on the Saskatchewan. Settlers, ranchers, and soldiers are soon caught in the storm, with sieges at Battleford, a grim blockade, and the battle of Cut Knife ahead. Flight across ice and capture by Poundmaker's men raise the danger.

Mackie follows his heroes through judgment halls, stampedes, and bold bids for liberty, in the adventure style of his day. The novel's view of Riel and the rising is partisan and dated, but its pace never flags. It offers a vivid, if one-sided, tale of the Canadian prairie war.
13160-an-iron-will:
Orison Swett Marden's 1901 An Iron Will, with help from Abner Bayley and portraits of famous men, teaches that will is the core of character. Marden quotes Emerson, that the education of the will is the object of existence, and Mill, that character is a completely fashioned will. His chapters train the will through work, struggle, and example.

Examples run from Nelson, who always fought when unsure, to Horatius holding a bridge with two friends, and Leonidas at Thermopylae. Marden also lists humble births: Virgil son of a porter, Horace of a shopkeeper, Shakespeare of a wool stapler, Cromwell of a brewer. The book is classic American self-help, earnest and full of lives held up as proof.
13310-the-complete-poetical-works-of-jam:
The Complete Poetical Works of James Russell Lowell, cabinet edition from Houghton, Mifflin in 1902, gathers the poems Lowell edited for the Riverside edition, plus later pieces from his executor C. E. Norton. A publishers' note traces the text from Lowell's own definitive edition to the Cambridge edition. The volume runs from early lyrics to satires and odes.

One satire shows a bard singing for reform and slave freedom, hitting foes with Thor's mallet and preaching brotherly love with a sling stone. Another, in Yankee dialect, weighs copper companies, quack medicine, and letters from the other side before choosing where to anchor. Lowell's verse is witty, learned, and American in voice, from high ode to low dialect.
13332-fifteen-years-in-hell:
Luther Benson's 1885 autobiography tells of fifteen years lost to drink. He begins with childhood, parentage, and schooling, then follows the slow road into heavy drinking: broken work, ruined health, friends lost, and homes blighted. He blames his own choices as much as habit, and names the friends who stayed beside him.

William Beck, who fetched him home from Connersville in his worst days, stands out as a faithful helper. The book closes with Benson speaking in public, first embarrassed before a packed Raleigh audience, then steadier as he turns his story into warning. It is a temperance life story, meant to show both the cost of drink and a way back.
13556-behind-the-line-a-story-of-college:
Ralph Henry Barbour's 1902 story of college life and football follows heroes in moleskin through new quarters, changed minds, and a critical season. Barbour thanks Lorin F. Deland of Boston for the football play described in chapter fifteen, and C. M. Relyea illustrates the book.

Neil, gasping on a window seat, warns Fletcher and Livingston that rivals plan to run off with a player, urging escape by the back way and round by the railroad. Sydney and Mills debate a play that will leave a man horribly banged up but stop the opposition, asking whether any player may rightly be placed where punishment is certain. Barbour mixes campus fun, loyalty, and hard tackling.
13851-the-downfall:
Émile Zola's La Débâcle, translated by E. P. Robins as The Downfall, follows the Franco-Prussian War of 1870. French troops camp near Mülhausen under a lowering August sky, with tents and stacked muskets along the lines. Defeat, retreat, and the fall of the Second Empire follow across three parts. Soldiers, officers, and civilians share the disaster.

Zola studies war as a vast, impersonal force crushing ordinary men. Battles blur into hunger, confusion, and flight. A foreboding sense of calamity settles over orchards and grain stacks as night falls. The novel closes the Rougon-Macquart cycle's political arc with grim power. It stands among the great war novels of the nineteenth century.
13963-ireland-since-parnell:
Captain D. D. Sheehan, barrister and former MP for Mid-Cork, wrote Ireland Since Parnell in 1921. Chapter one, A Leader Appears, defends Parnell against critics who deny his stature. Some claim lieutenants made him, or that his talents were mediocre. Sheehan answers that Parnell could never hold his place in history without real leadership.

Later chapters trace Parnell's watchwords to farmers and his achievements in the years that followed. Sheehan writes as a Nationalist who knew the movement from inside. The book covers the troubled years after Parnell's fall. It suits readers of Irish political history. Its partisan warmth reflects its author and moment.
14216-st-george-s-cross-or-england-above:
H. G. Keene's 1887 tale, neither pure fiction nor absolute truth, pictures Channel Island life two centuries past. A prologue finds William Prynne, suspended member of Parliament, at a Strand window in September 1649, watching Thames barges at high water. Keene leans on Dr. Hoskins's Charles the Second in the Channel Islands for background, and Guernsey printing gives the book local color.

Love and law drive the island plot. Rose and Marguerite debate marriage, with M. le Gallais proposed by others and England's freer ways preferred by the younger sister. Alain Le Gallais later stands trial before the lieutenant-bailiff and six jurats, defended strenuously by Advocate Falle, yet found guilty and sentenced to death. Rose spends money she can ill afford, and secret service funds stretch Mme. de Maufant's borrowing. Royalist politics darken as Charles attends church, dines in public, and touches for king's evil.
14228-bracebridge-hall:
Washington Irving's Bracebridge Hall, in an 1877 Macmillan edition illustrated by R. Caldecott, sketches an English squire's household and village. Contents run from the hall, busy man, and family servants to the widow, lovers, family relics, an old soldier, Ready-Money Jack, bachelors, a literary antiquary, horsemanship, love symptoms, falconry, fortune-telling, and gipsies. The chivalry of the hall, frontispiece shows, prepares to take the field.

Books and schoolboys supply comedy. A little parson devours Dibdin's Bibliographical Tour as a boarding-school girl devours a sentimental novel, planning an expedition greater than Africa or the North Pole. Slingsby, once horsed at school, returns to sway the rod of empire in that same schoolhouse, honored by squire and Mr. Tibbets, yet restless each spring to rove again. Irving writes Old England with affection and gentle irony, preserving customs already fading in his own day.
14348-ma-pettengill:
Harry Leon Wilson wrote these linked tales in 1919, round the ranch of Mrs. Lysander John Pettengill. The narrator strolls up from the Arrowhead corrals on a still Sunday afternoon to the ranch house. Ma Pettengill rules her spread with wit, nerve, and a sharp tongue. The tales follow her household, her hands, and the folk of Red Gap. Wilson tells them in a dry, first-person voice that loves a good yarn.

One tale turns on the animal kingdom of the ranch, with foremen, towheaded boys, and a man who quits over the swarm of young ones. Another follows Lon and Vernabelle, whose poster for villa sites looks more like an ad for bath soap. Dulcie's winter sports and her talk of Bohemia stir Red Gap, where being thought smart in New York counts for much. The book charms as a set of ranch yarns, told with warmth and bite.
14430-purcell:
John F. Runciman's short 1909 life of Henry Purcell belongs to a series of small books on musicians. Purcell, who died in 1695 at thirty-six, served as organist of Westminster Abbey and composer to the Restoration court.

Runciman surveys his anthems, odes, songs, and the opera Dido and Aeneas, and he weighs Purcell's blend of old polyphony with newer Italian and French styles. A list of works and illustrations closes the volume. Runciman also notes Purcell's short life and lasting fame. The book is a compact, admiring introduction, written when English music was rediscovering its seventeenth-century master.
14489-nightfall:
Anthony Pryde's novel Nightfall opens at Wanhope, a large old manor house with a dark chestnut hall and Flemish glass, where Laura Clowes calls Bernard to tea on a June afternoon. The family motto over the gate reads Fortis et Fidelis.

Bernard, Laura, and their circle face debts, dinners, and country society, while younger members such as Isa watch grown-ups with sharp eyes. Pryde writes with Edwardian ease about houses, meals, and manners, letting tension gather beneath polite talk. The novel is a domestic drama of an old family at dusk, graceful and slowly unsettling.
14575-bylow-hill:
George W. Cable's 1902 novel is set in a Southern town where a rector, his bride, and a young district attorney form a close circle. Illustrations by F. C. Yohn accompany the Scribner edition.

Ruth and Godfrey, Isabel, and Arthur and Leonard move through courtship, church work, and public scandal, as a storm gathers over reputations and a lantern is quenched. Cable, known for Louisiana tales, writes here of New Orleans society with sympathy. The novel mixes romance with moral judgment, and its title hill stands for a community watching its own.
14597-the-woman-thou-gavest-me-being-the:
Hall Caine's 1913 novel tells the story of Mary O'Neill in her own voice, from girlhood through marriage, honeymoon, love, motherhood, loss, and recovery. Caine warns that he disguised real sources to defeat identification.

Mary grows up in a convent school and marries. She then learns the world's talk of infidelity, passion, and duty, debating with Alma and a countess whether a wife may answer a husband tit for tat. Caine's melodrama is earnest and moralizing. The novel was a bestseller of its day, and it shows Edwardian popular fiction at its most earnest.
14608-jimmy-lucy-and-all:
Sophie May's 1900 children's book, part of the Little Prudy's Children series, follows Jimmy, Lucy, and their friends through tallyho rides, dinners, gold mines, and a zebra kitten. Lee and Shepard published it in Boston.

Chapters include a knitting woman, an air-castle, Grandma Graymouse, stealing a chimney, and Nate's cave, all told in simple, lively prose for young readers. Edith photographs the children, and small mishaps turn into lessons. The book is gentle Victorian children's fiction, full of country play and family warmth. Sophie May wrote dozens of such books for American children.
14671-dorothy-vernon-of-haddon-hall:
Charles Major's historical romance Dorothy Vernon of Haddon Hall, in the Mary Pickford photoplay edition, follows Dorothy Vernon and her lover through Elizabethan Derbyshire. Grosset and Dunlap published it in 1908.

The narrator rides down to Haddon, faces the iron, the seed, the cloud, and the rain, and pursues Dorothy through Derby town, tribulation, and a tryst at Bowling Green Gate. Mary Stuart and Leicester enter the plot. Major writes a swashbuckling romance of the old hall, and the photoplay pictures tie the novel to its silent film version. Mary Pickford starred in the film of Dorothy Vernon.
1529-all-s-well-that-ends-well:
All's Well That Ends Well follows Helena, a physician's daughter. She cures the King of France and claims as her reward the husband of her choice: Bertram, a young count who scorns her low birth and flees to war in Italy. Helena pursues him with wit and patience, using a bed trick to claim her marriage rights.

Bertram's pride, Helena's resolve, and a comic pair of braggarts drive this problem comedy, which ends in forgiveness rather than triumph. Shakespeare leaves the moral questions open. The play is a sharp, bittersweet study of love, rank, and a woman who refuses to be refused.
1552-the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-i:
Julian Hawthorne edits this volume of the Lock and Key Library, gathering the most interesting stories of all nations in mystery and detection. Tales from many countries sit side by side, chosen for suspense and surprise. Hawthorne, son of Nathaniel Hawthorne, edited the Lock and Key series for American readers.

Hawthorne's series aimed to show the detective and mystery tale as a world form, not an English one alone. Readers who enjoy a varied anthology will find here a strong mix of famous and forgotten writers. The all-nations volume widens mystery beyond England, to France, America, and beyond.
15851-love-conquers-all:
A humour book by Robert C. Benchley, issued in 1922 with pictures by Gluyas Williams. Benchley, a wit of the Algonquin circle, writes essays on family life and the art of watching. His pieces treat ordinary pastimes as if they were grand sports. The tone stays light, self-mocking, and sharp.

Contents include the Benchley-Whittier correspondence, family life in America in three parts, and rules for watching auction bridge. How to watch a chess match, watching baseball, and spring planting follow, with a Christmas spectacle and the Manhattador. The book charms as classic American humour: a man who does little, watches much, and laughs at himself first.
15976-puck-of-pook-s-hill:
A children's history fantasy by Rudyard Kipling, first issued in 1906 by Macmillan and Company in London. H. R. Millar's pictures are omitted from this text-only version, proofed against a 1911 reprint. Two children on Pook's Hill meet Puck, the old spirit of England, who summons figures from the past. Kipling joins story to song in each chapter.

Weland's Sword, Young Men at the Manor, and The Knights of the Joyous Venture open the set. Old Men at Pevensey, A Centurion of the Thirtieth, and On the Great Wall follow, with The Winged Hats, Hal o' the Draft, and Dymchurch Flit. The Treasure and the Law closes the book. Kipling's tales still teach history as adventure: Romans, Normans, and smugglers, speaking in their own voices.
16397-larry-dexter-s-great-search-or-the:
Howard R. Garis sends young reporter Larry Dexter on the hunt for a missing millionaire in this 1909 boys' book. Larry, already known from From Office Boy to Reporter, uses a newsman's nose for clues, interviews, and chases through the city. The frontispiece catches him crying out over a find, in the best dime-novel style.

Garis writes fast, clean adventure for boys, with a new puzzle at each turn and honest pluck as the hero's chief tool. The book belongs to the Young Reporter series, but it stands alone. Young readers who like reporter heroes and city mysteries will enjoy the chase from first page to last.
16575-an-inquiry-into-the-permanent-caus:
William Playfair asks why wealthy and powerful nations fall in this inquiry, copied from the first edition in the British Library and checked against the second. Book one opens with the plan, then treats the general causes, within and without, that pull risen nations back to the level set by their size, soil, and people. Wealth destroying power in ancient nations gets full treatment.

Playfair writes as an economist and chart-maker, with tables and a chart of universal commercial history from 1500 BC. The book is dense but bold, applying commerce to history's great question. Readers of economic history will find an early, original attempt to chart the rise and fall of nations.
1736-thomas-lord-cromwell:
The Life and Death of Thomas, Lord Cromwell, attributed in part to William Shakespeare, follows the blacksmith's son from Putney to the height of Henry VIII's court. Young Thomas leaves his father's shop and travels to Antwerp and Bologna. He rises through service to Wolsey and the king, while old friends, merchants, and rivals cross his path.

The play is written in the crowded, episodic manner of the early history plays, with a chorus and a large cast of citizens, dukes, and bishops. Its authorship is uncertain, and that doubt is part of its interest: a Tudor rise told in Shakespeare's neighborhood, in verse that sometimes sounds like him and sometimes does not.
17388-andrew-marvell:
Augustine Birrell wrote this life of Andrew Marvell for the English Men of Letters series, edited by John Morley, published in New York and London by Macmillan in September 1905. Marvell, the seventeenth-century poet and member of Parliament, is followed from early days at school and college, through a happy garden state, to service as a civil servant under the Commonwealth.

Chapters cover Marvell in the House of Commons, his Rehearsal Transprosed, his last years in Parliament, his final satires and death, and his work as a man of letters. Readers get a compact, literary biography, more interested in Marvell's writing and wit than in archives. Birrell's portrait suits readers meeting Marvell for the first time.
1741-the-white-moll:
Newspapers call her the White Moll, a woman thief whose daring has made her a legend. She moves through New York's night world under aliases such as Gypsy Nan. A code message, a room numbered eleven, and a rendezvous with fellow thieves set the plot in motion.

Packard writes the crook melodrama of his day with full energy: secret meetings, narrow escapes, and a heroine who outthinks the men around her. The book's pull is the Moll herself, cool and resourceful, and the question of whether a life built on daring can end anywhere but on the brink.
1754-the-sea-gull:
Around a country estate gather an actress, her son the young writer, and the girl next door who dreams of the stage. A failed play and a shot gull mark their lives. A failed play, an unhappy love, and a shot gull become the marks by which the characters measure their lives.

Chekhov lets the drama sit in talk and inaction: people long for art, love, and fame, and settle for less. Masha trails her life behind her like an endless scarf, in her own bleak phrase. The play's sadness comes from that gap between what its people want and what they will do. It is the work that made Chekhov's name in the theatre.
17801-milly-darrell:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon wrote Milly Darrell, first run in Belgravia from 1870 to 1871, and printed here in a Paris copyright edition of 1873. The volume also holds Old Rudderford Hall and The Splendid Stranger, two shorter tales by the same hand.

Milly, just nineteen, leaves her father's house to serve as pupil teacher with the Miss Bagshots at Albury Lodge in Yorkshire. Her father is a poor country curate with a sick wife and four children, and Milly must earn her keep. Braddon writes brisk sensation fiction, with secrets, pride, and young love, in the style that made her a best-seller.
18385-vera-nevill:
Mrs. H. Lovett Cameron, author of Pure Gold and In a Grass Country, published this novel at Philadelphia in 1893. Vera Nevill, or Poor Wisdom's Chance, takes its subtitle from Moore's Melodies: poor wisdom's chance against a glance is now as weak as ever. The book follows a young woman through society, love, and the choices that test judgment.

Chapters open with the vicar's family and Kynaston Hall, then fan dead ashes, bring a lay rector, little pitchers, and a soiree at Walpole Lodge. Later chapters give an engagement, a meeting on the stairs, a meet at Shadonake, peacock's feathers, a wedding dress, and an unlucky love letter. Readers get a Victorian society novel, where a glance can undo wisdom and a letter can change a life.
18759-from-the-ball-room-to-hell:
T. A. Faulkner, a former dancing master, published this warning tract at Chicago in 1892 with the Henry Publishing Company. Faulkner, once owner of the Los Angeles Dancing Academy and Pacific Coast champion in fancy and round dancing, says he writes plainly from duty to God and neighbor. He began to dance at twelve and spent most of his life in dance parlors and academies.

His target is the ballroom and dancing academy as a danger to young girls, with parents blind to the risk. He urges readers to leave a life of selfish pleasure for a purer, happier one in faith. The book is a blunt, period example of moral reform writing.
18829-winner-take-all:
Larry Evans published this western novel with Grosset and Dunlap in 1920. It opens with Blue Jeans, twenty-two, riding into hard times toward the poor town of Reservoir, his mare Girl o' Mine worn down by weary miles and short grain.

A month earlier he had been a man of ambition with a dream, helped along by an Eastern scholar hunting prehistoric bones under the hills. Chapters ask whether luck is a lady, send him riding as a cowboy, and carry him through business talks, pots and pans, and a final winner-take-all contest. The novel follows a young rider trying to win back his standing and his luck.
19114-foe-farrell:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch wrote this novel. He dedicated it to anyone who supposes he has a worse enemy than himself. It unfolds in nights, from John Foe and a meeting at the baths. Then come a grand research, police station scrapes, and a picturedrome outrage. Later come a chase, a vendetta, and at last castaways on an island. The structure is episodic and theatrical.

A coroner's inquest scene shows the book's detective flavour. A wild stranger demands sight of a body, and a juror swoons. Press men are barred from a second viewing. Readers get a rich, old-style romance of enmity, pursuit, and self-knowledge, told with Quiller-Couch's literary flair.
19302-dinosaurs-with-special-reference-t:
W. D. Matthew, curator of vertebrate palaeontology, wrote this book on dinosaurs with special reference to the American Museum collections. Chapters cover the age of reptiles, North America then, kinds of dinosaurs, carnivorous, amphibious, and beaked forms, distribution, and collecting. A skull of a great carnivorous dinosaur fronts the work.

Matthew describes a North America strange in coast and mountains, shaped by rain, rivers, volcanoes, and slow rises and falls, with shallow seas covering low lands in times of overflow. Readers get a classic, readable dinosaur survey from the museum age of discovery.
1995-the-divine-comedy-volume-1-hell:
Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy opens with Hell, in Charles Eliot Norton's translation. It is dedicated to James Russell Lowell, who read the proofs of the volume in the last year of his life. Dante, lost in a dark wood, is guided by Virgil through the nine circles of the underworld, from the unbaptized to the traitors frozen in ice.

The canto-by-canto journey gives the poem its shape: sinners who tell their stories, punishments that fit their crimes, and a guide who explains what Dante sees. Norton's prose translation, made for readers who want Dante's meaning clearly, remains a trusted way into the poem, and this volume is its necessary first step.
19975-base-ball:
John Montgomery Ward wrote Base Ball as an insider's guide to the young professional game. Ward pitched and played shortstop for the New York club. He opens with the doubtful circumstances of the ball's own invention. History's accuracy about the first ball, he jokes, is itself in doubt. From there he treats rules, positions, and the game's growth. Ward was a Columbia-trained lawyer as well as a star.

Ward later helped found the players' Brotherhood and a rebel league. His book is both manual and manifesto for the sport. It dates from 1888, when baseball was becoming big business. Players' rights simmer under his technical chapters. Historians of the game still quote Ward constantly. He remains the thinking ballplayer of his century.
20058-the-napoleon-of-notting-hill:
G. K. Chesterton wrote The Napoleon of Notting Hill, his first novel, set in a future London. The sample verse speaks of starry streets that point to God. It names the great grey water-tower on Campden Hill. A child dreams that epic hour and dreams it still, the poem says.

Chesterton imagines a king who makes each London borough guard its own pride. Notting Hill then takes that game of flags and walls in earnest. The book mixes farce, swordplay, and deep talk about place and loyalty. It has drawn fans of both comic tales and serious ideas ever since.
20163-the-jolliest-school-of-all:
Angela Brazil published The Jolliest School of All in 1922, a girls' school story. A girl empties the bottom cupboards of a big bookcase at speed. Her method is not tidy at all, the book admits freely. Soon books, papers, paint-boxes, and music lie in a jumble around her.

Brazil wrote dozens of school tales loved by girls for decades. Her schools are bright, loyal, and full of scrapes and games. Chalks, stamps, crests, and knitting wool show a schoolgirl's full world. Readers get classic Brazil: cheer, friendship, and school pride in full flood.
20245-a-narrative-of-some-of-the-lord-s-:
George Müller of Bristol told, in his Narrative, of the Lord's dealings with him. Müller built orphan houses run on prayer and gifts alone. A reader from 1844 would not know how the work has grown since. By the time of writing, it had grown three or four times larger.

And still it kept growing, Müller reports with calm wonder. He never made direct appeals for money, by his own firm rule. Food, funds, and helpers came, he believed, in answer to prayer. Readers get a famed record of faith, charity, and Victorian orphan care.
2031-the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-i:
Julian Hawthorne edits this Lock and Key volume of real-life detective stories and true stories of modern magic, the second in the series. Part one draws on actual cases, part two on feats that seemed supernatural. Real-life detective stories, drawn from police records, give this volume its documentary edge.

Hawthorne presents the tales as fact, or as near fact as memory allows, letting readers judge where detection ends and wonder begins. The volume appeals to lovers of true crime and stage magic alike. Modern magic tales, of mediums and illusions, test how far a reader will believe.
20379-a-narrative-of-some-of-the-lord-s-:
George Müller of Bristol became famous for running orphan homes while refusing to ask anyone for money. He wrote this narrative to tell how God had led him, step by step, through his life and work. He says many souls were blessed by what he told them in person.

Müller felt it his duty to print the account so others, whom he could never meet, might gain from it too. The book records answers to prayer, hard trials, and steady trust. It remains a key first-hand record of one of the best-known faith missions of the Victorian age.
20416-the-annual-catalogue-1737-or-a-new:
The Annual Catalogue for 1737 lists the books published in Britain that year, with short accounts of many titles. Such catalogues helped booksellers and readers track the flood of new print. Each entry gives a taste of the book it names.

Among the lives on offer are memoirs of Madame de Brinvilliers, who poisoned her father and two brothers. Another book tells of an impostor who fooled a man's wife and family, and puzzled the Parliament of France for a long time. Crime, scandal, and wonders sold well in 1737, and the list proves it.
2043-the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-i:
Julian Hawthorne edits this American volume of the Lock and Key Library, gathering riddle stories and tales of mystery from Poe, Hawthorne, Irving, Bierce, and others. The Gold-Bug and The Oblong Box sit beside The Minister's Black Veil. Hawthorne's American volume follows the English one, showing a younger nation's taste in mystery.

Hawthorne's introduction traces the detective tale back to Poe's Dupin stories, before the name detective story existed. The collection offers a strong survey of American mystery writing, from early romance to sharp, modern puzzles. Poe's tales anchor the book, since American detective fiction begins with his Dupin stories.
2047-the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-i:
Julian Hawthorne edits this Lock and Key volume of stories by modern French novelists, including Victor Cherbuliez's Count Kostia and Paul Bourget's Andre Cornelis. French mystery and romance take the lead here. Cherbuliez, a French novelist of the late nineteenth century, wrote Count Kostia as a romance.

An anonymous tale, The Last of the line, and other pieces round out the set, showing French writers at their most dramatic. The volume suits readers who want classic crime with a Parisian flavour. Bourget's Andre Cornelis, a study of a son and a murder, gives the volume its psychological depth.
20480-palmistry-for-all:
Palmistry for All, by the famous palmist Cheiro, teaches readers to read character from the hand. Cheiro promised a skill anyone could pick up. His method rested on the lines, mounts, and shapes of the palm.

The book aims at quick, practical judgments. Many readers, it says, want to gain at a mere glance a grasp of the leading traits of people they meet. Businessmen and hosts alike were told the hand would not lie. Cheiro's guides sold widely, and this one shows the rules by which a generation tried to read strangers at sight.
20634-the-sleeping-bard-or-visions-of-th:
Elis Wyn's The Sleeping Bard is a Welsh classic, first written in the early eighteenth century. Its full title promises visions of the world, death, and hell. A bard falls asleep and is carried in dream through each realm in turn, seeing the fates of men.

Scholars have traced where Wyn found his plan. The idea of the Vision of the World, this study shows, was clearly taken from an earlier prose vision. The Vision of Death came from another, and the Vision of Hell from the sties of Pluto. The English text lets new readers judge the fierce Welsh satire for themselves.
20749-st-ronan-s-well:
Sir Walter Scott published St. Ronan's Well in the 1820s, and the 1894 text keeps its period praise. Critics quoted here hail its character work and well-told story. Names like Lady Penelope, MacTurk, and Touchwood fill the cast at a spa town.

Scott sets pride, love, and scandal loose in a fashionable watering place. A secret from the past poisons hope for more than one figure. The novel is his only tale set in his own day, which makes it stand apart. Readers see Scott turn his sharp eye from old battles to drawing-room wars instead.
21050-the-master-of-the-shell:
A nasty house-master, trapped, tied, and left all night in a boot box, fronts The Master of the Shell. No boy will own the deed when daylight brings the reckoning, Reed notes. Talbot Baines Reed sets that bold prank near his school tale's heart.

The Shell, a famed form (class) at St. Domingo's, and its master drive the plot. Boys test a new master's worth by prank, sulk, and slow respect. Reed turns school lore into a tale of character on both sides. The Master of the Shell ranks high in his school canon, shrewd about boys and the men who earn their trust.
21376-will-of-the-mill:
In a Derbyshire dale with a Huguenot past, the vicar's son and the silk mill owner's son are fast friends in George Manville Fenn's tale. A visiting artist lodging with a mill worker falls down an old mine shaft, and the boys find him before the rescue party arrives. Then the mill catches fire in the night.

The fire pump has been disabled, and only just repaired in time by the artist's host, a man named Drinkwater, in French Boileau. Drinkwater goes mad with hatred for the mill owner, and suspicion falls on him for the fire. When autumn rains burst the mill dam and flood the village, the question of his guilt drives a dramatic finish.
21480-sunshine-bill:
Bill, son of a Portsmouth wherryman and an apple seller, loses his father in W. H. G. Kingston's Sunshine Bill. The harbour accident leaves a large, cheerful family hard pressed to eat and dress. Captain Trevelyan then offers Bill a boy seaman's place in his ship, the Lilly.

Bill sails knowing four years may pass before he sees home again. His messmate Tommy Rebow is a weaker lad, and the crew are decent folk. Hurricanes, men overboard, fights with the French, sharks, and short rations test them all. Thanks to God marks each escape in this warm, gritty tale.
21667-hollowmell:
E. R. Burden sends a schoolgirl on a mission in Hollowmell, or A Schoolgirl's Mission, printed at Glasgow in 1881. Minnie Kimberley hunts her lost books through cupboards, desks, and under tables. Her books always turn up in the least likely places, as her friends well know.

Minnie's plan grows through preparations and a first essay at doing good. A dispute is settled, Mona suffers defeat, and a success crowns the work. The tale runs short, some nine chapters from plan to end. The Society style of improving fiction shapes it, with Minnie's bright face and quick temper giving it life.
2175-you-never-can-tell:
A London drawing room full of gilt ornaments, glass lustres, and a clock that no longer keeps time sets the stage for George Bernard Shaw at his most playful. You Never Can Tell is a comedy of manners in which a family, a dentist, and a waiter collide over love, respectability, and who gets to judge whom. Shaw fills the room with talk that is sharp, funny, and pointed.

Beneath the jokes runs a serious argument about marriage, class, and the freedom of young people to choose their own lives. Characters say the unexpected, change their minds in public, and expose the rules polite society pretends to live by. The play rewards readers who enjoy wit that bites as well as entertains.
22034-a-narrative-of-some-of-the-lord-s-:
George Müller of Bristol became famous for running orphan houses on faith alone. He never asked any person for money, yet thousands of orphans were fed and housed. His Narrative of Some of the Lord's Dealings, written by himself, tells how it happened. This second part continues the record of his personal life and work.

Müller describes the doubts that tested him when he first published his account. He tells of the Scriptural Knowledge Institution and its schools, Bibles, and missionaries. Day by day entries note sums received, often at the last hour. The book became a classic of its kind, read wherever Christians spoke of answered prayer.
22066-the-long-roll:
Mary Johnston of Virginia published The Long Roll in 1911 as the first of two novels on the war between the States. A wintry day opens the tale: the small town breathes hard with excitement. It might have climbed rapidly from lower land, so heightened are its pulses and so wide its prospect. Old red-brick houses and leafless trees look out between the mountain ranges as Virginia moves toward war.

Johnston follows her Virginians into Stonewall Jackson's campaigns. She had researched the war for years and wrote battle as few novelists could. Romance runs beside the marching in her stately prose. The Long Roll was a bestseller and fixed the Shenandoah war in popular memory.
22128-bessie-costrell:
Mrs. Humphry Ward, the best-selling author of Robert Elsmere, wrote the novella Bessie Costrell in 1895. The scene is Clinton Magna, an English village, at harvest time. An old labourer counts this his last harvest after fifty-six years of work, man and boy. A curious pleasure stirs him at the thought of change, though age has bent him.

Into this village world comes Bessie, and with her the money that tests every bond. Ward watches trust, thrift, and temptation work on simple lives. The tale is short, close, and unsparing. It is often counted among Ward's finest pieces of fiction, a village tragedy told without melodrama.
22148-a-narrative-of-some-of-the-lord-s-:
The third part of George Müller's Narrative of the Lord's Dealings with him carries his famous record forward. Müller, who ran Bristol's orphan houses without ever asking for money, published each part for the same reason. He wanted readers to see that God still answered prayer in ordinary days. This part's preface repeats the reasons given for the second.

Accounts run here to the end of 1840 for the orphan houses. Personal matters continue a little further. Entries list gifts received, needs met, and children housed, almost day by day. Together the parts form one of the most read faith memoirs of the Victorian age, still printed by the Müller charities.
22163-the-rover-boys-on-the-farm-or-last:
Arthur M. Winfield, Edward Stratemeyer's pen name, wrote The Rover Boys on the Farm as a late Putnam Hall story. The subtitle calls it Last Days at Putnam Hall, and the boys know their schooling is ending. Rover adventures here mix school rivalry with farm life. Friends join the brothers for adventures, some comical and some strange and mystifying.

At school the old rivalries burn as keen as ever. On the farm, mysteries and practical jokes take over the plot. The Rovers prove their worth more than once, as the preface promises. The volume closes a long chapter of the series, sending its heroes toward the wider world of the later books.
22171-the-radiant-shell:
Paul Ernst wrote The Radiant Shell, a science fiction tale printed in Astounding Stories in January 1932. Ernst was a German-American engineer who turned to pulp writing. His story opens in a hushed conference room. White-faced men stare at each other across the table, weighing an incredible report: a world in which there is no United States of America.

A man on a metal plate is seen vanishing in the cover picture's scene. Parallel worlds and secret weapons drive Ernst's plot in the early pulp style. The tale mixes politics with dimension-hopping wonder. It survives as a sample of the brash, idea-first fiction that built American science fiction's first generation of fans.
2246-all-s-well-that-ends-well:
Helena, a physician's daughter, cures the King of France and earns the right to choose a husband, picking the reluctant Count Bertram. All's Well That Ends Well follows her pursuit of a man who flees to war rather than wed her, and her bold bed trick to claim the marriage. Shakespeare mixes fairy tale with a hard look at class and desire.

The play's mood is uneasy: Helena wins, but the victory feels strange, and Bertram's repentance comes late. Its prose and verse shift between comedy and near-tragedy. Readers who like Shakespeare's problem plays will find this one provocative and unresolved.
23009-a-modern-idyll:
A practiced voice performs in A Modern Idyll, a story by Frank Harris. It is not probable you will hear many more from me, the speaker says. A shade of sadness enters his lower tone as he ends the phrase. He lets the sad note drift in unconsciously, though long practice has made him an artist in managing his voice.

Harris watches that artistry the way a duelist watches hands. His idyll is modern because its lovers, if lovers they are, act their feelings as much as feel them. Sincerity becomes the story's open question. The prose stays smooth and slightly cold, matching its subject. Readers who enjoy psychological fencing in period dress will find this brief tale neatly made.
23221-the-story-of-the-little-mamsell:
Charlotte Niese's The Story of the Little Mamsell is told through a child's memories of an old storyteller. As a girl, the narrator spent coins from her own slender pocket money to coax the old man into telling his tales. She was not always successful in buying a story.

He had gloomy spells and said almost nothing. On better days, he shared tales from his own past freely, and his life had not lacked variety. Niese frames the little mamsell's story inside that exchange: a child's eagerness set against an old man's silence, memory, and hard-won tales.
23281-the-peacock-at-home-a-sequel-to-th:
Written by a lady and printed in London in the early eighteen hundreds, this verse sequel to The Butterfly's Ball imagines the peacock holding his own party at home. Birds and beasts, stirred by the butterfly's mirth, gather in feathered finery for song and dance.

The poem, in its twenty-seventh edition with notes, charms by its animal society: bees, gnats, and birds each play a part. It belongs to the golden age of children's animal verse, light, musical, and full of good humor. The Butterfly's Ball and the Grasshopper's Feasts stir the spleen of birds and beasts, who answer with a party of their own.
23637-the-bishop-of-cottontown-a-story-o:
John Trotwood Moore published this 1906 novel about life around the cotton mills of the American South. Its four parts follow cotton itself — bloom, boll, gin, lint — and the people whose work and wages depend on each stage. Field hands and mill workers, managers, preachers, and the families caught between them all have a part in the story.

Richard Travis, Jud Carpenter, Hillard Watts, and Alice Westmore move through midnight burials, factory floors, and mutual understandings, as Moore shows a mill town's hopes and hardships without flinching. The book's faith, drawn from the author's own mother, gives it a moral center: the real heroes are the ordinary people who keep the town running.
23652-the-entertaining-history-of-jobson:
Near the sign of the Bell lived Jobson and Nell, and cobbling shoes was his trade — so begins this illustrated verse chapbook published in Philadelphia by Morgan and Yeager. Sold for eighteen cents plain or thirty-one cents colored, it told its comic tale in rhyming stanzas, each paired with a humorous engraving for young readers.

The trouble starts because Jobson loves whiskey, which makes him frisky and careless with his customers' shoes. When the parson sends shoes for Sunday church, Jobson swears he will cobble no more, and poor Nell must coax him back to work. It is a light, old-fashioned cautionary rhyme about drink, duty, and a patient wife.
24168-a-little-miss-nobody-or-with-the-g:
Amy Bell Marlowe wrote this girls' school story, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1914, with pictures. It belongs to her books for girls, beside The Oldest of Four, The Girls of Hillcrest Farm, and Wyn's Camping Days. The frontispiece shows the moment a girl exclaims over the heroine, goodness me, you are a perfect Miss Nobody, on page ninety-eight.

Chapters open with Miss Nobody from Nowhere, then a boy, and the girls of Pinewood Hall, the school where the tale is set. Marlowe writes for young readers about fitting in, friendship, and finding a place. Readers get a cheerful school story of a girl who starts as nobody and earns her standing among friends.
24241-judy-of-york-hill:
Ethel Hume wrote this school story for girls, published by Houghton Mifflin Company in Boston and New York in 1922, with pictures by Harold Cue. It is dedicated in the words of Henry Newbolt's verse on school fellowship. The verse bids readers set the cause above renown, love the game beyond the prize, and treasure the bond joining brave people everywhere.

Chapters follow beginnings, important things, dressing up, a supper party, and enough as good as a feast. Later come putting it through, Christmas and Easter holidays, castles in the air, an anonymous letter, Judith playing detective, friends, the messenger, Judith winning the tennis cup, and prize-giving. Readers get a warm school tale of Judy, who grows from newcomer to winner.
24451-the-blue-wall:
Richard Washburn Child published this novel in New York in 1912, subtitling it a story of strangeness and struggle. Its narrator moves in the orbit of Judge Colfax, whose study and courtroom anchor the early chapters. He becomes entangled with a household shadowed by a mysterious moving figure, and by MacMechem, whose problem gives the first book its title.

Later books introduce a woman of twenty-two, a pledge to the judge, and a torn scrap of evidence. A figure called the Automatic Sheik appears as the mystery deepens into obsession and delusion. Child mixes courtroom drama with psychological suspense. The novel rewards readers who enjoy early twentieth-century tales of troubled minds and hidden pasts.
24465-jack-and-jill-and-old-dame-gill: Published in London on 17 March 1806 by J. Aldis of Moorfields, this tiny chapbook retells the nursery rhyme of Jack and Jill in a longer, joking form. Jack falls down the hill fetching a pail of water and breaks his crown. Jill comes tumbling after. Old Dame Gill plasters his head with vinegar and brown paper, while a dog and a pig dance a jig.
24810-the-better-germany-in-war-time-bei:
Harold Picton published The Better Germany in War Time with the National Labour Press, offering facts toward fellowship between Britons and Germans during the First World War. Picton argues that hate as a policy ruins the hater, and that the belief at home that every German is an incurable barbarian is simply wrong.

The book gathers testimony from chaplains, officers, and prisoners: camp lofts and boxes fitted with bunks, teas shared sixteen to a room, and kindness across the wire. Its epigraphs quote William Morris on fellowship as heaven. The volume stands as a brave wartime plea for seeing the enemy as human, written while the guns still fired.
25390-tabitha-at-ivy-hall:
Ruth Alberta Brown's Tabitha at Ivy Hall, published by Saalfield in 1911 with illustrations by Alfred Russell, follows a girl who hates her name. Tabitha chooses a new name, adopts it, and takes trouble and comfort in turn, in chapters that move from home to boarding school.

A dog and a cat feature early, and a brave little cat arrives half-starved from a mountain trail, black as coal with a crooked tail and cropped ears. Later Tabitha writes her first letter to a father she does not know, survives a fire in the night, and keeps Christmas at Ivy Hall. The book ends in a happy home.
25670-sea-dogs-all:
Tom Bevan, author of Red Dickon the Outlaw and The Fen Robbers, writes this 1911 tale of forest and sea, published by Thomas Nelson in London, Edinburgh, Dublin, and New York. A front picture shows Dolly near the fire, her face rosy with heat.

Contents open with the man in black, the plotters, two friends, and Johnnie Morgan taking a walk. Master Windybank, a sinister meeting, a hunt, darkness and the river, and snaring a flock of night ravens follow. A double fight, Westbury Steeple, a letter from court, and a journey to London close a boys' adventure of plotters and sea dogs.
25691-joyce-morrell-s-harvest-the-annals:
Emily Sarah Holt writes Joyce Morrell's Harvest, annals of Selwick Hall, one of a series about a late sixteenth-century family, between Lettice Eden and It Might Have Been. The book uses Elizabethan English, which may trouble readers unfamiliar with Shakespeare's plays.

One evening, three teenage girls and their aunt Joyce decide to start a shared journal. The idea draws scoffs, since nothing ever happens in their corner of the world, yet exaggerated examples of daily events follow. They get paper, pens, and ink from their father and take turns writing up their days at home.
25788-the-english-utilitarians-volume-2-:
Leslie Stephen writes volume two of The English Utilitarians, on James Mill, published in London by Duckworth in 1900. Contents treat Mill's early life, his role as Bentham's lieutenant, and his leadership of the utilitarians.

Reform movements follow, from political change and law reform to economic and church reform and sinister interests. Political theory, Malthus, Ricardo, economic heretics, and psychology complete the volume. Malthus chapters cover starting point, ratios, moral restraint, social remedies, political application, and rent, in six sections. Stephen traces how Mill and his circle shaped British thought. Stephen's chapters move from Mill's early life to his work as Bentham's lieutenant and then to his leadership of the utilitarians.
25991-frank-of-freedom-hill:
Samuel A. Derieux tells tales of a great red Irish setter in Frank of Freedom Hill, printed by Doubleday in 1922. Dan, sixth of his breed and most superb, springs to his feet at the baggageman's rattle, wavy bronze in color, head erect, eyes eloquent with upward looking appeal. Chapters run from the destiny of Dan to paradise regained, the bolter, old Frank seeing it through, an act of God, Comet, and a crisis.

A trial in Tom Belcher's store, a pursuit, a little boy in a blackberry patch, blood money, and the call of home follow. One scene shows a field trial in confusion. A judge wheels his horse away, Marian Devant rides to the bewildered dog, and a master runs through the crowd with a terrible face. Derieux writes of dogs, men, and loyalty with warmth.
26027-puck-of-pook-s-hill:
Rudyard Kipling tells history through magic in Puck of Pook's Hill, printed by Doubleday in 1906 with pictures by Arthur Rackham. Two children meet Puck, Robin Goodfellow, on Pook's Hill, and he brings folk from England's past to tell their tales. A centurion of the Thirtieth, men of the Great Wall, winged hats, Hal of the Draft, a Dymchurch flit, and treasure and law follow. Songs frame each tale, from Puck's song to a tree song.

A Roman born in Britain tells of Hadrian's Wall, built across North Britain to hold off the painted Picts after a Pict war of twenty years. Theodosius chased the little beasts far north before the tale teller was born. Kipling writes of Roman Britain, Norman manors, and Saxon shores with verve, and Rackham's pictures give the tales a green, haunted light.
26155-two-wonderful-detectives-or-jack-a:
Old Sleuth's 1898 dime novel sends detectives Jack and Gil after a fortune with no known owner. A banker brings them a strange case: a dying man, a trail that points to Monmouth County in New Jersey, and millions waiting for an heir. Chapter headings promise sharp cross-examination, white sand and Jersey mud, an old trunk, a railroad diary, and a sealed letter lost for years.

The pair work from slight clues, old memories, and a portrait to rebuild a life cut short. The chase builds toward a long-lost letter that may settle who the money belongs to. It is a fast, old-style detective yarn, full of surprises and bold claims for its heroes' skill, written for readers who liked their mysteries solved by pluck and logic.
26160-dave-porter-and-his-rivals-or-the-:
Edward Stratemeyer's Dave Porter and His Rivals, copyrighted in 1911, returns to Oak Hall school for a term of sport and scrapes. Contents list an automobile ride, a missing rowboat, a midnight feast, a football meeting, and a great game with Rockville. Later chapters add a runaway motor-boat, a race on skates, and a game of ice hockey.

Dave's chums Phil Lawrence, Roger Morr, and Ben Basswood stand by him, while foes Jasniff and Merwell stir trouble with girls Vera and Mary. A strange request from Hooker Montgomery leads to a discovery and a dash for liberty. The book mixes school loyalty, fair play, and old rivalries, and it closes with another victory for Dave and his friends.
26258-elizabeth-hobart-at-exeter-hall: Jean K. Baird's 1907 book, illustrated by R. G. Vosburgh and issued by the Saalfield Publishing Company, is named for Elizabeth Hobart at Exeter Hall. Baird, already known for Danny, Cash Three, and The Honor Girl, puts her heroine at the centre of a school tale. A frontispiece shows Elizabeth raising her cup to a toast.
26281-happy-thought-hall:
F. C. Burnand's Happy-Thought Hall, issued at Boston in 1872 and illustrated by the author, is a comic tale of a house and the party gathered in it. Early chapters weigh an idea, a plan on paper, cost, designs, staircases, and stables, with friends named Boodles, Jenkyns Soames, and Cazell debating each choice. The search leads to Blackmeer and a rambling old house.

Inside wait a housekeeper, an oriel window, tapestry, armour, mice, rats, and a ghost. A secret door, a white lady, and cruel jokes test the narrator's nerves. Later, a party must be chosen, with grandmothers, aunts, and chaperons proposed, and a Mrs. Boodles deposed for a Madame Regniati. The book offers light, chatty humour throughout.
2643-the-history-of-john-bull:
John Arbuthnot, a physician and wit, wrote the book that fixed John Bull as the name and character of the English people. Henry Morley's introduction notes that Bull appears at times thin and long nosed from trouble, but generally ruddy and plump, with cheeks like a trumpeter.

John Bull is an honest tradesman, simple and straightforward, easily cheated, yet formidable when he takes his affairs into his own hands. Arbuthnot's satire, aimed at the War of the Spanish Succession, made Bull a lasting symbol. The book remains the founding text of England's most famous personification.
26533-rainbow-hill:
Josephine Lawrence published this girls' farm story in 1924 with Cupples and Leon, following the Willis family into a summer away from home. Doctor Hugh plans to add offices to the house, and the noise of ripping and building sends his mother, Rosemary, Sarah, and little Shirley off to Rainbow Hill. Plans, looking forward, and first impressions open the book.

Farm days bring delight, storms, and scrapes, with a nervous Winnie, an adventure for Sarah, and a hired man named Jack. The Gay family, the Gay finances, and the poor farm widen the story beyond one household. A little girl lost, a circus joiner named Bony, and summer's end close a warm tale of sisters, neighbors, and country work.
26537-the-windy-hill:
Cornelia Meigs published this children's novel with Macmillan in 1921, opening on a hot June afternoon in Medford Valley. Oliver Peyton trudges up a dusty road, refusing lifts and hiding his errand, until he reaches the windy hill and its beeman. Cousins, neighbors, and a hateful stranger soon cross his path, and old stories begin to surface.

Chapters move from the beeman and the seven brothers of the sun to a garden wall, a ghost ship, and the portrait of Cicely. Janet's adventure, a fiddler of Apple Tree Lane, a man of straw, and three cousins carry the tale toward Medford River. Meigs weaves present-day children into the valley's past, letting family history explain the grudges and kindnesses of the present.
26665-the-cause-of-it-all:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this short play in two acts, and this hosted text presents the single play from his Plays Complete Edition, whose front matter sits in a companion volume. Its characters are Akulina, a brisk, dignified, old-fashioned woman of seventy. Her son Michael, thirty-five, is passionate, self-satisfied, vain, and strong. Martha, his daughter-in-law, grumbles and speaks much and rapidly.

Act One opens in autumn in a peasant's hut, where Akulina spins, Martha kneads bread, and ten-year-old Parashka rocks a cradle. Martha worries because Michael went to town to sell firewood and may drink half of it, with buffoon Ignat beside him. Taras, the village elder's assistant, quarters a restless tramp on the household in turn, and Akulina gives the stranger bread.
27110-the-eternal-wall:
Raymond Z. Gallun's science-fiction story The Eternal Wall opens with Ned Vince hurrying to Hurley to see Betty, the girl he loves. At Pit Bend, another car leaps into view past Jurassic rock. Ned's car crashes through a white-painted rail, tumbles down a slope, and arcs into the Pit's dark waters fifty feet below.

Death follows, a scream of brakes and a splash into icy, alkaline depths, but Ned Vince lives again a million years later. His mummy, disengaged with small sharp tools, wakes to creatures whose minds hold an incredible science millions of years old.
27126-all-s-well:
John Oxenham's All's Well, published by Doran in 1916, gathers wartime poems for a nation at war. The dedication runs to his son Hugo, second lieutenant of the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders, to all his comrades in arms on land and sea, and to sorely-tried hearts at home.

Part One, All's Well, asks Watchman, what of the night, prays for the men at the front, and sings of the cross still standing. Part Two, The King's High Way, closes with hero-blood that never runs to waste, in verse sure that since God is, right must win.
27225-a-woman-s-will:
Anne Warner's A Woman's Will, published by Little, Brown in 1904 with illustrations by J. H. Caliga, unfolds in three parts: the rise of the storm, the beating of the waves, and the breaking of the barriers. It opens with Jack waving a handkerchief to Rosina from a departing liner's deck.

Later scenes meet on the Maximilianbrücke and in Leipzig, where a professor taught one character all he knows and gave him his music, which is his life. Warner writes a romance of will and feeling, where a woman's resolve meets the storms that test it.
27553-lord-john-russell:
Stuart J. Reid wrote this political biography of Lord John Russell, the ninth volume in his series The Queen's Prime Ministers. The series gives photogravure portraits and copies of autographs, and its frontispiece here reproduces an unpublished picture by G. F. Watts.

Companion volumes treat Beaconsfield, Melbourne, Peel, Gladstone, Salisbury, Palmerston, Derby, and Aberdeen. Russell's volume takes its place among lives of Victoria's chief ministers. Readers get a compact, illustrated account of a leading Whig and Liberal statesman, in a series made for general readers. Reid also wrote The Life and Times of Sydney Smith.
27624-how-to-marry-well:
Mrs. Hungerford, known as The Duchess, published this advice piece in The Ladies' Home Journal of Philadelphia in March 1890. She addresses girls starting in life, and the mothers who hear the words marry well more clearly than their daughters do.

Some girls think snubbing the opposite sex will bring men to their feet, but Hungerford calls such imaginings vain. A man may be amused by coquettish impertinence, yet in the end he hastens to lay his name and fortune at a more modest girl's disposal. She also laments girls' low educational standard: a smattering of French, a word of German, and an idea of music from scales. The piece is period advice, plainly given.
2786-jack-and-jill:
Louisa May Alcott wrote this village story for the schoolmates of Ellsworth Devens, whose lovely character, she says, will not soon be forgotten. The book is affectionately inscribed by their friend, L. M. A., in 1880.

Jack and Jill tumble down a hill in the opening catastrophe, and two penitent invalids learn patience, friendship, and good humor in Ward Number One and Two. Secrets, surprises, and Jill's mission follow. Alcott writes with warmth and moral cheer, and the book remains a beloved children's classic. Alcott's village feels real, from schoolroom to sickroom.
2842-black-heart-and-white-heart-a-zulu-:
H. Rider Haggard gathered three South African tales in Black Heart and White Heart, dedicating the volume to the child Nada Burnham, who died of war hardship at Buluwayo in 1896. The stories center on Philip Hadden, King Cetewayo, a prophet called the Bee, and a doom pool where ghosts are said to gather. Haggard's author's note frames the book as tales of faith tested against violence and death.

The longest interest lies in the clash between Zulu custom, missionary belief, and the ambitions of white adventurers. Prophecy, hunting, and a woman named Nanea carry the plots through fear and loyalty. The collection shows Haggard's late romance style, vivid in setting and direct in its moral contrasts.
28504-the-rival-campers-ashore-or-the-my:
Ruel Perley Smith's The Rival Campers Ashore, Or, The Mystery of the Mill, published by the Page Company of Boston with copyright 1907, sends two boys on an inland voyage. A morning train from Benton drops them at a small station overlooking a pond, beside a weather-beaten house signed Spencer's. Their canoe, trunk, and boxes land on the platform as the adventure starts.

Chapters follow the old mill, a trout pool, a long race, and the conquest of rapids. Henry Burns makes a gift, Colonel Witham gets the mill, and a golden coin is found, lost, and sought again. Granny Thornton's secret and a strange admission close the mystery for young readers.
28654-dave-porter-and-the-runaways-or-la:
Edward Stratemeyer wrote this 1913 boys' adventure about Dave Porter and his school friends in their last days at Oak Hall. A letter brings news of a wild man in the woods behind the school. Soon Dave, Roger, Phil, and Ben are tracking runaways, a cabin on an island, and a blown-up bridge. The schoolmaster Mr. Job Haskers and the bully Nat Poole add trouble of their own.

The plot builds through a bonfire night, a serious accusation, a storm, and a flood before the runaways are found and the wild man is caught. It is a fast, plain tale of schoolboy loyalty and outdoor daring, written for readers who liked a new scrape in every chapter. The book closes Dave's Oak Hall days with a farewell to the school itself.
29225-the-battle-of-bunkers-hill:
Hugh Henry Brackenridge wrote this dramatic piece on the Battle of Bunker Hill, in five acts and heroic measure, by a gentleman of Maryland. Brackenridge lived from 1748 to 1816, and the volume's introduction notes that the battle stirred whatever dramatic activity America had at the Revolution. A play on the subject, it argues, belongs in any representative collection.

The piece stages the battle with generals, soldiers, and speeches, including Lord Pigot among its figures, and adds an ode and a speech. Brackenridge writes in the elevated verse of the age. Readers get a Revolutionary verse drama, formal and patriotic, that shows how early Americans turned a battle into theatre while the war was still fresh.
29254-the-monkey-that-would-not-kill:
Henry Drummond wrote this children's story, published by Dodd, Mead and Company with sixteen full-page illustrations by Louis Wain. The copyright dates to 1897. Its hero is Tricky, a monkey who upsets everything, survives a night outdoors, shakes salt-water off, and begins with the parrot. A shepherd bolts like wildfire, and all is ready for a grim test.

The frontispiece shows Tricky with a stone in his arms, walking calmly toward the shore. Later illustrations show him heaved over a cliff with monkey and stone, yet holding back a baby. A second story, Gum, completes the volume. Readers get a Victorian animal tale, illustrated with Wain's charm, about a monkey who will not be killed and will not quite behave.
29305-sielanka-an-idyll:
Henryk Sienkiewicz wrote this idyll, translated by Vatslaf A. Hlasko and Thomas H. Bullick and published in New York in 1898 by R. F. Fenno and Company, copyrighted in 1897. Sielanka, Polish for an idyll, opens in deep woods, in an open glade where the forester Stephan keeps house. His house is built of logs packed with moss, roofed with straw thatch.

Two outbuildings stand hard by, a fenced piece of ground lies before it, and an old well with a long, bent sweep holds green-edged water. Sunflowers and wild hollyhocks grow opposite the windows, with poppies, sweet peas, morning-glories, nasturtiums, marigolds, primroses, and asters close to the ground. Readers get a lyrical Polish country idyll, gentle and richly flowered, from the Nobel laureate.
29560-m-p-s-in-session-from-mr-punch-s-p:
Harry Furniss drew this 1889 book from Mr. Punch's Parliamentary Portrait Gallery, showing members of Parliament in session. Printed by Bradbury, Agnew and Company, it opens with Mr. Punch as cartoonist in chief, crying that he knows all the old models and wants some new character. Portraits follow, among them Lord Claud Hamilton, late of Liverpool, and sketches of the House of Commons' manner.

Furniss caricatures MPs with a sharp, fond eye, catching pose, dress, and temper in a few lines. The book is both art and political gossip from the late Victorian Commons. Readers of cartoon history and British politics will enjoy a lively gallery of the men who made, and mocked, the laws.
29615-james-boswell:
W. Keith Leask wrote this life of James Boswell in the Famous Scots Series, printed in Edinburgh by Oliphant, Anderson and Ferrier. Its chapters run from early days and meeting Johnson in 1740 to 1763, through the Continent and Corsica, to the Edinburgh bar and the Stratford jubilee. Love affairs, the literary club, and later years follow.

Leask notes Boswell's foible with Scott's contrast: what was a foible in Scott was a passion in Boswell, who thrust his genealogical tree forward on many occasions. The book traces the biographer behind the great Life of Johnson. Readers of Scottish letters will find a compact, classic life of a famous, flawed, and lovable Scot.
3021-a-boy-s-will:
Robert Frost published A Boy's Will as his first book of poems, gathering lyrics of youth, love, and nature. The contents give each poem a gloss, from Into My Own, where the youth forswears the world to be more himself. Ghost House, My November Guest, Love and a Question, A Late Walk, Stars, and Storm Fear follow. The boy courts autumn, winter, and spring in turn. A poem of woodland love has two figures pausing like gnomes hidden from the moon.

Listening in a hush, they hear a brook, a slender tinkling fall making drops like pearls and a silver blade. Frost's New England scenes carry a young man's fears and hopes. The book shows the poet already sure of voice, music, and image.
30255-the-skull:
Philip K. Dick sets a hunter against a stranger he has never seen. The tagline gives the bargain plainly: Conger agreed to kill a stranger, but would make no mistakes because he had the stranger's skull under his arm. Conger faces a council Speaker. The Speaker recalls his illegal trading business, now gone, leaving only six more years in a cell. A situation requiring peculiar abilities awaits him.

Conger was a hunter, skilled at trapping, hiding in bushes, and waiting at night for game, and the Speaker plays on the chase and the stalking as a source of satisfaction. Conger cuts him short, asking who he must kill, and the Speaker answers softly that all comes in proper sequence. A car stops at night on a dark street, a guard presses his arm, and a door opens onto damp sidewalk. Dick turns a prison deal into a grim puzzle.
31038-the-real-hard-sell:
William W. Stuart wrote this science fiction story, published in If: Worlds of Science Fiction in July 1961. Its opening line asks whether human work was naturally more creative, more inspiring, and more important than robot drudgery. It poses the question in both directions: was this the world's most important task, or was it not? The story's hero is Ben Tilman, waiting after hours to see the Old Man.

Tilman sits in the easiest of easy chairs in a lush, plush waiting room, where the motto runs that the customer's ease is the sales manager's please. He picks up a magazine, flips pages, stands, snaps his fingers, walks to the view wall and back, and sits again. He is fidgety about nothing, and irritated at nobody, at the world, and at himself, with no clear reason for it. It is a sly story about selling, robots, and human worth.
31675-the-annals-of-willenhall:
Frederick Wm. Hackwood's local history, published at Wolverhampton in 1908, traces the Staffordshire town of Willenhall from its name and antiquity through Saxon settlement and the Norman Conquest. Early chapters cover the battle of Wednesfield, the founding of Wulfruna's church in 996, and the town's chapel and church life.

Later passages follow disputes over who might nominate a minister, the value of the curacy's land, and the claims of lords, townspeople, and church authorities. Readers get a detailed town chronicle, built from records and local lore, that shows how one English community grew around church, manor, and trade.
31839-john-brown-an-address-at-the-14th-:
Frederick Douglass's address on John Brown, delivered at the fourteenth anniversary of Storer College, Harper's Ferry, West Virginia, on May 30, 1881, was published at Dover, New Hampshire, the same year. Proceeds from its sale were to endow a John Brown professorship at Storer College, an institution mainly devoted to the education of colored youth.

Douglass looks back to Boston two decades before, when a crowd attacked him and fellow speakers and forced them out of Tremont Temple for praising Brown in the same spirit. Now he could stand freely at the very spot of Brown's offense and commend him without reserve as a hero and martyr in the cause of liberty. Readers get a landmark speech on memory, courage, and change.
31847-dog-stories-from-the-spectator-bei:
Dog Stories from the Spectator, with an introduction by J.
