St. Loe Strachey and published in New York by Macmillan in 1895, gathers anecdotes of the intelligence, reasoning power, affection, and sympathy of dogs, selected from the correspondence columns of The Spectator. Strachey says the idea came from Mr. Fisher Unwin, who saw that scattered newspaper stories of dogs would form a readable volume.

Its sections cover syllogistic dogs, the reasoning power of dogs, and emotion and sentiment in dogs. Strachey argues that a single clever-dog story may be dismissed as accident, but six showing the same kind of intelligence carry real weight. Readers get a Victorian collection that treats dogs as thinking, feeling creatures.
31928-a-golfing-idyll:
A Golfing Idyll, or The Skipper's Round with the Deil on the Links of St Andrews, appeared in its third edition of 1897 from St Andrews and Edinburgh. It is a Scots verse tale of golf, drink, and conversion. It opens by asking the skipper what made him mount the ribbon blue and join the Templar crew. Six months gone, he was a drunken devil leading the ball in waste and revel.

Now the skipper sits grim, well washed and well clad, his blue beard shaved, telling how the smell of drink makes him scunner, as meek as an elder before the session. Readers get a comic Scots idyll, illustrated by A. Islay Bannerman, in which a round with the devil on the St Andrews links reforms a hard drinker.
31929-big-pill:
Raymond Z. Gallun's short story Big Pill was printed in Planet Stories in September 1952. It opens beneath Saturn's glow and rings, where five airdomes of a new colony on Titan still stand inflated, enormous bubbles of clear, flexible plastic. The sixth has flattened. Beneath its collapsed roof, a dozen men in spacesuits have lost all hope of rescuing the victims.

Bert Kraskow, an Oklahoman turned space-freighter pilot and now just a colonist, reports nine dead and no survivors into his helmet radio. Readers get a colony story whose title points to its gamble: a child of the now ancient H-bomb, new and untested, that might sweep Titan from space or make a paradise-colony.
32177-a-y-girl-in-france-letters-of-kath:
Katherine Shortall's A Y Girl in France, published in Boston by Richard G. Badger at the Gorham Press, gathers her letters home from France. Shortall writes to her family as the only woman among some fifteen hundred men, apologising when more than a week passes between letters. Those days are full of events, she explains, and in the brief intervals between them she must rest to keep her energy in reserve for whatever came next.

Her letters promise the whole story, told as it happened, from a woman holding her own among soldiers. Readers get a wartime correspondence, warm and direct, from a Y worker in France writing to dearest family. The book's charm lies in its voice: tired, determined, and unwilling to slump, even when events crowd every day.
330-where-there-s-a-will:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's comedy opens after the excitement, with Mr. Sam saying goodbye at a spring-house. Where There's a Will follows a household tangled by a will, a missing owner, and a conspiracy. Miss Patty arrives, a prince appears, and a doctor is fetched.

Chapters promise a warning, a way, a wanted owner, and a mutiny, with indigestion and burglary along the way. Rinehart mixes mystery with domestic farce in her brisk style. The novel's thirty chapters build to a big night and a cupboard full of rye. It shows Rinehart's popular touch.
33120-the-forward-pass-in-football:
Elmer Berry's Forward Pass in Football, published in New York in 1921, is a coach's manual for the play that changed American football. Berry, coach at Springfield's Y.M.C.A. College, dedicates the work to Dr. J. H. McCurdy, the man who earliest developed the forward pass.

Chapters cover the coming of the forward pass, legal restrictions on it, and the spiral pass from center. They also cover the technique of forward passing, fundamentals of a successful passing game, and suggestive formations and plays. Berry writes for coaches and players who wanted to use the new weapon well and within the rules. As sports history, the book captures football at the moment the pass opened the game up, and it still reads as a clear coaching text.
33277-john-dene-of-toronto-a-comedy-of-w:
Herbert Jenkins's comedy follows John Dene of Toronto, a Canadian who comes to Whitehall and sets official London in a stir. Published in 1920, in a fifth printing, its chapters move from Dene's coming and his way of doing things to Department Z, gingering up the Admiralty, and Dene's leaving Whitehall. Jenkins, author of Bindle, writes with the same comic verve, now aimed at wartime bureaucracy.

The tale's fun lies in watching a plain, practical outsider cut through red tape and pomposity, to the dismay of officials and the delight of readers. Its wartime setting, from 1915 to 1919, gives the jokes a real edge. For fans of British comedy, John Dene offers a bright, satirical romp through the corridors of power.
33499-stories-that-end-well:
Octave Thanet's Stories That End Well, copyrighted in 1911, gathers tales. Their closes bring hope, not gloom. Thanet, author of The Man of the Hour and The Lion's Share, offers an adventure in Altruria. Other tales bring a tale of the terrors of the law, the real thing, the old partisan, and Max, or his picture. Later tales bring the stout Miss Hopkins and her bicycle, and a spellbinder, among others.

The collection's charm lies in its humane, Midwestern voice, where good sense and kindness win through trouble. Its stories suit readers who like a tale with a satisfying end, earned by character rather than chance. For fans of Thanet, Stories That End Well offers a warm, well-told set of short fiction from America's heartland.
33660-the-year-when-stardust-fell:
Raymond F. Jones writes a 1958 science fiction novel about a comet whose dust brings disaster to Earth. Twenty chapters trace the fallout. These include a comet, breakdown, power failure, spreading disaster, theft, a scientist's work, dust from the stars, attack, judgment, victory of the dust, sick animals, decontamination, mobilization, battle, and finally reconstruction. The opening essay frames human history as an endless struggle between light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance.

Jones follows ordinary people and scientists as they confront a strange agent that upsets the balance of nature and invites fear, witchcraft accusations, and organized resistance. The novel blends disaster plotting with reflection on how societies respond to the unknown. Fans of classic science fiction will enjoy its clear prose, its escalating crisis, and its hopeful close.
33971-witching-hill:
E. W. Hornung, author of Raffles, wrote this set of linked tales, reprinted in London in 1914. A young estate agent on Witching Hill Road watches a new suburb grow over ground with an older, darker past. Tales of unhallowed ground, a house with red blinds, a locked room, and a temple of Bacchus follow.

Each story turns on a resident, a secret, or a sudden act of violence that the hill seems to draw out. Hornung mixes crime, mystery, and a touch of the uncanny. The book offers a moody portrait of a place where new houses cannot bury old deeds.
34127-morphological-variation-in-a-popul:
Laurence M. Hardy and Charles J. Cole wrote this 1968 study of variation in a population of the snake Tantilla gracilis, in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. The paper, pages 613 to 629 of volume seventeen with six figures, thanks Charles W. Myers of the Gorgas Memorial Laboratory for suggestions on traits examined.

Hardy and Cole measure how one population varies in form, giving field and museum workers a careful baseline. The paper serves snake students who need exact, measured accounts of a small, little-known species. It remains a solid piece of mid-century herpetology.
34538-the-hole-in-the-wall:
The Hole in the Wall is a novel by Arthur Morrison, first published in 1902. Eyre and Spottiswoode issued the London text. The tale is told by Stephen, the publican's grandson. His grandfather kept the Hole in the Wall at Wapping. That inn stood on the river's edge. The contents move between Stephen's tale and scenes in Blue Gate.

The narrator calls his grandfather a publican and a sinner. His sins are the record of the book, he says. The old man owned a small wharf on the Lea as well. His name, Nathaniel Kemp, was also the father's name. Morrison made his name on tales of London's East End. Jago's world of docks and thieves is his ground. This novel joins crime to a family chronicle. The river trade and its rough men fill its pages.
34689-the-wishing-well:
Mildred A Wirt wrote The Wishing Well, a Penny Parker mystery issued in nineteen forty-two. Penny Parker is a high school girl who solves cases in Riverview. Wirt wrote many tales for girls, both mysteries and trailer stories.

Penny sits at her desk, books stacked, waiting for the closing bell to free her. Chapters lead her to an old house, a covered well, and a record cut on rock. Strangers come from Texas, lights move at night, and prowlers stir. A silken ladder, lost pearls, and a grand ball follow. Penny's find beneath the flagstones drives the case to its close.
34690-dorothy-payne-quakeress-a-side-lig:
Dorothy Payne, Quakeress is a biography by Ella Kent Barnard, issued in 1909. Its subtitle calls it a side-light on the career of Dolly Madison. A portrait of Dorothy Payne Todd fronts the book. Four chapters carry her life in order. Early years and scenes open the tale. Marriage and widowhood follow. Washington and the White House form the third part.

The illustrations show the ground of her youth. A Friends' meeting house in North Carolina appears. Portraits of Patrick Henry and Colonel Byrd follow. Scotch Town and Hanover Court House mark her Virginia days. Harewood, where she wed James Madison, is shown. Barnard writes from the Quaker side of her subject. Dolly's plain upbringing shaped her later grace, the book argues. The life runs from meeting house to presidential rooms.
34778-nooks-and-corners-of-cornwall:
Nooks and Corners of Cornwall is a walker's guide by Dawson Scott. Eveleigh Nash published it in London with a map. The book belongs to a series of like county guides. A companion volume on Devon was in preparation. The price was half a crown net.

A section of warnings opens the guide. Cornwall, Scott quotes Borrow, can only be seen by walking. Big names on the map may shrink to a few cottages. Inns are fewer than travellers expect. The cheerful Cornish are mostly Nonconformist and Sabbatarian. Bathing on the north and west coasts is unsafe. Big Atlantic rollers come in without warning. Cliff paths hide dangerous blow-holes. A chapter then treats the crosses and churches.
34793-address-to-the-first-graduating-cl:
Address to the First Graduating Class of Rutgers Female College is a printed speech by Pierce, delivered at New York on Sunday evening, June 2, 1867. Henry Pierce was president of the college, and he spoke in the Fourth Avenue Presbyterian Church. The trustees asked for its publication. The Agathynian Press printed it the same year.

Pierce first traces the school's growth. The Rutgers Female Institute was founded in 1839, after long consultation, from a growing sense of women's duties. A quarter century had changed the education of women greatly. Now the institute stood as a college. Pierce then states his views on woman's true position, claiming for her an equal place beside man.
35607-the-spell:
The Spell is a novel by William Dana Orcutt, held under a 1909 copyright and printed by Harper and Brothers in New York and London. Gertrude Demain Hammond drew the plates. Orcutt gives the book to his friend Guido Biagi of Florence.

A front plate carries the line that there may be some difference in men, but all husbands are alike. A second plate tells that slowly the spell began to work on Inez brain. She was no longer in the present, but a woman of Italy four centuries back. A third plate has a contessa say that beautiful paintings do not possess husbands. The tale thus joins a modern marriage to an old Italian echo. Romance fans get love, jealousy, and a past that will not stay past.
35958-a-review-of-edwards-s-inquiry-into:
A Review of Edwards's Inquiry into the Freedom of the Will, by Henry Philip Tappan, was published in New York in 1839. Jonathan Edwards had argued that the will is always moved by the strongest motive, a doctrine Tappan feared had done real harm. The review states Edwards's system, draws out its consequences, and then examines his arguments against a self-determining will.

Tappan writes as both philosopher and believer, claiming full liberty of thought while expecting inquiry to confirm moral duty. He insists that knowledge of the will matters because duty and religion rest on it. The book is a clear American answer to Edwards, and it helped shape the long debate over freedom, necessity, and responsibility in American theology.
3616-the-o-conors-of-castle-conor-county:
Anthony Trollope writes a short story about his first taste of Irish country life, drawn from his Tales from All Countries. The narrator, Archibald Green, never forgets his first day's hunting in Ireland or the evening that followed, and he remains grateful for the hospitality of the O'Conors of Castle Conor. A polite note at an inn first offers him a bed at the castle.

Trollope describes Irish gentry hospitality, hunting, and evening talk with the warmth of a guest who was won over. The story gives a friendly, if romantic, view of County Mayo society in the nineteenth century. It suits readers who enjoy Trollope in short form and a tale where kindness, not plot, carries the day.
36686-the-vicar-of-wrexhill:
The Vicar of Wrexhill is a novel by Frances Trollope in one volume. Bentley of London put out this new revised edition in 1840. The book stands as number seventy-eight in the Standard Novels line. Trollope had writ Domestic Manners of the Americans before this tale. Lines from Molière on the title page warn against false devotion.

True devotees are not those who make the most grimaces, Molière says. Hypocrisy and devotion should never share one name or one honour. A frozen blandishment smooths the proud vicar's face in one picture. He receives sycophants with his lady beside him in that scene. Oak-sheltered Wrexhill shows few spots in England of greater beauty. The narrator owns the spot has been sketched too often to linger. The vicar's rule over that fair parish makes the tale's dark heart.
3700-the-courtship-of-susan-bell:
Anthony Trollope writes a short novel about the courtship of Susan Bell, daughter of a widowed mother at Saratoga Springs. Susan's father, John Munroe Bell, had been a lawyer in Albany who thrived well until his early death left his widow with young daughters. For ten years the Bells lived in a cottage at the Springs, taking boarders in summer, old ladies and the occasional old gentleman whose pockets suited the widow's moderate charges.

Into this quiet life comes a suitor, and Susan must choose between love, duty to her mother, and the world's judgment. Trollope writes with gentle humor about American manners and family feeling. The story suits readers who enjoy Trollope in brief form, with a heroine whose heart and conscience pull both ways.
37245-the-piskey-purse-legends-and-tales:
Enys Tregarthen wrote The Piskey-Purse, a book of tales and old lore from North Cornwall. J Ley Pethybridge drew the plates for the London book. A first plate shows an ugly small sprite who flees, chased by three wee hares. The Cornish word piskey names the small folk of the moors.

Five long tales make up the book, each with its own world of spells. A magic pail, a witch in a well, and lent eyes and ears follow the first. A small white hare closes the set of tales. Plates show shoes that bear a girl past a dread bog, and a great stone on the moor. A tin mine, a lane of shrubs, and the glow of a set sun ground the tales in place. Young readers get old Cornish lore in tale form.
37269-the-triumph-of-jill:
The Triumph of Jill, a novel by Mills Young, was published in London by John Long in an edition dated 1903. Chapter one opens in a poorly furnished studio. An artist gazes at a half-finished canvas on an easel, then at the small girl beside him. She has posed for him since infancy, and has always proved a poor model by his lights.

Art, he tells her, is the only thing worth living for, and the worst trade for bread. With bread in plenty it adds butter, even preserves. He is sorry he chose it, for her sake, and calls his life's work a grind and a failure. The girl slips her hand into his and begs him not to talk so. Young sets a tale of a painter's daughter inside the art world's hard economics.
37358-determinism-or-free-will:
Determinism or Free-Will?, in a revised and enlarged edition of 1919, is Chapman Cohen's short book on the oldest puzzle in philosophy. The Pioneer Press of London printed it for common readers. Cohen says a wide public wants philosophy without the jargon of the schools. A trade publisher once offered to print the work if he would pad it out for a higher price.

He refused, holding that hard subjects get clearer when squeezed, not swollen. Chapters state the question, then unpack the words freedom and will. Consciousness, deliberation and choice come next. Cohen answers the fears said to follow from determinism, takes on Professor James and his dilemma, and ends with character and environment.
37610-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume is slice eight of volume eleven of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, running from Germany to Gibson. The text opens with the transcribers' notes on marks, roots and Greek letters. A long list corrects misprints found in articles such as Germany, Gettysburg, Ghazni and Ghost.

The articles then run in strict letter order through scores of short entries. Place entries cover Germersheim, Gerona, Ghent and Ghazipur. Life entries cover the painter Gérôme, Elbridge Gerry and Lorenzo Ghiberti. Longer pieces treat Germany itself, the ghetto and the gerrymander. The slice shows the great reference work at full stretch, mixing towns, artists, peoples and ideas.
37748-how-to-collect-a-doctor-bill:
How to Collect a Doctor Bill is a business manual for physicians by Frank Davis, secretary of the Oklahoma State Board of Medical Examiners in the years before the war. The Physicians Drug News Company of Newark published it in 1913. Davis had also run a state institution and edited a medical magazine.

Eight chapters teach the money side of practice. The first defines the successful physician, and the second fixes his attitude toward debtors. Then come the proper time to collect, books and bookkeeping, letters and forms, statutes of limitations, and exemption laws and their application. The last chapter prints extracts from the exemption laws of all the states. The keynote, Davis insists, is system: to conduct any enterprise successfully, business methods must be adopted, and the simplest system is the best. A cash system, he argues, is by far the simplest of all.
38430-the-philosophy-of-mr-b-rtr-nd-r-ss:
Philip Jourdain edited this playful volume on the philosophy of Bertrand Russell, whose name the title page stars out. George Allen and Unwin of London and the Open Court Publishing Company of Chicago first published it in 1918. An appendix adds leading passages from certain other works, and a list of abbreviations keys the many books quoted, from Alice's Adventures in Wonderland to works on the algebra of logic.

Forty-three short chapters treat the indefinables of logic, identity, the law of contradiction, symbolism and meaning, and denoting. Russell's logic is set out with a straight face and a comic effect. Chapters treat the mortality of Socrates, the mathematical attainments of Tristram Shandy, and the hardships of a man with an unlimited income. Later chapters take up the paradoxes of logic, the hierarchy of jokes, and laughter itself.
38614-cornwall:
Cornwall is a roam book with paint plates by Nicholls and words by Mitton. A Black house of London brought it out in nineteen fifteen. Twenty full page plates in hue show the duchy in this print. Land End stands as front plate of the set in its list. Part one treats the stock views folk hold of Cornwall at start.

Far as you can go is a Brit pull, that part holds at its head. Gate of the duchy, the toe of Cornwall, and far west and south fill ranks. King Arthur land and north shore sand strands stand mid part scheme. South shore creeks, Cornish towns, and Cornish ways close the scheme. Plate themes run from Carbis Bay and Kynance Cove to Truro town. St Ives lanes and Fowey port stand in that hue plate list too.
38621-doctrine-of-the-will:
Doctrine of the Will is a work of philosophy by Asa Mahan, president of the Oberlin Collegiate Institute, published at New York in 1845. Mahan asks whether the human will is free or bound by necessity. The book opens with rules for the inquiry itself, then sorts the faculties of the mind before reaching its main fight.

Mahan defines liberty and necessity, and argues that liberty, not necessity, is the true mark of the will. He answers the objections of the necessity school and appeals to consciousness as proof. A final line of argument rests on the fact that all minds hold the idea of liberty. The book is a clear statement of the free will side in an old debate.
38676-adenoids-and-diseased-tonsils-thei:
Margaret Cobb Rogers wrote this study of the throat and the mind, printed at New York in April 1922. It is the fiftieth book in a set of the files of the study of the mind, from Columbia. The theme is set in its full head: growths in the nose and sick glands in the throat, and their force on the wit of the child in the main. The list of parts shows the plan of the work.

The first part looks at the past books on the tie of faults of the nose and throat to wit. The next part sets out the way of the probe: a count by sums, and a probe of the gain past cure. The tests and the choice of cases are told there.
38771-the-little-princess-of-tower-hill:
The Little Princess of Tower Hill is a tale for the young by Meade, put out at New York with six full page plates. Her past tales for girls are named on the title leaf. The host print holds three more short tales in its back parts. Their names are kept in a note at the front of the host text. The list of parts for the main tale runs to three teen.

All the young folk who knew her thought Maggie a most blest small girl. She was at times spoke of by the name of the book. For Tower Hill was the name of her sire's place, and Maggie was his sole child. The young folk of the town close by spoke of her with great awe.
39582-the-rival-pitchers-a-story-of-coll:
The Rival Pitchers is a boys' novel of college baseball by Lester Chadwick, published in New York by Cupples and Leon in 1910. It belongs to the College Sports series, beside a football story, A Quarter-Back's Pluck. A frontispiece shows Phil winning the game amid a riot of cheers.

Tom, the hero, carries the tale. Chapters open with the old bell clapper and a good throw. A baseball meeting, a hazing, and a scrub game set the college scene. The pole rush and practice follow, then a game with Boxer Hall. A coil of wire and an electric shock bring the mystery in. Tom holds his own, does not tell, and works on his curves. A girl and a game, a sophomore trick, and a discovery fill the middle chapters. Chadwick's series gave schoolboy readers the whole ritual of college sport, rivalry and all.
39935-twelve-good-musicians-from-john-bu:
Twelve Good Musicians from John Bull to Henry Purcell is a music history book by Sir Frederick Bridge, printed in London in 1920. Bridge was organist of Westminster Abbey and held chairs at London and Gresham. The book grew out of a university course he gave in the session of 1919 to 1920.

His opening quotes Sir Hubert Parry's hard claim that the seventeenth century is, in music, almost a blank. Bridge thinks that verdict a little severe on England. His course, and this book, set out to give a useful view of what English musicians did in that century. Twelve lives carry the story, from Dr John Bull at one end to Henry Purcell at the other. A front plate shows Bull from the painting in Oxford's Music School.
40566-moth-and-rust-together-with-geoffr:
Moth and Rust is a novel with two shorter tales by Mary Cholmondeley. John Murray published the volume in London in 1902. Cholmondeley also wrote Red Pottage and Diana Tempest. A Rossetti line on rust in gold fronts the title page. The contents give page places to the three pieces. Moth and Rust fills the bulk of the book. Geoffrey's Wife and The Pitfall follow as shorter tales. A dedication to Essex says birth and place did not make the friendship.

The novel opens in a little church during a sermon. The vicar gives out the text on treasures upon earth. Moth and rust corrupt such treasures, the text warns. The congregation settles peacefully to listen to the exposition. Only the quality in the carved pew have much treasure, it notes. The poor keep a pig laid up for Christmas rent. Sermon and parish frame Cholmondeley's tale of wealth.
40668-a-quarter-back-s-pluck-a-story-of-:
A Quarter Back’s Pluck, a story of college football by Lester Chadwick, was copyrighted in 1910. Cupples and Leon of New York published it in the College Sports Series. The Rival Pitchers, a baseball tale, stands as its companion volume. Smash and hammer, hammer and smash, cries a plate caption in the front.

Moving Day is the title of the first chapter of the contents. Langridge Has a Tumble and Phil Gets Bad News follow in the list. Football practice, a clash, and a professor’s objection fill the next chapters. The first line up and a plot by Langridge and Gerhart raise the stakes. Chadwick wrote the series for boys who lived for the autumn game. Pluck at quarter back is the moral as much as the title.
41206-batting-to-win-a-story-of-college-:
Lester Chadwick wrote Batting to Win, a tale of college baseball issued in New York in 1911. A front plate shows a batter slamming a three base hit. Chadwick had built a College Sports Series round Randall College, with tales of rival pitchers and of football pluck.

Thirty four parts open in a dusty college room with Sid Henderson, Tom Parsons, and a strange message. Sid is caught, then charged, then spiked in a game, and he keeps silent under a grave charge. Games against Boxer and Fairview, a petition, and hard times with cash fill the middle. A perilous crossing and a title game end the run, with Tom's last appeal and the ban lifted.
41512-the-young-continentals-at-bunker-h:
The Young Continentals at Bunker Hill is a Revolutionary War tale for boys by John McIntyre, printed at Philadelphia in 1910. McIntyre also wrote of the same heroes at Lexington and at Trenton. Ralph Boyer drew the pictures. Eighteen chapters follow young Ezra Prentiss.

Ezra hears of a stranger, meets Gilbert Scarlett, a soldier of fortune, and slips into Boston. He rides with Prescott toward Bunker Hill and stands in the battle itself. Then he carries the news and meets General Washington on the road. The tale ends with Ticonderoga's guns starting their famous journey. McIntyre mixes invented boys with real men and real fights.
41783-king-arthur-in-cornwall:
King Arthur in Cornwall, by Howship Dickinson, a fellow of Caius College, Cambridge, was issued by Longmans in 1900. The contents open with an introductory chapter on the subject. Traditions and history bearing on the life of Arthur follow. Arthur’s last battle and the doubts on his burial place take the third chapter.

Dickinson weighs the Cornish claims on the Arthur legend in this study. Tintagel, Slaughter Bridge, and Glastonbury all press their rival tales. A doctor of medicine turned antiquary sifts fact from romance here. His method is to test each tradition against the records. Cornwall keeps Arthur as her own king above all other shires. The book is a careful walk through that beloved maze. Local pride and hard evidence meet on every page.
41787-reports-of-the-committee-on-the-co:
A congressional report on the Fort Pillow massacre, printed in May 1864. The Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War produced it. Congress had ordered the inquiry by joint resolution in April. Rumoured slaughter of Union troops after surrender demanded facts. The Senate ordered twenty thousand extra copies printed. Senators Wade and Gooch formed the investigating subcommittee.

The two men left Washington at once with a stenographer. Cairo and Mound City, Illinois, were their first stops. Survivors and witnesses gave testimony there. The report asks a second question as well. Could Fort Pillow have been reinforced or evacuated in time? The Tennessee garrison included many Black soldiers. Their fate after the fort fell made the report a searing Union document.
4224-mr-hogarth-s-will:
Catherine Helen Spence set this novel in the south of Scotland, where the sudden death of Mr. Hogarth of Cross Hall gathers his household for the reading of his will. His two orphan nieces, whom he raised as daughters, learn how tightly his odd rules and bequests bind their futures.

Much of the story turns on those conditions: the nieces must live under terms that test their judgment, their suitors, and their sense of duty. Spence uses the will as a device to examine how women of their rank were educated, limited, and expected to behave, and what happened when they pushed against those limits.
42437-aunt-jimmy-s-will:
Mabel Osgood Wright wrote a novel printed in New York in 1903, with pictures by Florence Scovell Shinn. Wright was known for Birdcraft. A line from Alcott fronts the book, to aim at the highest and never mind the money. Wright gives the book to her godchild Mary Elizabeth Miller. A lawyer clearing his throat fronts the tale.

Red Pineys, Uncle John, and Aunt Jimmy enter in early chapters. A caged bird, cousins, and a summer in New York follow. A pewter tea pot, telltale trousers, and a fire escape mark the climb to freedom. The bird is freed in the last chapter head, a promise of the will's true gift to a young life held too tight.
42462-barbara-rebell:
Mrs Belloc-Lowndes wrote this novel of Barbara Rebell and her godmother. Dodge printed the authorized edition in New York in 1907. Gilbert White drew the frontispiece of Barbara for the book. A prologue opens on her tenth birthday, June 9, 1870.

That day brought her first meeting with her godmother at last. The lady name had stood in her nightly prayers since childhood. It also brought the greatest of her childish disappointments then. St Germains, her French home, stayed home to her for years after. War in July and August 1870 would soon mar that ordered French town beauty.
42817-lord-randolph-churchill:
Lord Randolph Churchill is the biography of the Victorian statesman by his son Winston Churchill, published by Macmillan in 1906 in two volumes. The younger Churchill, already a member of Parliament and an author of war books, dedicates the life to the Duke of Marlborough. This first volume opens with the deed of trust that governed his father's papers.

Lord Randolph had signed the deed in 1893, two years before his death. It gave his political and state papers, kept in tin boxes at his bank and at Grosvenor Square, to Viscount Curzon and Ernest Beckett, to use at their absolute discretion. Papers touching the India Office or the Foreign Office needed a secretary of state's written consent before use. The deed, printed whole, is both a source note and a son's credential: the biography that follows rests on an archive its subject himself arranged.
43197-the-golden-boys-and-their-new-elec:
Wyman, dean of Pennsylvania Military College, wrote The Golden Boys and Their New Electric Cell, published by Burt in New York in 1922. The Golden Boys series, for boys of twelve to sixteen, had sent its heroes to a fortress, the Maine woods, the lumber jacks, and the river drive. This volume turns to invention. In a basement workshop in Skowhegan, Maine, Jack and Bob Golden finish a new electric cell.

Jack is unsure the thing will work. The theory is right, he says, but practice is a cat of another colour. Everything rides on the test: the Jenkins boys have a new boat that will run circles round the Sprite unless the cell succeeds. A picture shows the Sprite creeping up foot by foot until the two boats race side by side.
43796-tom-fairfield-s-schooldays-or-the-:
Allen Chapman starts a school series with Tom Fairfield's first term at Elmwood Hall. Cupples and Leon issued it at New York in 1913. The frontispiece shows a bull rushing a crowd of students.

The contents promise school sport and school trouble in equal shares. Tom hears strange news, then finds a drifting boat. He makes an enemy and finds a chum in the first six chapters. The call of the pigskin leads to Tom's touchdown. A coward's trick and a class warning follow. A runaway iceboat and a skating race vary the fun. Chapman wrote shelves of such series under this and other names. His school tales taught fair play, pluck, and loyalty to the house.
44041-the-mystery-of-arnold-hall:
Helen Persons wrote The Mystery of Arnold Hall for the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron and New York, copyrighted in nineteen thirty-four. She had earlier written Finding the Lost Treasure. A caption under the front matter sets the tone: Rhoda helps the others scramble up rough stones slippery with moss. The contents promise a school story with trouble in it, from Pat's Chance and Anne through the Alley Gang, a meddler, and a fall.

The first chapter opens on a cool late August evening. Patricia's mother calls from the living room, where she is starting a fire, as the doorbell rings hard. Patricia hurries from putting away the supper dishes, a tall girl with short wavy yellow hair, big brown eyes, and a green jersey dress. Later chapters bring a fire, an arrest, a robbery, a weird experience, and the solutions.
44411-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-0:
Grenville Kleiser put in order The World Great Sermons, a set of ten books put out in New York and London. Book four held rights from 1908 and runs from L Beecher to Bushnell. 

Lyman Beecher leads with a talk on the rule of God as a thing to be wished. Channing gives a talk on the traits of Christ, and Chalmers one on the push of a new love. Campbell speaks for the cause of men sent to preach abroad. Irving, Arnold, and Wayland add talks on prayer, on life in God, and on a day in the life of Jesus. Newman and Bushnell close the book, on the will of God and on the sway we shed in sleep of mind. A life note tells of Beecher and his famed talks on strong drink.
44557-an-unsentimental-journey-through-c:
Unsentimental Journey is a Cornwall travel book by the author of John Halifax. Macmillan of London issued the pictured account in eighteen eighty four. Napier Hemy drew the views, from Saint Michael Mount to Cornish coves. Contents divide the trip into sixteen days of travel across Cornwall.

Views list Falmouth from Flushing, Saint Mawes Castle, and a fisherman cellar. The Lizard lights by night, Cornish fish, and Poltesco follow in the plates. Cadgwith Cove, the Devil Frying Pan, and Mullion Cove show the coast. Crabbers, seine boats, and hauling lines show the fishing life there. Readers tour the Cornish shore day by day with a plain eyed guide.
45010-oliver-cromwell:
Oliver Cromwell is a biography by Samuel Rawson Gardiner, the great historian of the Stuart age. Gardiner's works fill the front pages: a ten volume history of England to the outbreak of the Civil War, four volumes on the war itself, and four on the Commonwealth and Protectorate. This life stands in crown octavo with a frontispiece, offered at five shillings net.

Gardiner also wrote Cromwell's Place in History, from six lectures given at Oxford, and school histories that taught a generation. His life of Cromwell distils the store of those vast works into one volume for the general reader. It treats the soldier and statesman who rose from the fens to rule England, by the hand that knew the records best.
45316-footprints-of-former-men-in-far-co:
R S Hawker, vicar of Morwenstow, gathers the legends and worthies of old Cornwall in sketches edited by C E Byles. John Lane issued the book at London and New York in 1903. J Ley Pethybridge drew the pictures.

Byles warns the reader with a smile. Hawker never let facts, or the lack of them, block his imagination. He had a Chatterton-like habit of passing off his own work as old manuscripts. His poem The Quest of the Sangraal survives as a fragment. Byles ranks it beside Hyperion. Hawker re-read Scott's novels each year at Christmas. In his small local field he did for Cornwall what Scott did for Scotland. The sketches mix true lives, tall tales, and pure romance along a wild coast.
45480-the-liberty-bell:
The Liberty Bell is a patriotic poem by William Ross Wallace, illustrated from drawings by John Hows. James Gregory published it in New York in 1862, in the second year of the Civil War. The poem opens with a sound like a tempest rolling through the land. The bell of freedom, it says, tolled at midnight and was heard through a fettered land.

A note ties the ringing to the announcement of the Declaration of Independence on July the Fourth, 1776. Later verses carry the chime over mountain and wave to cottage and hall. The old sabre is sharpened and the pioneer's blade drawn in answer. Wallace wrote the poem to stir Union hearts with the memory of 1776.
45703-water-supply-the-present-practice-:
Ernest Spon wrote a manual on the present practice of sinking and boring wells, published in London and New York in 1875. Spon belonged to societies of engineers and geologists. His preface notes that people now gather in large communities. Such towns need water gathered in one place for household, social, and industrial use.

Chapters begin with geological considerations, then the new red sandstone. Well sinking and well boring each get a chapter. The American tube well and boring at great depths follow. A long chapter gives examples of wells actually made and districts supplied by them. Tables and an index close a practical engineering handbook.
45869-the-story-of-doctor-johnson-being-:
The Story of Doctor Johnson is an introduction to Boswell's Life of Johnson by Roberts, a scholar of Pembroke College, Cambridge. The Cambridge University Press printed it in 1919. A second edition followed within months, in June of the same year. A portrait of Samuel Johnson fronts the book.

Roberts used the second edition to correct mistakes pointed out by friendly critics. He also added brief notes on Johnson's birthplace and on the Gough Square house, with a new photograph of the latter. The contents open with Johnson's world, then the boy at school, then Oxford. The book is a short, clear road into Boswell's great biography, written for readers who want the man before the monument. Its quick second edition shows how welcome it was.
45927-seets-i-paris-sammywell-grimes-s-t:
Seets i' Paris is a dialect travel tale by John Hartley, printed at London and Wakefield. Its full title tells of Sammywell Grimes's trip with his old chum Billy Baccus, his opinion of the French, and the French opinion of the exhibition he made of himself. Hartley also wrote Seets i' Lundun and Grimes's Trip to America.

In his preface Sammywell answers readers who may be disappointed to find no sights but what they knew before. They did not make a new Paris on purpose for him to visit, he says. To those who doubt the truth of his descriptions, he begs them to remember that we do not all see with the same eyes. If half the book is fact, that is worth sixpence, and if the other half is fancy, that is worth sixpence too. The tale is told in broad Yorkshire dialect.
46937-a-book-of-cornwall:
A Book of Cornwall is a land book by Baring-Gould, first out in eighteen ninety-nine and in a fresh form past seven years. Past thirty plates fill it. Baring-Gould was known for a shelf of like books on the west and south lands. Parts run from the saints of that shore to its tin mines and its towns.

Heads treat the holy wells and the stone marks of the land, its strong holds, and the trade of tin. Town parts take in the chief town of the north, a port town, and a town past a great stream. The cape of the end of land and the isles past it close the list. A part on the sly trade of the shore stands in the rows.
47378-mrs-darrell:
Foxcroft Davis wrote Mrs Darrell, a novel issued by the Macmillan Company in nineteen hundred five. William Sherman Potts drew the pictures. The book runs to eighteen chapters. Davis had earlier written a book on rule by one man and rule by the crowd.

The tale opens with a look back at old Washington. Once the town was a plain court of state, run by top officials and envoys. Few grand houses stood there then. Girls wore muslin to balls and rode trams with party bags. Two young British officers watch the big Charity Ball of the season. One is Captain Reginald Darrell, whose wife gives the book its name.
474-how-to-tell-stories-to-children-and-:
Sara Cone Bryant teaches the art of oral storytelling in this guide, first shaped for teachers and parents. She explains why telling beats reading aloud, how to pick tales children love, and how to cut, fill out, and shape a story for the ear. Voice, mood, and the seating of listeners all get practical advice.

Chapters use familiar tales such as The Three Bears and The Three Little Pigs as worked examples. Stories to tell follow the method chapters, ready for use. The book remains a handy manual for anyone who wants to hold a room of children with voice alone.
47474-huts-in-hell:
Huts in Hell, by Daniel Poling, was published in Boston in 1918, while the First World War still raged. Poling traveled with the American forces in France as a Christian Endeavor worker, and the title points to the welfare huts that served soldiers near the front. Chapters cover the voyage through the submarine danger zone, war capitals, Pershing, Seicheprey, and a dugout diary.

Poling writes of gas attacks, the first Croix de Guerre, and boys at the front, mixing reportage with appeals to readers at home. Photographs show troops marching through London and camps in France. The book belongs to the home-front literature of the war, honoring both the fighters and, in its dedication, the men and women of the Red Triangle who helped them fight.
47562-the-putnam-hall-encampment-or-the-:
The Putnam Hall Encampment, or the secret of the old mill, is a boys' school story by Arthur Winfield, copyrighted in 1910. Winfield had written three Putnam Hall books before, and the Rover Boys series besides. A front picture shows a fire that seemed to be everywhere. The contents open in a belfry, with a cadet named Jack in peril soon after.

A bully's confession, a bully punished, and a crabbed teacher making a find fill the early chapters. Word of weight arrives, the girls have something to tell, and the school marches off for its encampment. Wagons are trailed, a cave found in the woods, and the camp pitched by a lake. A swim, a game of baseball, and danger of fire follow in the open air chapters.
47837-the-mysteryes-of-nature-and-art-co:
John Bate, writing as I B, published a book of secrets of nature and art at London in 1634, in four treatises. The first treats water works, the second fire works. The third covers drawing, coloring, painting, and engraving. The fourth gives diverse experiments, both serviceable and delightful. Bate tells the reader the work lay by him long in a confused heap.

Friends pressed him to share what he had gathered, practiced, or found out by industry. He promises no elegance of phrase, only plain terms for the meanest capacity. The mixed experiments of part four he entitles Extravagants. The book is an early English manual of practical wonders and stage effects.
48273-lincoln-day-entertainments-recitat:
Sidelar put in one book all a school needs for a Lincoln Day show. The book came out in Chicago in 1908. It holds verse to speak, plays, talks twixt two, and drills. Tableaux, dumb shows, quotes, and songs crowd its pages. A plate shows the famed Lincoln statue in Lincoln Park, Chicago.

Benton, Bryant, Best, and Cary give verse on Lincoln's life. Facts, tales, and praise bits fill the back of the book. Each piece is short and set for a school stage. Teachers can build a whole day's show from one shelf book. Young folk learn the great man's life by heart and act.
48729-the-strand-magazine-vol-17-no-97-j:
Volume seventeen of The Strand Magazine covers January to June 1899. George Newnes edited and published the illustrated monthly in London. Number 97, the January issue, opens with a Conan Doyle story. Round the Fire is the frame; its eighth tale tells of a japanned box. A private tutor narrates how he lost his best situation. He went to Thorpe Place, in the Avon country of the Midlands.

The tutor taught two small boys of a widower, Sir John. A governess cared for the little girl of seven. That governess later became the tutor's wife, the tale confesses. Shakespeare's own country frames the scene: stone walls and lichened roofs. The most English part of England, the narrator calls it. Fiction of this polished kind was the Strand's staple fare.
48997-back-from-hell:
Back From Hell, by Samuel Cranston Benson, was published in Chicago in 1918. A front note calls Benson a man who went to war as a pacifist but came back a fighting American. Forty-two chapters trace his path from doubt to front-line work in France and Belgium during the First World War.

Early chapters cover red tape, enlistment, mud on the northwest front, gas, and the Red Cross. Later ones tell of Verdun, barrage fire, the heroism of the wounded, and Benson's capture and trial as a spy. He writes of ruin in Louvain, a night in no man's land, and his escape back to France. The tone is frank, patriotic, and often grim.
49352-the-pictorial-field-book-of-the-re:
Benson J Lossing wrote The Pictorial Field Book of the Revolution, Volume Two, issued by Harper and Brothers in 1852. Several hundred engravings on wood by Lossing and Barritt aid the text. Most are from original sketches by the author. A note warns that the first eight chapters of this volume repeat the last eight of Volume One and are not duplicated here.

Chapter Nine opens with verses on a desolate and dying year. Lossing left New York on November 22, 1848, to visit the Southern states. Those states were made memorable by the War for Independence, he says. He notes the lack of public travel facilities for such a tour at that time. Sketches of scenery, relics, and traditions fill the journey. Biography and history are woven with the road tale in the Lossing manner.
4997-two-boys-and-a-fortune-or-the-tyler:
Matthew White Jr.'s Two Boys and a Fortune opens with a man on a bridge, a miser's home, and Mr. Tyler's will, which sets twin brothers Rex and Roy on different paths. Breaking the news, Rex's trip to town, Reginald's humiliation, and a mystery about Sydney follow, with an alarming discovery and midnight happenings to come.

Rex determines to take matters into his own hands and arrives in New York, where he sees a horrible sight that changes the story's stakes. White keeps the plot moving through offices, homes, and city streets. Readers get a boys' mystery of inheritance and enterprise, where a will is only the beginning of the adventure.
50940-wailing-wall:
Wailing Wall is a science fiction story by Roger Dee, illustrated by Ed Alexander, first published in Galaxy Science Fiction in July 1952. The magazine's blurb promises an enormous weapon that forces people to keep their troubles to themselves. The hero, Farrell, wakes naked and weaponless in the underground dome of the Hymenops, an insectoid alien power on the planet Sadr the Third.

Farrell has no idea how long he has been lost in the honeycombed dark. Above him lie silent audience chambers; outside, by a silver river, his companions wait in the disabled ship Marco Four, as far away in effect as Earth, five hundred light-years off. He darts into an opening and finds a Ringwave generator, at once alien and familiar.  The story runs on that trap: a human mind driven where something wants it to go.
5120-vandrad-the-viking-or-the-feud-and-:
J. Storer Clouston's adventure novel is set in the Viking north, where a feud and a supposed spell drive Vandrad from sea voyages and island halls into danger. Chapters move from the west sea sailing to a holy isle, a hermit's cell, a king's feast, and a trial by the sword, as old wrongs pull Vandrad toward revenge.

Magic, runes, and a magician stand beside seamanship, loyalty, and blood debts, giving the tale the colour of saga literature. Readers looking for a brisk historical romance will find swordplay, sea travel, and island politics woven through a story about whether a man can escape the feud that shaped him.
51404-plain-living-a-bush-idyll:
Plain Living, a bush idyll by Rolf Boldrewood, author of Robbery Under Arms and The Miner's Right, was published in London and New York in 1898 by Macmillan. Chapter one brings Stamford riding slowly homeward at dusk. He follows the dusty track to the Windahgil station in late autumn light. The ride sets the scene of a pastoral tenant's life in Australia.

Boldrewood grants that such a life is mostly free and pleasant. It lacks the cares that gnaw at modern men in cities. Then come the striking exceptions. A dry season falls, in bush speech, and the drear months follow. Grass withers, waters shrink from the footstep, and flocks and herds suffer. The idyll is a station tale with drought as its dark undertow.
5150-the-ear-in-the-wall:
Arthur B. Reeve's mystery collection follows Professor Craig Kennedy through cases that mix crime with the new technology and social tensions of the 1910s. Chapters run from a vanisher and a safe robbery to a suffragette secretary, a woman detective, a jury fixer. A Wall Street wolf appears among them, each case turning on a clue Kennedy reads by science.

The title points to eavesdropping and hidden listening, a theme that suits stories of black books, anonymous letters, and society scandals. Readers get brisk, invention-filled detective tales, in which typewriters, photographs, and phantom circuits matter as much as motives and alibis.
51576-shatter-the-wall:
Sydney Van Scyoc wrote Shatter the Wall, a tale in a galaxy magazine of 1962. A family charms everyone, and everybody loves them to death. Especially Amanda, the tag line adds, with a knife in the words. Bass McDowall stands life-size on the Wall in the first scene. His image bends over a girl-image on the screen.

Kippie, sweetie-bug, his mellow voice gasps from the Wall. Amanda thrusts savagely upward on an ebony lever, and the idols vanish. Kathryn leaps up, crying to turn it back on. He was going to kiss her, the girl protests in anguish. Amanda bars the lever to speak first with her daughter. Kathryn is the youngest person living in this city, she says. Everyone has to call me Kippie, the girl snaps back. Van Scyoc gives a future of screens and borrowed selves.
5187-miss-minerva-and-william-green-hill:
Frances Boyd Calhoun's Southern humour novel opens with a scandalised Miss Minerva receiving a small boy who arrives by bus, perched beside the driver in a huge raincoat. William Green Hill, mischievous and credulous by turns, soon turns her orderly house upside down with rabbits, riddles, tall tales, and a humble petition or two.

Calhoun writes in the dialect humour tradition of the period, letting Billy's literal mind collide with adult respectability. The book is a gentle comedy of a spinster aunt and the boy she did not expect. It offers readers a warm, old-fashioned portrait of Southern small-town life.
51920-the-old-soak-and-hail-and-farewell:
Don Marquis wrote The Old Soak and Hail and Farewell, for Doubleday at Garden City in 1921. Sterling Patterson drew the line pictures for the book. Its hero, the Old Soak, comes in from his home in Flatbush in no jovial mood. Friends tell him some hope for beer and light wines under the law. Hope, he says, is a fine thing, but it does not gurgle when poured from a bottle.

He would rather have despair with a case of bourbon than all the hope in the world alone. Home-made booze from a tea-kettle and hose is his next target. One friend, scared of his brew, tried it first on his wife's parrot Peter. Home liquor is good to take grease spots out of rugs, he holds, but not for the human stomach. Marquis gives dry-era talk at its funniest.
5232-sejanus-his-fall:
Ben Jonson's tragedy Sejanus His Fall dramatises the rise and ruin of Sejanus, favourite of the emperor Tiberius, in ancient Rome. Jonson added hundreds of scholarly notes, mostly in Latin, grounding the play in Tacitus and other Roman historians. The five acts follow Sejanus from power through conspiracy to a sudden, brutal fall.

The play is Jonson's most learned Roman tragedy, austere where his comedies are lively. It shows his belief that drama should teach history. Readers will find a dark study of ambition, flattery, and tyranny, with a Senate, a palace, and a city watching one man's fortune collapse.
53414-dave-porter-and-his-classmates-or-:
Edward Stratemeyer wrote a school tale of Dave Porter and his mates at Oak Hall. Long lists at the front name his many sets for boys, from Old Glory to Lakeport. Dave Porter books alone run past a dozen in the list shown. A big touring car racing past a carryall fronts the tale as a plate.

Dave and his classmates face tests of honor, sport, and nerve at school. Rivals, runaways, and searches fill the wider set, and this book keeps that brisk pace. Plain talk and quick scenes carry each scrape to a clean end. Boys of the time read Dave as a model of pluck and fair play.
53898-thomas-campbell:
Thomas Campbell is a life of the Scots poet by Hadden, in a set of lives of famed Scots. The set list at the front names past thirty lives, from the sage of the north to the bard of the plow. The book is given to the writers wife, whose calm help eases his life of the pen. Its front note owns a great debt past.

A past life of Campbell by a friend was the stay of the poets last years, and no tale of him can skip it. One past judge of books said as much in a great sheet of the past age. Hadden adds his thanks to a set of tales of the man by a next hand, ill put in a row yet rich in fact. The life thus stands on the work of those who knew the poet best.
5400-project-gutenberg-complete-works-of:
The Complete Project Gutenberg Edition of the Works of Winston Churchill gathers the American novelist's books in one record, with a note distinguishing him from the British statesman of the same name. Its contents include The Crossing, The Dwelling Place of Light, Mr Crewe's Career, A Far Country, Coniston, The Inside of the Cup, Richard Carvel, A Modern Chronicle, The Celebrity, and The Crisis.

The edition adds Dr Jonathan, a play, A Traveller in Wartime. The Crossing and its borderland chapters open the edition. Readers get Churchill's whole fictional career in one place, from frontier romance to novels of politics, faith, and modern life.
5405-the-ne-er-do-well:
Rex Beach's Ne'er-Do-Well, dedicated to his wife, opens with victory. A trail divides, then the story follows Kirk Anthony through a gap and new acquaintances. A remedy is proposed, until he is greatly surprised. Chapters bring El Comandante, Spanish law, a change of plan, the truth about Mrs Cortlandt, a night at Taboga, and Chiquita.

Later chapters follow the path that led nowhere, an alias as Jefferson Locke, a number. Garavel the banker enters, as Kirk's fortunes in Panama shift. Beach writes a brisk adventure of the canal zone, with romance, intrigue. The comedy of a young man out of his depth runs through it, in the manner of his popular novels.
54639-the-naturalist-s-repository-volume:
The first volume of a Regency natural history miscellany. Its full title is the Naturalist's Repository, or Monthly Miscellany of Exotic Natural History. Elegantly coloured plates form its core. Each plate carries scientific and general descriptions. Quadrupeds, birds, fishes, insects, and shells all qualify. Rarity is the selection rule throughout.

The work hunts novelties from every part of the world. Some creatures remained entirely undescribed before its pages. Others had escaped proper notice from earlier naturalists. Transcriber notes reveal the plates' quirks. Two plates were bound reversed and have been swapped back. Index entries sometimes point to background plants only. Such monthly parts built Georgian cabinets of curiosity in print. Five volumes eventually gathered the series.
55654-the-deep-sea-s-toll:
James Connolly wrote tales of the deep sea and the men who pay its toll. The book came out in New York in September 1905. Aylward and Reuterdahl drew its plates. Connolly wrote Out of Gloucester and The Seiners. A front plate shows a skipper who shouts for Tommie in a gale.

The Sail-Carriers leads the set of eight sea tales. The wicked Celestine and the truth of the Oliver Cromwell come next. Skill at sea, dory mates, and a bark's save fill the mid set. Georges Shoals and Patsie Oddie's black night close the book. Salt talk and true seamanship rule each tale in full. Gloucester men stand at its heart.
557-puck-of-pook-s-hill:
Rudyard Kipling lets Puck, the old spirit of England, tell children the past in this story cycle. Dan and Una, playing near Pook's Hill, meet Weland the smith, a Roman centurion, Saxons, Danes, and smugglers, each with a song. Puck's opening song traces guns, mills, and camps across Sussex downs.

Kipling writes with rich, musical prose, mixing tale and verse. Each visit teaches how England grew from tribes, legions, and crafts into one land. The book endures as a beloved history in story form, where the past walks and talks beside two children at play.
55982-forward-pass-a-story-of-the-new-fo:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote this school tale of the new football, with its daring forward pass. Barbour's Hilton School and Big Four books stand on the list at the front. The hero here is Dan, a boy bound for Yardley school.

Off to School opens the tale, then Hall 56 and Tubby Jones, who gives in in chapter six. Payson the coach, the first game, and a hard drop from the squad test Dan. A rescue, a rich man's son, and a plot thicken the school year. Gerald comes to Yardley, and an afternoon afloat rests the team. The front plate shows a boy staggering round the goal post for the score that wins the day.
56088-john-marshall:
John Marshall is a life of the great chief judge by James Bradley Thayer. It is number seven of a set of shore lives and came out in nineteen one. Thayer drew with free hand past a talk he gave at a great law school that year. A plate past a small paint of the judge heads the book. Parts treat his life past his post, his talks, and his law views.

That first part tells his sire was a school mate of the first chief of the land and served with him as a land measurer. Both men won wealth past that work past a great lords wide lands in the west. The judge him self was born past a great stream in the south state, Thayer notes past his own life of that chief. His kin, his last days, and his notes take the last parts.
56970-mrs-farrell:
Mrs Farrell is a short novel by Howells, in an edition of 1921. The hosted text opens with a long list of his books. Annie Kilburn, April Hopes, and A Hazard of New Fortunes stand there. Mrs Farrell itself appears among the titles. A family note tells the story's first life in print. It ran in the Atlantic Monthly of 1875. Its first title was Private Theatricals. Howells was then editor of that magazine.

Henry James's Gabrielle de Bergerac came just before it. Neither short novel was republished by its author, the note says. This late printing rescued a piece of his youth. Howells became the dean of American letters. His early tales of manners are slighter than the great novels. Mrs Farrell shows his hand before the fame. Private theatricals and village love drive its slight plot.
57453-kelly-of-the-foreign-legion-letter:
Russell A Kelly letters form Kelly of the Foreign Legion, to which is added an historical sketch of the Foreign Legion, issued in New York by Mitchell Kennerley in nineteen seventeen. A photo of Kelly faces the title page. The book is given to the memory of the Marquis de Lafayette. A preface is dated New York, May nineteen seventeen. Ten sections fill the book.

Section one is Voyage to Bordeaux and Enlistment. On Election Day, November third, nineteen fourteen, Kelly left New York on the good ship Orcadian. The cargo was six hundred fifty horses for the war, he writes. His letter from Bordeaux is dated November twenty fifth, nineteen fourteen. Training at Depot de Lyon and In the First Line Trenches follow. The Battle of Artois closes the letters. War readers get an American legionnaire letters home.
57512-john-bull-s-womankind-les-filles-d:
John Bull's Womankind is a humorous book by Max O'Rell, author of John Bull and His Island. The French title, Les Filles de John Bull, stands beside the English one. The Leadenhall Press issued the work at London, and this copy is of the twenty fifth thousand. The price was half a crown, or three and six in cloth.

The front pages carry adverts for a famed ladies' tailor, quoted from Paris and London papers. Such matter frames the book as light reading on English life and manners. O'Rell wrote as a French observer amused by his neighbours across the Channel. His earlier book on John Bull himself had made his name with English readers. This companion volume turns the same comic eye on English women. Its sketches trade in national types, dress, and social custom.
57627-mrs-gaskell:
Mrs Gaskell is a study of the novelist Elizabeth Gaskell, written by Esther Alice Chadwick. Herbert and Daniel published the book at London in the Regent Library series. A portrait after George Richmond faces the title page. A calendar of the main events of Gaskell's life stands near the front.

Chadwick sorts her matter by kind, from poems to novels to tales. The novels section weighs the great social tales first. Mary Barton and its Manchester strike fill many pages. North and South and Cranford supply the humour and the charm. Chadwick notes that forty six years after her death, the books still found eager readers. A centenary the year before had swelled the fame. The study served the new readers that revival brought.
5780-the-rover-boys-at-school-or-the-cad:
Winfield introduces the Rover Boys at school in this first Putnam Hall adventure, where Dick, Tom, and Sam learn they are bound for boarding school at last. Tom cheers the news to Sam, who fears false hopes, until Tom reports that Uncle Randolph told Aunt Martha he would not keep the boys in the house another week. The brothers head for Putnam Hall as cadets, ready for lessons, drills, and scrapes.

It offers the series formula in its freshest form: three brothers, a strict school, rivals, and pranks that test loyalty. The school setting gives the adventure its shape, with classrooms, dormitories, and playing fields as stages for courage. Young readers who enjoy vintage school stories will find brisk chapters, earnest heroes, and a brotherhood that carries every plot.
58036-the-miller-in-eighteenth-century-v:
Colonial Williamsburg published this account of the miller and his craft. The 1978 booklet treats mills in eighteenth century Virginia life. It also describes the windmill near the Palace in Williamsburg town. An opening note clears today master of Robertson windmill of blame.

Old millers bad repute is no slur on present men, it says. Chaucer millers stole corn and meal, sly and accustomed well. His pilgrim miller had a thumb of gold, the tale notes. Honest miller proverb cut a broad swath, the account adds. The account opens by addressing a reader of open mind and charitable temper at Williamsburg.
58107-for-the-story-teller-story-telling:
For the Story Teller teaches the art of telling stories to children. Carolyn Sherwin Bailey wrote the manual. The Milton Bradley Company published it in 1913. Bailey had written several children's books before it. Thirteen chapters treat the teller's craft. A sheaf of stories to tell follows them.

Early chapters build the theory. Sense appeal and suspense earn chapters. Climax and memory training follow. The instinct story and the dramatic story divide the kinds. Fairy stories get a chapter on imagination. Making over old stories closes the teaching. The story section adapts tales from many hands. Andersen and Wilde appear in it. Bailey dramatises the gingerbread boy herself. A Swedish fairy tale opens the set.
58558-christmas-at-thompson-hall:
Anthony Trollope's Christmas at Thompson Hall was issued at Boston by Joseph Knight in 1894, in the Cosy Corner Series. The tale had been copyrighted in 1893. Five chapters follow the Browns: a success, a failure, an attempt to escape, an escape, and arrival at Thompson Hall. The story opens on the severe Christmas of a year the narrator will not name. Paris, he says, feels bad weather worse than London does, being built for gaiety.

Snow turned to slush floods the streets, and half-frozen rain falls through the twenty-third of December. At ten that evening an English couple reach the Grand Hotel on the Boulevard des Italiens. The narrator hides their real names and calls them the Browns. An illustration list promises a large woman thought by some to be handsome and a scene where she looks like Lady Macbeth.
58583-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of John Stuart Mill is a finding list compiled by David Widger. It gathers Mill's writings as held in the Project Gutenberg collection, with the tables of contents of the volumes. Mill is the great English philosopher of liberty and utility.

The roll of works is the canon itself. On Liberty stands beside Utilitarianism and the Principles of Political Economy. The Subjection of Women, the Autobiography, and the Considerations on Representative Government are all here. The System of Logic appears in two volumes, with the essay on Auguste Comte and positivism nearby. The Contest in America recalls Mill's voice in the American Civil War. Such an index serves the reader who wants the whole shelf of an author in one view, and students who need a chapter found fast.
58696-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of the Project Gutenberg works of Robert Ingersoll. Twelve volumes of the works are listed first. Single pieces follow: The Ghosts with its hell lecture, About the Holy Bible, the oration on Thomas Paine, The Christian Religion, Heretics and Heresies, Humboldt, and Individuality. Mistakes of Moses and the trial of Reynolds stand in the roll.

The index then prints detailed contents of the volumes. Volume one holds lectures: The Gods, Humboldt, Thomas Paine, Individuality, Heretics and Heresies, The Ghosts, and the liberty of man, woman, and child. What Must We Do to Be Saved takes the gospels and the churches one by one. An honest God is the noblest work of man, The Gods begins from 1872. Readers of the great agnostic get a map of his whole shelf here.
58703-key-and-guide-to-native-trees-shru:
Norma Stillwell of Dallas, Texas, wrote this key to the native trees, shrubs, and woody vines of Dallas County, printed at Dallas in April 1939. A glossary opens the book, defining axil, deciduous, dioecious, lenticel, and the parts of flowers in plain terms. Plates show flowers and twigs: spike, cyme, umbel, panicle, and catkin forms.

Drawings teach leaf shapes and edges: lobed, rounded, pointed, oblong, and heart forms, with crenate, serrate, and notched margins. Winter buds and leaf scars help name a tree bare of leaves. The guide serves walkers, teachers, and gardeners in one Texas county, giving them a working key to the woody plants at their doors.
5873-farewell:
Honore de Balzac's Farewell, translated by Ellen Marriage and dedicated to Prince Friedrich von Schwarzenberg, opens in a hurry toward dinner. A deputy of the Centre is urged to mend his pace, jump, and keep up, if the party means to sit down to dinner when everyone else does. From that brisk, comic opening, Balzac unfolds a tale of memory, war, and a farewell that echoes far beyond one evening.

Readers meet Balzac's gift for turning a small social scene into a large human drama, with soldiers, marquises, and dinner parties as his stage. The story favors character and irony, letting past wounds surface in present manners. It suits readers of Balzac's shorter fiction, and those who enjoy French realism where a farewell carries the weight of history.
59005-the-cadets-of-flemming-hall:
Anna Chapin Ray wrote The Cadets of Flemming Hall, for Crowell in 1892. Crowell sold it at New York and Boston, illustrated, for a dollar and a quarter. Ray had written Half a Dozen Boys and Half a Dozen Girls. A Detroit paper praised her quiet sly humor in a front notice. Her everyday events take dramatic interest, that notice adds.

A plate shows guests seating themselves as their tastes suggested. Boy school stories had gone on multiplying in those years, her preface owns. An American tale of a new senior at Andover stands in her survey. A French tale of school life stands beside it in the same note. Ray adds her own school of cadets to that growing shelf. The book gives schoolboy honor, scrapes, and friendship in her warm mode.
59111-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger made this list of the works of Lewis Carroll held by Project Gutenberg. It is a guide, not a tale: a roll of names with the heads of their parts. At its head stands the line of Alice. The roll names the first form of the tale, made from the author's own hand. It names the full tale of Wonderland in more than one shape, with the form made for the cradle room as well.

Through the Looking-Glass comes next, then The Hunting of the Snark. The pair of tales of Sylvie and Bruno stands by verse and jest in Phantasmagoria. The works of sums and of signs have their place too: The Game of Logic, Symbolic Logic, and A Tangled Tale.
59238-an-easy-introduction-to-spanish-co:
An Easy Introduction to Spanish Conversation, by Velazquez de la Cadena, is a small self teaching book. The New York edition is dated eighteen seventy two, with rights from eighteen forty nine. Its title promises all that is needed to make rapid progress in Spanish talk. It is designed for persons with little time to study, or who teach themselves.

The preface calls its aim much in little, in a Latin tag. A short survey of the Spanish tongue comes before the word lists. That survey stresses the joining of verbs, which the learner must master well. The author advises learning five nouns, adjectives, or verbs each day by heart. A month of that plan yields more than five hundred common words of daily use. Dialogues then let the learner vary questions and answers with ease.
59314-snowball:
Poul Anderson's Snowball ran in Worlds of If Science Fiction in May 1955. Simon Arch, thirty-two, is a physicist working for himself in Westfield, fifty miles north of Boston. Royalties from a patented electronic valve freed him from teaching. He and his wife Elizabeth built a house with a walled garden and a separate laboratory. Their latest project, the headnote warns, is a new source of power anyone can manufacture in a kitchen oven.

The story asks what happens to the world economy when such power turns snowball-cheap. Colin Culquhoun, the huge red-haired professor of physics at the local college, is Arch's closest friend and political opposite. Arch calls himself a reactionary; Culquhoun holds radical opinions. The opening chapters set the two men arguing over dielectrics. Anderson grounds his wonder in one couple's postponed children and tight budget.
59391-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Bertrand Russell is a finding tool compiled by David Widger. It lists the works of Russell held by Project Gutenberg and gives the table of contents of each volume. The works named include Proposed Roads to Freedom, The Analysis of Mind, Political Ideals, The Problems of Philosophy, The Problem of China, Bolshevism, Mysticism and Logic and Why Men Fight.

The contents show the span of Russell's writing. Political Ideals takes up capitalism and the wage system and the pitfalls in socialism. The Problems of Philosophy runs from appearance and reality to idealism, induction and the world of universals. The index lets a reader see the shape of each book before opening it.
59522-biltmore-house-and-gardens-biltmor:
Biltmore House and Gardens is a visitor guide to the Biltmore Estate. The estate at Biltmore Asheville in North Carolina opens to visitors year round. A three mile drive winds through shrub plantings and pine forests to the house. The mansion then comes into view with startling suddenness, the guide says.

George Vanderbilt completed the great house in eighteen ninety five on that drive. Richard Hunt designed it on the lines of French Renaissance chateaux. Blois and Chambord gave the chief models for its grand form. Frederick Law Olmsted planned the landscape setting of mansion and estate. Many call that estate the finest landscape design in all America.
59623-change-signals-a-story-of-the-new-:
Change Signals, a Story of the New Football, is a school novel by Ralph Henry Barbour. Appleton published it in New York and London in September 1912. Barbour's shelf of Yardley school tales stands listed at the front. An illustration shows a kicked ball sailing true over the crossbar.

The contents begin with a mass-meeting and a joke played by Towne. Kendall, the hero, makes a call and learns of a plot against the team. He foils that plot before the first game of the season is played. A mysterious kicker enters the story at its midpoint in the contents. Golf with Broadwood and a chapter on mushrooms give the term its lighter side. The title arrives as a chapter near the end of the book.
59707-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Edward Sylvester Ellis is a catalogue compiled by David Widger. Ellis was a prolific writer of tales of the American frontier. The index lists his works held by Project Gutenberg, title by title. Under each title it gives the parts or chapters a reader will find in that work, the part shown suggests.

The contents name dozens of his books in a row. Among them are lives of Thomas Jefferson and Kit Carson. Tales such as The Lost Trail and The Huge Hunter appear, some of them twice. Deerfoot tales fill a long run of the list. Launch Boys adventures and Boy Patrol books show his series work for boys. A life of Daniel Boone and tales of Texas and the Ozarks round out the part shown.
60178-leaves-from-the-note-books-of-lady:
Leaves from the Note Books of Lady Dorothy Nevill was shaped by her son Ralph Nevill and printed in London by Macmillan in 1907. A portrait of Lady Dorothy, painted by G F Watts in 1844, stands at the front. Her scrap books held a long life in high society.

The first part ranges from a female politician of other days and old election souvenirs to political caricatures and old menus. Names crowd the list, from Bernal Osborne to Lord Randolph Churchill and his giving up of office. The second part treats society and talk, the Duke of Wellington hate of publicity, and Peel wedding at Apsley House. Matchmaking, American influence, and famous hostesses fill the pages. Readers get Victorian and Edwardian society from a sharp insider notebook.
6018-the-journal-of-a-tour-to-the-hebrid:
James Boswell records his tour to the Hebrides with Samuel Johnson, dedicating the journal to Edmond Malone. Boswell insists that authenticity matters above all in history and biography, and he appeals to Johnson's friends to judge from internal evidence whether the many conversations are correctly related.

He recalls General Paoli, who fought to preserve his country's liberties and found asylum in Britain, as a judge of truth in an earlier work. The journal that follows gives talk, travel, and character in close detail. Boswell's portrait of Johnson rests on what was said, heard, and remembered on the road.
60414-the-viking-s-skull:
John Carling wrote a tale of a Viking skull, a rune ring, and a lost throne. The book came out in Boston in March 1904. Carling wrote The Shadow of the Czar as well. An English lady starts the tale, and a rune ring comes next. A past look and a dire death close the first long part.

The Ravengars of Ravenhall lead the main tale in full. A shrine's riddle and Idris come back from death's door in it. The ring's key and the oft borne throne's shade drive the plot. Fires of the old gods and a tomb's core mark its turns. Lorelie Rivière brings love to the weird tale.
60765-the-young-mechanic-containing-dire:
The Young Mechanic came from Putnam at New York and London in 1896. Its entry was made in 1871, from the English edition, with corrections. The author had written The Lathe and Its Uses before it. Directions for the use of all kinds of tools fill the book. The construction of steam engines and mechanical models stands in the title.

The art of turning in wood and metal is included in its scope. The American editors believe they are supplying a long-felt want. Young mechanics of this country had no book like it, they hold. No book in England or America explains tools so clearly, they add. It is written for boys and beginners, yet serves the practical mechanic too. The first six chapters treat tools for working wood, from the simplest on. A boyish faith that tools enough can make anything is corrected early.
61100-charles-w-quantrell:
Charles Quantrell is a history of guerrilla warfare by John Burch. Burch printed it at Vega, Texas, with rights held in 1923. Captain Harrison Trow, who followed Quantrell through his whole course, told it. Plates show Quantrell and Trow in the front of the volume. Contents open with an introduction and a piece called The False Jonah.

The early life of Quantrell and why the guerrillas organized follow there. His first battle, fights at Independence, and the Tate House come next. Jayhawkers, the Low House fight, and a hunt for ammunition ensue. The battle and capture of Independence and Lone Jack fill later heads. Border war on the Missouri and Kansas line, 1861 to 1865, is the theme.
61334-when-whirlybirds-call:
Frank Banta wrote this tale of Five-Gun DeCrabbe and the whirlybirds. The story ran in Worlds of If in January 1963. Featherton folk cheer from windows, fearing to come out that morning. DeCrabbe rides down main street with his coupe bubble slid back.

He ignores the menace from the skies with haughty self confidence. Five-Gun had come to clean up the town of whirlybirds. He checks needle pistols, an explosive pellet rifle, and an N-ray gun. Mayor Alson Prince waits under the City Hall marquee to greet him. A rocket powered stun gas spray gun fills his hands as he strides to meet them.
61635-americans-all-immigrants-all:
Americans All, Immigrants All is a set of twenty-six radio plays for broadcast. The shows put the gifts of the many cultural groups of the United States in the spotlight. They trace what those groups have given to the growth of the land in wealth, in social life, and in public life.
