The shows were put on by the Office of Education of the Department of the Interior with the Columbia Broadcasting System.

The Service Bureau for Intercultural Education worked with the makers, and the Works Progress Administration gave aid. The front matter names the heads of the plan: Harold L. Ickes as Secretary of the Interior and John W. Studebaker as Commissioner of Education. Rachel Davis-DuBois led the Service Bureau. Philip H. Cohen ran the shows, and Gilbert Seldes led the writing in the staff list as shown.
61968-the-ballad-of-blaster-bill:
Nelson Bond wrote this science fiction ballad in verse for Planet Stories in the summer of 1941. Its opening tells how crews hurtling round the sun, on the run through the asteroids from Jupiter to Mars, may sight an unwinking beacon in the everlasting night. Every man aboard gravely salutes it: the final resting place of Blaster Bill.

The ballad then introduces the freighter Dotty Sue and her master engineer, surly Jonathan McNeer, gruff and foul-mouthed but a better grease-pot never sheared the blue. His torment is Bill the Blaster, a lazy, good-natured oaf with boulders for forearms and lead for brains, whose duty is the rocket-blasts and motors. Bill breaks things by the dozen and practices vivisection on every machine he touches. Two months out of Io City, with the asteroids thirty hours away, McNeer orders the hypatomic motors taken down for cleaning.
62251-the-poems-of-alice-meynell:
The Poems of Alice Meynell, in a complete edition, was issued at Toronto by McClelland and Stewart in 1923. A front portrait of the poet comes from a drawing by Sargent. A bibliographical note at the front maps her books of verse. Preludes, her early volume, stands first in that history.

Poems of 1893 ran through nine impressions before 1913, the note records. Later Poems of 1901 joined the collected edition of 1913. A Father of Women, and Other Poems appeared in 1918. This volume contains the whole of her poetry in one place. Meynell wrote lyrics of faith, motherhood, and London streets with rare finish. Her verse was praised by poets and read in two hemispheres. The complete edition is her monument in a single book.
62702-the-city-of-the-sacred-well:
Willard wrote The City of the Sacred Well, for the Century company in 1926. His book tells of the discoveries and diggings of Edward Herbert Thompson. Thompson worked in the ancient city of Chichen Itza in Yucatan. Discourse on the culture of the Mayas fills the same covers. Their art and architecture reveal that culture, the title says, with photographs.

A front plate shows a bride hurtling far out over the sacred well. Contents open with Yucatan, the land of the Mayas, and a church legend. The first Americans, the ancient city, and an idle day in the jungle follow. Sixty feet under water tells of diving in the well for its treasures. The finding of the date-stone and the tomb of the high priest come later. Thirty years of digging closes the contents in a long retrospect.
62807-old-chelsea-a-summer-day-s-stroll:
Old Chelsea, subtitled A Summer-Day's Stroll, is a topographical walk through London's Chelsea by Benjamin Ellis Martin. Fisher Unwin published it in London in 1889, with illustrations by Joseph Pennell. The stroll described is imagined as taken during the summer of 1888, with all dates brought down to that moment.

Martin's note thanks Lady Holland for a curiosity. The ware on the cover copies a plate from a set once Doctor Johnson's, now in Holland House. The plates guide the walk. They show the statue of Thomas Carlyle by Boehm, the embankment, Chelsea Hospital's river front, Paradise Row, and Tite Street. The gateway of Rossetti's old house also appears. A statue of Sir Hans Sloane in the Botanic Gardens also appears. The book strolls a literary riverside village inside the growing city.
63050-be-polite-to-all:
Be Polite to All is number 43 in Dean's Illustrated Farthing Books, published in London by Dean and Son. A motto heads the tale: you cannot judge a man by the coat he wears. The story opens at a busy station, with the engine puffing, porters rushing with trunks, and crowds scrambling for seats.

A carelessly dressed man stands quiet on the platform, paying little heed to the rush. He is lame, and at a glance seems a man of no wealth or weight. The conductor slaps his shoulder, calls him Limpy, and tells him to get a seat or be left behind. The man answers, cool and unmoved, that there is time enough. The farthing tale teaches children not to mock what they misjudge.
63051-oliver-cromwell:
Oliver Cromwell is a biography by Theodore Roosevelt, issued in New York in 1900. Scribner published it with illustrations. A portrait by Walker serves as frontispiece. Milton's sonnet to Cromwell stands as its motto. The contents run to six chapters. The times and the man open the study. The Long Parliament and the Civil War follow.

The second civil war and the death of the king come next. The Irish and Scotch wars fill the fourth chapter. The Commonwealth and Protectorate are then weighed. A chapter on personal rule closes the book. Roosevelt wrote it while governor of New York. He treats Cromwell as a soldier-statesman of faith and force. The preface is dated from the Executive Chamber at Albany. Few presidents have written lives of foreign rulers.
63310-the-chapel-on-the-hill:
Chapel on the Hill is a tale by Alfred Pretor, a fellow of a Cambridge college. Pretor also wrote Ronald and I, his title page notes. The Cambridge edition is dated nineteen oh four. A line from Cymbeline heads the book: some falls are means the happier to arise. The book is dedicated to the memory of a dog named Judy, with lines from Byron.

Chapter one opens from a rector's study window. Two large bay windows look onto a terrace and a lawn fringed with gay flower beds. A flood of light and air streams in, the narrator says. Sadness would be out of place in such a room, he muses. Impossible to write a gloomy sermon here, he jokes. Beyond the meadow, reaping is in progress. A glimpse of the sea and an island closes the view.
63708-total-recall:
Total Recall is a science fiction story by Larry Sternig, first printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1946. It opens in the office of Brian Wargan, chief of the Solar Bureau of Investigation. Wargan, gray with strain, tells the young agent Roger Kay that the Corvo North business is almost a myth by now, but it is their only chance.

The department has located the old scientist. His laboratory stands on Ganymede, some distance from the spaceport, in the mining district. He has been doing research for the Inter-Planetary Mining Syndicate. Wargan puts Kay through by visi-communicator, and North's daughter appears on the screen. She says her father is in the lab and will not let her disturb him. The tale's promise is stark: buried under layers of horror in the old scientist's brain is the one thing that can save the System.
63720-through-the-asteroids-to-hell:
Through the Asteroids, to Hell, by Leroy Yerxa, ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1946. Blair Freedman pilots the X26 on a run he has made past counting. Trip number seven thousand twenty two, the chart says, for the rest of his life. He sighs and calls Jerry Graham from the navigation desk. For a moment he wants to miss the tunnel mouth. A straight hit on the asteroid wall tempts him. Graham stiffens at the thought.

Freedman pulls himself together and flies true. The guard ship trains its guns as he flashes his colours. Inside, the ship's lamps splash light on twisting walls of death. The Cutter, a huge ship built by Planet Control, keeps the tunnel open. Freedman, the blurb warns, would die to keep it open, but not with the girl he loves.
64010-the-android-kill:
The Android Kill is a science fiction story by John Jakes, first published in Planet Stories in January 1952. Its villain-hero is Caffrey, a freighter captain shipping a cargo of android slaves. The magazine's blurb gives the twist away: someone made this batch of androids too perfect, and Caffrey laughs at the irony as he ponders sending his ship into the sun.

The opening is brutal. In the ship's vast gym the blue-gray androids exercise on bars and rings under Caffrey's eye, men, women and children who do not sweat and do not look at him. They know, the narrator says, that they were dead when they were born. When two of them rest and talk, Caffrey beats them with his Venus wood cane until the anger boils out of him. The story builds its horror from the overseer's certainty that his slaves are things.
64015-last-call:
Last Call is a science fiction story by Bryce Walton, taken from Planet Stories of January 1952. The headnote frames it: a soldier of the Disciplinary Corps had not cracked up in all the years of Captain Morrow's service. Bronson was the first. Bronson reckoned he was one of the rare beings who had heard the Call from Mars.

The small cargo rocket is halfway to Venus when Bronson takes it over. The robot waits there, meant for the radioactive areas of Venus where no human could go. Morrow, conditioned to be amoral and unemotional, is shaken. No Corpsman has cracked before. Bronson answers that there is a death penalty for going to Mars, and that the Call comes from there. Walton's tale is a mutiny driven by a signal no one was supposed to hear.
65315-turner-s-water-colours-at-farnley-:
Turner's Water-Colours at Farnley Hall studies the great collection of Turner drawings kept at a Yorkshire house. Alex J Finberg wrote the text, and The Studio published the volume in London, Paris, and New York. The Farnley pictures came from the painter's friendship with the house's owner.

Walter Fawkes of Farnley Hall became Turner's patron and intimate friend. Finberg admits it is not known exactly when or how they met. Several biographers place the meeting about 1802, during a Yorkshire sketching tour. Turner was then making drawings for topographical works by Dr Whitaker, the vicar of Whalley. Finberg tests that story against Whitaker's books and finds it wanting in detail. The essay models careful provenance work. The Farnley collection itself remains among the richest stores of Turner's watercolour art.
6635-a-romance-of-billy-goat-hill:
Alice Hegan Rice, known for Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch, sets a Kentucky romance in gay, bursting springtime. A colonel, a doctor, a letter burned on a hearth, a shot in the night, and a plea for pardon all flash past in the picture list. The opening chapter lets spring rush through highways and byways, heedless of frost.

Love, wrong, and forgiveness drive the plot, as folk on Billy-Goat Hill weigh pride against heart. Rice writes with warmth and humor, in a Southern voice that feels lived-in. A Romance of Billy-Goat Hill is a gentle, old-style love story, full of Kentucky color and kind feeling.
66550-farewell:
F W Harvey wrote this book of poems, printed by Sidgwick and Jackson of London in 1921. Harvey had written A Gloucestershire Lad at Home and Abroad and Gloucestershire Friends, poems from a German prison camp. Comrades in Captivity told his life in seven German prisons. Nature poems open the set, with four prayers at their head.

The Hollow Land, On Birdlip, Out of the City, and Gloucestershire from the Train root the verse in his home county. Love poems follow, with sonnets on native land and on death. A prayer in the back pages praises the God of bright colours: rainbows, peacocks, daffodils in March, and the red flare of autumn. Harvey writes as a soldier-poet come home, saying farewell.
66623-the-road-to-bunker-hill:
The Road to Bunker Hill, by Shirley Barker, is a story of the American Revolution for younger readers, published in New York in 1962. Barker also wrote novels such as Peace, My Daughters and Rivers Parting, and a Trojan Horse tale for the same young audience.

The first chapter finds Eben Poore on the wharf at Newburyport, complaining that nothing ever happens in his town. His friend Dick Moody wishes for a tea party like the one Boston had, and says he would gladly dress as an Indian and heave a chest of tea overboard. Chapters follow readiness to march, the great Ipswich fright, and fun while it lasted. A pipe-smoking man saves the hero, and a tryst with the enemy follows. The book ends with a terrible black day, the world turned upside down, and hanging and wiving.
67079-the-red-lodge-a-mystery-of-campden:
The Red Lodge, a mystery of Campden Hill by Victor Bridges, was printed at Garden City, New York, in 1924. Doubleday, Page held the copyright, and this is the first edition. Bridges gives the book to Margaret, as he had his earlier Greensea Island.

A dark green Rolls-Royce slides round the corner of Sydney Place and stops in Fulham Road. Its owner, a tall man of about fifty, steps out before Saint Christopher's Hospital and tells his chauffeur to wait. The porter nudges his friend: that is Sir George Onslow, and some poor beggar is for it. The famous surgeon climbs to the second landing, unknowing of the gibe at his trade. He walks into the house surgeon's room without troubling to knock.
67173-the-missing-will:
Agatha Christie wrote The Missing Will, a Hercule Poirot case. Miss Violet Marsh writes a brisk, businesslike note asking for an appointment. She arrives punctually at eleven: tall, handsome, plainly dressed, and clearly a young woman who means to get on in the world. Hastings, who narrates, owns he is no admirer of the New Woman. Her business, she says, is of a somewhat unusual nature.

She is an orphan. Her father was the younger of two sons of a small Devonshire yeoman farmer. The elder brother, Andrew, emigrated to Australia and grew rich on land speculation. Her father became a clerk, married an artist's daughter, and died when she was six. Her mother followed when she was fourteen. Uncle Andrew, returned rich, bought Crabtree Manor and raised the girl as his own. His will makes Christie's puzzle.
67784-sussex-painted-by-wilfrid-ball:
Sussex is a county picture book in a London series of painted and described shires, with water colours by Wilfrid Ball. A list of corrections at the front shows the book's range along the coast. On one page east should read west; on another, Shoreham should read Seaford; on a third, a headland's name is set right. Such small slips mark a text full of named places.

The publisher's pages push the match volume for Wessex, painted by another artist of the series. Thomas Hardy himself wrote to that painter in praise, the advertisement quotes. To their truth in form and colour I can testify, Hardy said. He praised the mood of each spot caught under the view, belonging to that place and no other on earth. The Sussex volume works to the same pattern: colour plates with companion prose.
67805-rivals-for-the-team-a-story-of-sch:
Rivals for the Team is a school and football story by Ralph Henry Barbour. Appleton brought the book out in New York and London in 1916. Relyea drew the pictures, Go it, you Winslow among the plates. Barbour had writ Danforth Plays the Game and The Purple Pennant. Twenty-six chapters run from after practice to Hugh unmasked at last.

Players and coach, a moonlight plunge, and I'm Ordway fill the start. Hugh finds a word, the awkward squad, and his grace the duke follow. Battle, Cathcart proctor, and thirteen to ten crowd the early games. Two in a canoe, back to the fold, and Bert confides come midway. A broken rib, friends in need, and benched darken the late list. Hobo wins fame before Hugh goes to the village near the end. Ted Trafford eases his tired body to a window-seat first.
6788-wilhelm-tell:
Schiller's Wilhelm Tell, in Theodore Martin's translation, opens with a long cast. Gessler governs Schwytz and Uri. Baron Attinghausen, his nephew Rudenz, Stauffacher, Tell, and Furst join folk of Schwytz, Uri, and Unterwald. Herdsmen, huntsmen, fishermen, and a priest join them, with wives, sons, and a rich heiress, Bertha of Bruneck, in the wings.

From that crowded stage grows the Swiss legend of apple, arrow, tyranny, and freedom. Schiller writes with a dramatist's fire for liberty and home. Wilhelm Tell is a noble, stirring play, still the classic telling of Switzerland's founding myth.
68712-the-secret-in-the-hill:
The Secret in the Hill is a tale by Bernard Capes, out at London in nineteen three. The book is given, with a bow, to a Miss Precision and to a small friend in fond marks. It stands in two parts, the first of past ten parts and the next of past fifteen. Names in the lists hint at a quake tale, a hunt for gold goods, and a storm.

The tale is told by a man who lost his mother as a small boy. His father, a law man of warm heart, was more loved than lucky at his work. That father took the boy on his last round of courts, where the boy heard the gay tales of the law men past their work. A first sight of a man, of a hill, and of its tale open the plot.
6880-the-coming-of-bill:
Lora Delane Porter, a rich and forceful woman, fills the opening of this novel with her daily drive and her firm grip on her family. Her daughter Ruth stands at the center of the tale, and the two books follow Ruth's plans, her marriage hopes, and the clash between her own will and her mother's designs. Chapter titles point to troubled waters, broken hopes, and a slow path toward peace.

Steve, a second leading figure, meets mischance and exile before he finds a way back, and the later chapters turn on rescue, tangled knots cut loose, and new pastures. Wodehouse shapes the whole as a light tale of love and family power, where pride gives way, bit by bit, to a fairer deal for all.
68930-beyond-the-wall:
Henry Leverage wrote a crime tale of a prison break, the first of a set of tales of the underworld. Leverage also wrote Thirst and The Harvest of the Deep. His man Chester Fay serves life and fifteen years at Rockglen prison. Fay is young, slim, and gray haired, and he works in the yard in the rain.

Fay plans an escape with old Charley O'Mara, who is sixty five and bent with age. A motor truck in the yard gives them their chance. Fay creeps close to a dozing guard, strikes him down, and makes his move. What comes next tests nerve, speed, and luck as the two men try to get past the wall.
70236-the-secret-of-the-old-mill:
The Secret of the Old Mill is a Hardy Boys tale by Franklin W Dixon, printed in New York by Grosset and Dunlap under a 1927 copyright. Walter S Rogers drew the plates. Twin books in the set are The Tower Treasure and The House on the Cliff.

A plate shows a boy dropping lightly to the roof of the old mill. Chapters open with a five dollar bill and counterfeit money. The Hardy boys at school, another victim, and curing the joker follow. The old mill, in the mill race, and Joe courage pace the mid tale. A man in a hurry, a chase, and what Lester said raise the stakes. The rug buyer, a note of warning, trapped, and the reckoning close the hunt. Boys of the day got a counterfeiting puzzle in a mill.
70523-remarks-on-the-speeches-of-william:
A pamphlet of 1716, sold in London at sixpence, took up the dying speeches of two men hanged at Tyburn. William Paul, a clergyman, and John Hall of Otterburn were put to death on July 13, 1716, for their part in the late rebellion. Their speeches are printed at length. The remarks that follow are the point of the piece.

The writer holds that the speeches were not the men's own work at all. All the rebel papers of that season, he says, come from one mint, framed to stir the faction to a fresh rising. Both men, he says, did all they could to save their lives. They would have cast off the Pretender and sworn fresh oaths, had pardon been offered on those terms. The pamphlet defends the government in church and state.
71350-hadrian-s-wall:
Hadrian's Wall is a walking and history book by Jessie Mothersole, first issued at London in October 1922. Fourteen illustrations by the author, with maps and plans, support the text. A front picture shows a castle built of stones taken from the wall itself. Second and third editions followed fast, in 1922 and 1924.

A note written as the book went to press reports fresh digging below a named fort. A scholar was completing work on the bridge over a river by the wall. No trace had been found of the bridge's western footing, likely washed away by the strong current. On the eastern side a whole series of footings had been uncovered. The river now runs much farther west than in Roman times, the author adds.
71529-a-call:
A Call, the Tale of Two Passions, is a novel by Ford Madox Hueffer. The author had won fame with his Tudor queen trilogy in past years. A folk song verse on the marigold stands at the front of the book. The novel came out in London in the year nineteen ten.

Robert Grimshaw is likened to a seal on watch at the start of the tale. His dachshund with great feet and bright eyes goes with him in all rooms. A wedding in the set opens the web of two loves and two bonds. Parts in letter form close the long tale of hearts at odds. Keen sight and slow turns mark the authors famed craft with mood.
71698-christmas-at-cedar-hill:
Christmas at Cedar Hill is a holiday story book by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, entered for rights in eighteen sixty nine. Guernsey had written Irish Amy, Straight Forward, and Winifred before this volume. The book was printed in New York by Thomas Whittaker at the Bible House. Its funds came from a Sunday school of Christ Church, Bay Ridge.

Seven chapters frame the book as a set of stories told by travellers. It opens with children setting out by train for their Christmas holidays. Agatha Bower, a pale girl in deep mourning, rides with three boys. Frank and Edward are brothers from Doctor Bower's private school in the tale. Herbert, a grave and thoughtful lad, completes the little party on the train. A rescue follows, then the stories of an old lady and a clergyman. A scholar's story and Agatha's story close the set before the end.
71743-wanderings-in-london-piccadilly-ma:
Wanderings in London: Piccadilly, Mayfair, and Pall Mall is a guide to old London by E. Beresford Chancellor, published in New York in 1909. Chancellor also wrote The Squares of London. The book holds twenty pictures of old London, four of them in colour. Maps inside the covers mark the district for walkers new to it.

The publishers' note mourns the passing of old London as new streets sweep its quiet corners away. Chancellor leads the reader street by street through the West End. He recalls the houses, clubs, and gardens tied to the leisurely life of the past century. The Carlton House gardens of 1784 appear among his pictures. It is a book for walkers who like history under their feet.
72521-astronomy-in-a-nutshell:
Garrett Serviss wrote Astronomy in a Nutshell for Putnam in 1912, explaining the chief facts and principles of the science in popular language for the general reader and for schools. Forty-seven illustrations help, beginning with a photograph of the lunar crater Copernicus.

The book works in three parts. The first treats the celestial sphere: horizon, zenith, and meridian, the placing of the stars, the ecliptic, the equinoxes, the zodiac, and the precession of the equinoxes. The second treats the Earth, its shape and mass, gravitation, tides, time, the seasons, and the calendar. The third takes up the solar system, starting with the distance, size, and heat of the Sun. Serviss was known for making hard science readable, and the plan is orderly throughout.
73098-a-gypsy-against-her-will:
A Gypsy Against Her Will, or Worth Her Weight in Gold, is a tale for girls by Emma Leslie, put out by Blackie and Son of London. Its heroine is Lizzie Betts, a girl in service. The first chapter shows her home, where her mother irons at the board. Lizzie is tired of her place and of cross tempers she must bear in silence. A thought strikes her: why not come home and help with the washing? Her mother takes in laundry to make ends meet.

The mother doubts they can afford it, but Lizzie presses her case. The table of chapters maps the tale to come. There is a fair, a fortune-teller, and a wax-work show. A strange disappearance comes into the tale, and a chapter of repentance stands near the end. Leslie was known for tales of working girls and their trials.
73614-a-book-of-the-west-volume-2-cornwa:
S Baring-Gould wrote A Book of the West, and volume two treats Cornwall as a guide and tale hoard. Methuen issued the book in London in nineteen hundred. Thirty three pictures show coasts, wells, and old stones. Cornish fishermen face the title page in a photo.

Saints of Cornwall lead the tour, with their holy wells next. Crosses and castles mark the old faith in stone. Tin mining gets a full trade chapter of its own. Town by town the road runs west from Launceston. Camelford claims King Arthur in its lore. Smuggling tales spice the coast from Fowey to Penzance. The Land’s End and the Scilly Isles close the long walk. Folk song and odd custom season each stop.
73705-fiddler-s-farewell:
Leonora Speyer wrote Fiddler’s Farewell, a book of poems of loss and love. Alfred A Knopf issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred twenty six. She gives the work to her husband in a short verse leaf. His smile listens well and long, that kind leaf says of him.

No fine feathers of phrase for her song, the first poem vows. Stark dress, a crying nakedness of words, is her bold aim here. The startled candour of the heart stands bare on her lips. Ballad of a Lost House opens the first part of the book. Hungry Heart knocks at a door that once was its own home there. A fiddle’s sound bids the heart step in, for music keys all locks. Friends make free in the lit hall, but the nursery stands dark. Three small children once filled that room with patter and games.
73951-the-second-shell:
The Second Shell is a tale of the air by Jack Williamson. It first ran in a press sheet of air tales in November of nineteen twenty-nine. A front note tells of a strange skin of the sky that turns back the waves of the wire free sets. No man has yet pierced that skin to learn what lies past it, the note says.

The tale opens at two in the night in a year past ten years past, in a press room of a great west town. Its voice is a young news man past a year of flight school. A night guest in rough garb shows a badge of the state guard and asks for him by name on hid work. The two walk out into the still street as the tale takes flight, in both senses of the word.
74421-foot-ball:
Foot Ball, Its History for Five Centuries, by Montague Shearman and James Vincent, opens the Historical Sporting Series. The Leadenhall Press of London issued the book. The authors state their object plainly in the preface. They have not tried to teach the art of football at all.

That art, they say, can only be attained by practice on the field. Their aim is to collect the scattered knowledge of an ancient pastime. Laws, bans, and village games mark the road of the ball through five centuries. Kings forbade the game, and parishes kept it alive in the streets. Shearman and Vincent gather that fragmentary record into one story. The book is a founding work of football history, written when the modern codes were young.
74744-the-windfall:
The Windfall, a novel by Charles Egbert Craddock, was published in New York in March 1907. Craddock, the pen name of Mary Murfree, had written The Prophet of the Great Smoky Mountains. Chapter one sets Hilary Lloyd in the Great Smoky Mountains. Green, purple, and bronze heights stun his theatrical sense. A clear river runs swift between crags. Yet Lloyd frets: his little street fair needs patrons, and the town of Colbury is remote.

Booths rise on the stony public square with sweat and loud talk. Tents collapse from clumsy handling. His partner slouches up in a loud plaid suit, chewing a straw. Well, partner, we have done it again, he says. The tale mixes mountain splendour with the hard luck of show folk.
74858-whitehall:
Whitehall: Historical and Architectural Notes is W J Loftie's guide to the old palace of Whitehall, published by Seeley and Company of London in 1895. A portrait of Inigo Jones, engraved after Van Dyck, forms the frontispiece. Loftie writes the history of a palace that survives mostly in pieces, above all the Banqueting House.

The plates reconstruct what fire and time destroyed. Rubens's Apotheosis of James I, the great ceiling painting, faces the early pages, and views of Whitehall in 1724 and from the river follow. Holbein's Gate and the King Street Gate appear in old engravings, and the first and second designs by Inigo Jones for rebuilding the palace are set side by side. The book is a scholar's walking tour of a vanished court, pieced together from prints.
74954-christmas-at-the-hall:
Christmas at the Hall is a volume of poems by Terrington, author of an earlier poem called Welton Dale. The title poem stands first, with The Hero's Grave and Night Musings named beside it on the title page. The book was issued at London and at Hull. Terrington inscribes it to Samuel Wilderspin, founder of infant schools, who was his father in law.

In his preface the poet owns a bias toward verse held for many years. That urge was often restrained rather than encouraged, he says. Yet turns in his life forced him back to it, and made him wish to test his true strength in the literary world. Welton Dale had been written twelve years before for the same purpose. Lack of confidence had held him back since, the preface admits.
75068-three-girl-chums-at-laurel-hall:
Three Girl Chums at Laurel Hall, or The Mystery of the School by the Lake, is a girls' school story by May Hollis Barton. It was copyrighted in 1926 by Cupples and Leon of New York. Barton also wrote The Girl from the Country and Plain Jane and Pretty Betty. Twenty-five chapters carry Jo Morley and her friends from home trouble to boarding school.

The chapter list promises fire, a rescue, a robbery, and a secret club. The girls face a mean trick, a tennis match, a boat race, and a plot the book calls dastardly. In the end the loot is recovered. The story opens with Jo telling Nan Harrison that she cannot go with her, and the trouble behind that news drives the first chapters.
75219-the-promise-of-the-bell:
The Promise of the Bell, a Christmas essay by Agnes Repplier, was published by Houghton Mifflin in 1924 with pictures by John Wolcott Adams. Its full title adds the words Christmas in Philadelphia. The subject is the Liberty Bell and what its ringing promised. Repplier writes as a Philadelphia essayist with a love for her city's past.

She argues that the bell did more than proclaim the Declaration of Independence. It promised the pursuit of happiness as a right joined to life and liberty. Her pages weigh what that liberty means beyond the casting of a ballot. She quotes Santayana on the liberty to grow wise and live in friendship. The essay ties the bell to English and Greek ideas of a well lived life.
75341-the-dreadful-dragon-of-hay-hill:
The Dreadful Dragon of Hay Hill, by Max Beerbohm, came out alone in 1928. Heinemann printed it in London that November. A new impression followed in January 1929. The tale had first stood in A Variety of Things, part of his collected works. A picture shows Thia and Thol, dated 39,000 years before Christ. The story opens at dawn on a golden summer day. Smoke rises thickly from Hay Hill, with sparks in it. No fire-brigade is called: none exists yet. Dover Street is not built.

Beerbohm walks the reader back past the Georgian hill he remembers. Deeper still: a green hill, higher and steeper, with two caves. Berkeley Square was then a green valley with a babbling stream. All Mayfair lay wild, cut by tiny brooks running to the Pimlico marshes.
75586-babe-ruth-s-own-book-of-baseball:
Babe Ruth's Own Book of Baseball, by George Herman Ruth, is a baseball manual and memoir copyrighted in 1928. It was published in New York by arrangement with Putnam's. The first chapter runs from the Baltimore riverfront and street-corner baseball to days at St Mary's school. It tells of his first contract and his climb to the big leagues.

The front matter names the A L Burt Company as publisher and credits an arrangement with Christy Walsh. The contents then turn to craft: pitching control and how to study a batter. One chapter weighs why young pitchers fail and what practice can fix. Another names the fast ball, the hook, the spit ball, the screw ball, and the knuckle ball. Later chapters cover the pitching motion and curve balls, then infield and outfield play.
77143-jack-hall:
Robert Grant wrote Jack Hall, or The School Days of an American Boy, published at Boston in 1888 and illustrated by Attwood. Grant had earlier written Face to Face and The Confessions of a Frivolous Girl. He dedicated this book to his three boys. Jack, the hero, is a medium-sized boy of thirteen.

The story opens on a bright February morning, with snow in perfect shape for snowballing. A snowball fight and a day of reckoning follow, then Jack goes off to a school called Utopia. Chapters treat the headmaster, first impressions, and a schoolmate named Haseltine who must make his choice. Baseball enters by way of a triple play in the pictures. The book gives a lively picture of American schoolboy life in the 1880s.
77938-the-stone-wall:
The Stone Wall is an autobiography by Mary Casal, published at Chicago in nineteen thirty. Chapter one opens in a garden where mullein plants, known in the East as Indian tobacco, show themselves. Weeds, she calls them, and lifts a hoe, but the velvety sage green leaves hold her hand. Memory turns on a sermon she once heard on the question, what is weeds.

A small boy at a fence, asking a minister that same question, carries her back many years. Casal's life story grows from such scenes of garden, church, and self questioning. The book is known as an early open account of a woman's love for women, told in code and plain speech by turns.
78214-jubilee-hall:
Jubilee Hall, or There's No Place Like Home, is a children's story by Mrs Greene. Nelson published it at London, Edinburgh, and New York. Nineteen chapters carry the tale. Joyful news opens it, in a schoolroom scene. Kathleen Malcomson bursts in on her two brothers at their lessons. She offers each of them three guesses at her grand news. It concerns the boys as well as her, she hints.

The journey to the hall and a bad beginning follow. Berry picking, a prize, and the voice of conscience mark the early lessons. A discovery in Aunt Marian's store room turns the plot. Watching his opportunity and a scene at dead of night raise the stakes. From bad to worse, gloomy forebodings, and the mischief discovered lead to a full confession. Home, sweet home, ends the tale.
78563-the-judgment-of-johan-coull:
Frederick Sleath wrote a sea tale of salvage work on the North Sea. Sleath also wrote Sniper Jackson and The Seventh Vial. Raymond Sisley drew the pictures. The tale opens in the saloon of the Seabird, a salvage ship of the Carn Shipbreaking and Salvage Company. Her crew works to raise a sunken liner named Warpindi.

Divers have patched the shot holes of the liner for weeks. One diver strays from the rest and finds a strange sight on the sea bed. Big Jim Martin, the firm chief, goes down with his mate to check the tale. Five German submarines lie side by side below, as if set there by a hand.
78698-the-spark-of-skeeter-bill:
The Spark of Skeeter Bill is a tale of the west by Tuttle, the hand of past tales named on the title leaf. Its host text starts with the tale it self, no title leaf at all. Skeeter Bill Sarg stop at the door of his shack of tar sheet and lath. He look back at the street as the tale starts. Skeeter was crane like in his build, the tale says.

His long legs were a bit bent, and his thin hands hung well past his thighs. He was one of those grave look men whose faces seem on the edge of mirth or of tears. Just now he seem in two minds on some point. He rub a thin hand past his chin and spoke soft to him self. Then he went in the house.
79606-the-last-poems-of-alice-meynell:
Alice Meynell left a last set of poems, issued in London in 1923. Burns, Oates and Washbourne brought out the slim book that year. Titles run from The Poet and his Book to The Poet to the Birds. Faith, death, verse craft, and quiet fields fill the short set.

One poem hears a child's hid knowledge of death in tears at night. The Wind is Blind sets sight in earth and sea against the blind air. More pieces treat sleep, silence, Christmas night, and a bird's voice in spring. Readers who like spare, grave verse will find a calm, deep close to a life's work.
79607-alice-meynell:
Alice Meynell's poems fill one small volume in the Augustan Books of Modern Poetry, a series edited by Humbert Wolfe. The series set Donne, Herbert, and Yeats beside newer names. Ernest Benn issued the book at London, with thanks to Wilfrid Meynell for leave to print.

Early poems open the choice, with A Poet's Song of Derivations and Singers to Come. Later pieces treat childhood, parting, and a girl's letter to her own old age. San Lorenzo's Mother, The Shepherdess, and The Lady Poverty show her Catholic cast of mind. The poems are short, grave, and finely wrought, in the manner readers prized.
8662-the-camp-fire-girls-at-sunrise-hill:
Margaret Vandercook opens her Camp Fire Girls series at Sunrise Hill, where Betty Ashton sighs over a book until its leaves quiver in her hand. Chapters follow the voice that calls the girls together, their first meeting, the law of the Camp Fire, work, health. Love, and the guardian who watches over them. Pipes of peace, the rose moon, Nan, Polly, and a surprising camp visit all appear before the summer camp ends.

The novel teaches the Camp Fire ideals of the time: outdoor life, service, friendship, and self-reliance, wrapped in a gentle story of girls learning to keep step together. Suspicion, a disappearance, and a warning add mild mystery. Young readers of the 1910s loved the series for its wholesome adventure. Modern readers will find a period piece about girls' organizations, summer camps, and the virtues adults hoped camp would build.
881-lemorne-versus-huell:
Elizabeth Drew Stoddard wrote this short story, first printed in Harper's New Monthly Magazine in 1863, about two months at Newport that shaped the narrator's fate. She stays with her Aunt Eliza Huell, ordered to the seaside for her health, and finds her aunt troublesome, for ill health is not her only trial.

Stoddard writes with sharp, unsentimental prose about family, money, and the wills of strong women. The tale turns on a clash between the narrator and her aunt, and on the choices that follow. It is a fine example of Stoddard's neglected art, praised by modern readers for its psychological bite.
9322-the-nation-in-a-nutshell:
George Makepeace Towle wrote this rapid outline of American history in 1886, called The Nation in a Nutshell. Contents run from American antiquities and discovery, through colonization, independence, and the Revolution, to Washington, the War of 1812, and the Mexican War. Slavery, Civil War, and the presidents follow in turn.

Later chapters treat material progress, letters, arts, and science, with political changes to close. Towle, known for young people's histories, writes briskly for general readers, in short chapters that move fast. The book remains a handy, old-fashioned survey of the republic's first century.
9614-the-case-of-richard-meynell:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote The Case of Richard Meynell in 1911, a novel of the Church of England and its creeds. Meynell, a clergyman, faces the power of the State Church, which owns cathedrals, crowns kings, and sits in the House of Lords through its bishops. Ward's foreword asks American readers to grasp that church's vast reach, from parish schools to public life. The novel turns on what a priest may believe and still serve.

Meynell's case tests faith, law, and conscience, as church courts and public opinion press him hard. Ward writes with grave care for doctrine and for human cost. A reader gets a serious Edwardian novel of religion and reform, rich in debate and in the fate of a good man caught by his church.
9927-the-bronze-bell:
Louis Joseph Vance's 1909 adventure romance opens with destiny and a babu, a girl and a token, and a hero marooned far from home. The chapters carry him through a goblin night and a red dawn, past masks and faces, toward the court of the Maharana of Khandawar.

Vance sets his tale in India, where a bronze bell, a photograph, and a long day's journey bind love to intrigue. His hero moves between British and Indian worlds, never quite belonging to either. Readers get a colorful, fast-moving romance of the Raj, full of color, danger, and disguise.
a-boy-s-will:
Robert Frost presents his first book of poems with a contents page that glosses each piece in a line. Into My Own opens the volume: the youth is persuaded he will be more himself for having forsworn the world. Ghost House, My November Guest, A Late Walk, Stars, and Storm Fear follow, each with its small summary.

Three parts gather lyrics of New England farms, woods, and weather, written in plain speech with strict forms beneath. A Prayer in Spring, Flower-gathering, and Rose Pogonias show the young poet's eye for small natural facts carrying large feelings. The glosses, likely added for English readers, let a first audience watch a major poet finding his ground.
a-desperate-chance-or-the-wizard-tramp-s: Old Sleuth tells a thrilling narrative of a desperate chance in the Rocky Mountains. A man and a youth sit by a campfire in a narrow gulch, days of travel from civilization. Their strange circumstances and the wizard tramp's revelation drive the tale. The story belongs to the dime novel tradition of adventure and mystery.
a-romance-of-billy-goat-hill:
Alice Caldwell Hegan Rice, named on her title page as the author of Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch, opens in a Kentucky springtime, gay and irresponsible, bursting through highways and byways. George Weight illustrated the book. Billy-Goat Hill is a poor neighborhood above Louisville, and its people guard their pride as carefully as the rich guard their money.

Thirty-one chapters follow a young woman of the hill, a young doctor, a shooting the illustrations hint at, and letters burned on a hearth. Rice mixes dialect comedy with real pathos, as she did in the Cabbage Patch. The romance tests whether love and forgiveness can cross the line between the hill and the town below.
all-s-well-that-ends-well:
William Shakespeare's comedy, printed here in old spelling, follows Helena, a doctor's daughter of low rank who loves Bertram, the young Count of Rossillon. Bertram wants glory and freedom, not a wife chosen for him. When Helena cures the King of France of a fistula, the King grants her the husband she names.

Bertram accepts the marriage under force, then flees to the wars in Italy and sets hard conditions before he will own her as his wife. Helena follows in secret, aided by a widow and her daughter in Florence. The closing scene tests whether cleverness and patience can turn a forced match into a real one.
an-inquiry-into-the-permanent-causes-of-: William Playfair enquires into the permanent causes of the decline and fall of powerful and wealthy nations, carrying his survey to the present year 1805. The inquiry weighs trade, debt, war, and luxury as forces that undo great states. Playfair's economic lens gives the work a modern edge among histories of decline.
an-iron-will: Orison Swett Marden writes An Iron Will, with the assistance of Abner Bayley and portraits, from the author of Pushing to the Front. The book preaches willpower, persistence, and self-help through lives of men who held on. Marden's earnest, encouraging tone made the volume a popular manual of character.
andrew-marvell: Augustine Birrell writes a life of Andrew Marvell, the poet and member of Parliament, from his chambers in Lincoln's Inn. The study follows Marvell from Hull to Westminster, through poetry, satire, and politics. Birrell's portrait is affectionate and readable, catching the wit and integrity of a singular Englishman. The life suits readers who love wit with principle.
b09-luther-bondage-will:
On the Bondage of the Will, from 1525, is Martin Luther's answer to Erasmus, the famed Dutch scholar. Erasmus had defended free will in his Diatribe, and Luther replied at length and without mercy. The Latin work argues that the human will, in matters of salvation, is bound and cannot turn itself to God.

Grace, in Luther's account, must do the whole work, or it is not grace at all. He praised the book in later years as his finest, a rare claim from him. Edward Thomas Vaughan's 1823 English rendering carries the text here. The debate with Erasmus still anchors talks on freedom, fate, and faith.
behind-the-line-a-story-of-college-life-:
Ralph Henry Barbour published this story of college life and football in 1902, illustrated by C. M. Relyea. Barbour thanks Lorin F. Deland of Boston for the football play described in chapter fifteen, a sign of the period's new science of the game. Heroes in moleskin opens the tale; Paul changes his mind, Neil makes acquaintances and shows his mettle, and Mills arrives as head coach.

A kidnapping, the gentle art of handling punts, and an injured shoulder fill the season. Trainer Simson installs Neil in an easy chair with a pillow behind the hurt shoulder, promising meals sent over and a few days indoors. Barbour writes the school-and-college sports story at its Edwardian height: clean rivalries, loyal roommates, and the big game approached through practice, injury, and pluck.
black-heart-and-white-heart-a-zulu-idyll:
H. Rider Haggard gathered three African tales in this volume of 1900 and explained each in his author's note. The Wizard, the first, tells of a missionary faith that triumphs over savagery and death. Elissa rebuilds the Phoenician city whose ruins stand in Rhodesia and imagines its fall. The title story gives the volume its name.

Black Heart and White Heart is a Zulu idyll of the time of King Cetewayo. Its chapters open at the king's court with the trader Philip Hadden, the black heart of the piece, and move through prophecy, a hunt, and the Doom Pool to the lovers' trials. Haggard calls it a story of the courtship and final union of a pair of Zulu lovers. The book is dedicated to a child who died at Bulawayo in the war of 1896.
bracebridge-hall:
Washington Irving published Bracebridge Hall, the Sketch Book's sequel of English country life, here in the Macmillan issue of 1877 with art by R Caldecott. Irving lodges his narrator with Squire Bracebridge and his house full of kin and guests. Geoffrey Crayon's mild eye runs over all.

Sketches treat the hall, its servants, the widow and her retinue, and Ready-Money Jack. Falconry, fortune-telling, gipsies, and May Day sports fill the middle. Master Simon rules the roost in most scenes. Lovers' troubles build toward a wedding at the close. Irving sighs in advance for the old hall's fall to coaches and trade. The set fixed the dream of old England for American readers: snug, droll, and already fading.
britannica-1911-accommodation-bill: An accommodation bill is a bill of exchange. Such a bill is a written order to pay money. Someone accepts or endorses it without receiving value in return. This entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines the term in one sentence. It sends readers to the article on bills of exchange for the machinery. The point of the device is help. The acceptor lends his name and credit. That gives temporary money aid to the person accommodated. He can then raise funds on the strength of that signature.
britannica-1911-achill:
Achill, meaning Eagle, is the largest island off Ireland, lying off the west coast of county Mayo across the narrow Achill Sound. Triangular in shape, it covers fifty-seven square miles and held about five thousand people in 1901. Mountains dominate it: Slievemore in the north and Slieve Croaghaun in the west both rise above two thousand feet, and the Minaun cliffs reach eight hundred.

Poverty and scenery sit side by side. Desolate bogs that cannot be cultivated alternate with the hills, and islanders live scantily by fishing and tillage or by seasonal work in England and Scotland. Rail and a swivel bridge across the sound improved contact, and summer visitors come for the jagged coast and the views over Mayo and Galway.
britannica-1911-airy-sir-george-biddell:
Airy, Sir George Biddell, British Astronomer Royal of 1801 to 1892, receives a long article within the hosted text of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Alnwick, he came from a farming branch of an old Westmorland family. At Trinity College, Cambridge, he was quickly recognised as the leading man of his year. He graduated as senior wrangler, the top mathematics student, in 1823.

Fellow of Trinity at twenty-three, Airy held the Lucasian chair of mathematics briefly, then became Plumian professor of astronomy and director of the new Cambridge observatory. His writings ranged across mathematics and astronomy, including works on light, tides, and waves. Honours crowded his later career: fellow of the Royal Society, its president in 1871, and holder of both the Copley and Royal medals. He was five times president of the Royal Astronomical Society and was made K.C.B. in 1872.
britannica-1911-apportionment-bill:
Apportionment Bill is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an act of the United States Congress. After each census, this act fixes how many members each state shall send to the House of Representatives. The constitution set the first ratio at one member for thirty thousand of the free population. The first House thus held sixty-five members.

At that ratio the House would in time have grown too large to manage. So Congress first settles a new, higher ratio after each census, then divides the seats by it. The article prints a table that runs from the constitution through the twelfth census. It shows the population, the year of each apportionment, the ratio used, and the whole number of representatives.
britannica-1911-babington-churchill:
Churchill Babington (1821–1889) was an English classical scholar and archaeologist, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his Cambridge career. He was born at Roecliffe in Leicestershire on the eleventh of March 1821. He was educated by his father until he was seventeen. He was then placed under the tuition of Charles Wycliffe Goodwin, an orientalist.

Babington entered St John’s College, Cambridge, in 1839 as a student. He graduated in 1843, seventh in the first class of the classical tripos. In 1845 he won the Hulsean Prize for an essay. That essay treated the sway of Christianity in ending slavery in Europe. In 1846 he was elected to a fellowship and took orders in the church. He gained his master degree that year, and a doctorate in divinity in 1879. From 1848 to 1861 he served as vicar of Horningsea.
britannica-1911-bagimond-s-roll:
Bagimond's Roll grew from a tax the council of Lyons laid in 1274: a tenth of all church revenues for six years to aid the Holy Land. Pope Gregory X gave the Scottish collection to Master Boiamund de Vitia, a canon of Asti, whose valuation roll then grounded church taxation in Scotland for centuries.

Boiamund meant to rate benefices at their true value, not the old conventional figures. Scottish clergy objected, met at Perth in 1275, and sent him back to Rome to plead for the old method; the pope refused, and collection went ahead on true values. No full copy survives, but a Durham fragment lists real values beside tenths for the Lothian archdeaconry, and later Scottish tax records rest on the lost roll.
britannica-1911-bakewell:
Bakewell is a market town in Derbyshire, England. It stands on the river Wye. Derby lies 25 miles south-east. The Midland railway serves the town. Its urban district held 2,850 people in 1901. All Saints church appears in Domesday.

Tradition gives the nave to King John's building. The tower's west side is older still. Fine encaustic tiles decorate the church. Vernon and Manners monuments stand inside. A runic rood-stone stands in the churchyard. Zinc and marble are worked nearby. Arkwright planted the cotton manufacture here. A chalybeate spring serves rheumatism cases. Baths attach to that spring. A jam-cake gives the town wider fame. The Bakewell pudding is that famous cake. Haddon Hall lies two miles away. Chatsworth's great domain lies eastward.
britannica-1911-bartlett-john-russell:
John Russell Bartlett (1805–1886), an American historical and linguistic student born in Providence, Rhode Island, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Raised partly in Kingston, Canada, he worked as a dry-goods clerk, book-keeper, bank cashier, and then a New York bookseller. From 1850 to 1853 he served as the United States commissioner surveying the boundary with Mexico, though lack of funds left the work unfinished.

Writing and records fill the rest of the entry. Bartlett's Personal Narrative of 1854 reported his explorations in Texas, New Mexico, California, Sonora, and Chihuahua, with much scientific and historical material. As Rhode Island's secretary of state from 1855 to 1872 he rearranged and classified the state records. Above all he is remembered for his Dictionary of Americanisms of 1848, a pioneer work on American speech that the entry still calls valuable, if no longer complete.
britannica-1911-base-ball:
Base-ball, named from the bases and ball used in play, is the national summer sport of the United States in a very long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It was also popular in Canada and Japan. Its origin is called obscure. Some authorities derived it from the English game of rounders. Others credited Abner Doubleday with devising it at Cooperstown, New York, in 1839, a claim the entry reports rather than settles.

Growth of the organized game fills the history. Schoolboy games called One Old Cat and town-ball came first, then clubs around New York, the Knickerbocker club's first regular rules in 1845, and a national association in 1858. Professional play followed with the Cincinnati Red Stockings, the National League in 1876, and the rival American Association in 1882. Tours to England and Australia failed to plant the sport abroad, the entry notes, even as it prospered at home.
britannica-1911-basket-ball:
Basket-ball is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a game usually played indoors in the cold season. James Naismith, an instructor at the YMCA training school at Springfield, Massachusetts, invented it in 1891. His class needed winter exercise to replace football and baseball, active but not too rough indoors. First published in the school paper, the Triangle, the game quickly spread across America and to England, for girls as well as men.

Play centres on a raised basket. The court described measures sixty by forty feet, with a net on a metal ring eighteen inches wide, set ten feet high at each end above a back-board. Players strike a large inflated ball with open hands and score by throwing it into the opponents' basket. Indoor matches used teams of five in set positions, under a referee and umpire. The side with most goals in two periods won.
britannica-1911-battle-abbey-roll:
Battle Abbey Roll is the name of a supposed list of William the Conqueror's companions in arms, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. By tradition it was kept at Battle Abbey, on the field of William's win over Harold. The text is known only from versions printed in the 1500s by Leland, Holinshed, and Duchesne, and all three are called flawed and corrupt. Holinshed's is the fullest, with 629 names, several of them repeats.

Doubt runs through the whole entry. Camden and Dugdale held that monks had slipped extra names into the list over time, to their own gain. Later writers went further: Brydges called the roll “a disgusting forgery,” and Freeman a “transparent fiction.” The entry's own view is calmer. The roll, it argues, was likely a list of family surnames, made in the 1300s, to show which houses had “come over with the Conqueror.”
britannica-1911-beddoes-thomas-lovell:
Thomas Lovell Beddoes is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Beddoes was an English playwright and poet born at Clifton in 1803. His father was a well known doctor. At school he wrote verse and a novel in the manner of Fielding. He went to Oxford in 1820.

The article follows his early plays and verse tales. His play The Bride's Tragedy won a small circle of fans in 1822. He was an early admirer of Shelley and copied his lyric style. Later he worked for years on a strange drama called Death's Jest Book. He kept revising it until his death, and it came out after he died. The text also notes his study of the human body in Germany.
britannica-1911-bill:
Bill is three separate English words with distinct roots, and the 1911 Britannica article treats them in turn. The first bill is a written document, once sealed. It comes from the Latin bulla, a seal, and is kin to the word bull. The second bill is a long-handled cutting weapon, cousin to the hedging tool still used on farms. The third bill is the beak of a bird, found in no other Teutonic tongue.

Most of the article goes to the document sense in law and parliament. A bill in parliament is a draft statute that becomes an act when passed. That system dates from the reign of Henry VI. Chancery bills, bills of exchange, and other legal papers get their own sections. The weapon section closes the piece. Billmen still marched in Tudor armies, but the pike pushed the bill aside. Watchmen kept it into the 17th century.
britannica-1911-blair-atholl:
Blair Atholl is a village and parish in Perthshire, Scotland, where the rivers Tilt and Garry meet. Its name comes from a Gaelic word for a plain. The parish held 1722 people in 1901, and the village only 367. The Highland railway ran through it, north-west of Perth.

Blair Castle, seat of the duke of Atholl, dominates the account. Its oldest part dates from 1269. The entry lists its wartime guests in turn. Montrose held it in 1644, and Cromwell's men stormed it in 1653. The Young Pretender stayed in 1745, and Cumberland followed in 1746. Viscount Dundee lies buried in the church at Old Blair. Highland games each September, fine castle grounds, and the falls of Bruar nearby are also noted.
britannica-1911-blaydes-frederick-henry-:
Frederick Henry Marvell Blaydes (1818–1908) was an English clergyman and editor of Greek plays. Born at Hampton Court Green, a distant kinsman of Andrew Marvell, he went to St Peter's School, York, and Christ Church, Oxford. He won the Hertford scholarship in 1838 and held a studentship at Christ Church.

Ordained in 1842, he served as vicar of Harringworth in Northamptonshire from 1843 to 1886. Almost all his long life went to the Greek dramatists. His editions are noted for bold guesses at mending corrupt passages, some in texts that seemed sound. Works listed cover Aristophanes in full, several plays of Sophocles, and Aeschylus. Honours came from Dublin, Budapest, and Athens, and he died at Southsea in 1908.
britannica-1911-boll: Boll is a short word entry in the 1911 Britannica, covering a pod and a measure. In botany a boll is a fruit pod, above all the pod of the cotton plant. The word comes from Old English bolla, the same root as bowl, a round vessel for liquids. A second family of senses is northern and practical. In Scotland and the north of England a boll is a measure of weight for flour, set at 140 pounds. It is also a measure of capacity for grain, with 16 pecks making one boll.
britannica-1911-bridewell:
Bridewell is a London district between Fleet Street and the Thames, named for the well of St Bride, or St Bridget, that once stood close by. From Norman times a castle or tower rose there by the Fleet ditch, used at times as a lodging for English kings. Henry VIII built a grand house on the spot for the emperor Charles V in 1525.

Royal use gave way to a sterner role. In 1553 Edward VI handed the place to the city as a penitentiary, a house of correction for vagabonds and loose women. The lord mayor took formal charge in 1555. Most of the building burned in the Great Fire of 1666, a new Bridewell of 1829 was pulled down in 1864. The name lived on as a common word for any reformatory.
britannica-1911-brill:
Brill is the name of a flat-fish, given the Latin names Psetta laevis or Rhombus laevis, that stands close kin to the turbot. Telling the two apart is the heart of the short entry: the brill carries very small scales, grows smaller, lacks the bony knobs found in turbot skin, and shows a reddish colour.

On parts of the British coast the fish is plentiful. For the table it ranks high, held only a little below the turbot itself, which says much given the turbot's fame as a food fish. Those few lines, kinship, marks of difference, home waters and table worth, make up the whole notice, a compact guide to naming the fish correctly.
britannica-1911-brisbane-sir-thomas-makd:
Sir Thomas Makdougall Brisbane (1773–1860) was a Scottish soldier and astronomer born on 23 July 1773 at Brisbane House near Largs in Ayrshire. He joined the army in 1789 and served in Flanders, the West Indies and the Peninsula. Sent to North America in 1814, he was recalled when Napoleon returned from Elba but arrived too late for Waterloo.

In 1821 he became governor of New South Wales, holding the post four years. Colonial finances fell into confusion on his watch, yet he pushed the vine, sugar-cane and tobacco plant, horse breeding and land reclamation. Sent out explorers, one party finding the Brisbane river that took his name. Stars were his lasting work: an observatory at Paramatta from 1822 yielded the Brisbane Catalogue of 7385 stars, printed in 1835. Back in Scotland he observed at Makerstoun, where magnetic studies began in 1841.
britannica-1911-broken-hill:
Broken Hill is a silver-mining town in Yancowinna county, New South Wales, Australia, 925 miles directly west by north of Sydney and linked by rail to Adelaide. It held 27,518 people in 1901. Mining made it, and one nearby mine, the Proprietary, is called the richest in the world.

Gold is found with the silver, and large quantities of lead, good copper lodes, zinc and tin also occur. Treating the sulphide ores at a profit was long the district's hard problem, and the entry says it has been practically solved here. Around the mines, Broken Hill also centres one of the largest pastoral districts in Australia, and the town is the seat of the Roman Catholic bishop of Wilcannia.
britannica-1911-bull:
Bull is a word study from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica that works through the many senses of one short English word. Its first sense is the male of cattle, above all the full male of the tame ox. The article traces the word back through Middle English forms and links it to like words in German and Dutch. It also notes its use for the males of other large beasts, such as the elephant and the whale.

The entry also gives the stock market sense of the word. On the London and New York exchanges, a bull buys in hope of a rise in price. He hopes to sell again at a gain before the day he must take delivery. The bear is his reverse, a dealer who sells in hope of a fall. A side note covers bullock, the young castrated male ox raised for beef.
britannica-1911-bunker-hill:
The 1911 Britannica article on Bunker Hill recounts a famous battle. It was the first considerable battle of the American War of Independence. It was fought on June 17, 1775. The ground was a peninsula north of Boston. Bunker Hill is joined by a ridge to Breed's Hill. The fighting in fact took place on Breed's Hill.

The article tells how the Americans moved first. About 1,200 men under Prescott and Putnam dug in by night. The British general Gage sent troops under Howe to drive them off. Charlestown was burned during the attack. The British climbed the steep slope in order. The Americans held their fire until the attack closed in. Their steady volleys broke the first assault.
britannica-1911-burton-john-hill:
John Hill Burton, a Scottish writer on history who lived from 1809 to 1881, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Aberdeen, he studied there, then moved to Edinburgh and trained for the Scottish bar. His rise as a lawyer was slow, and he made up his income with writing of many kinds.

His Manual of the Law of Scotland, in 1839, brought him notice. He helped edit the works of Jeremy Bentham and ran the Scotsman for a time. His Life of David Hume in 1846 won him high standing, built on fresh papers not used before. He went on to lives of Lord Lovat and Duncan Forbes, and a full History of Scotland. That history was done by 1870 and reissued in a better form in 1873.
britannica-1911-buxton-sir-thomas-fowell:
Sir Thomas Fowell Buxton (1786-1845) was an English philanthropist, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces his path from brewing to Parliament. He was born in Essex and studied at Trinity College, Dublin, where hard work made up for a neglected start and won him a name as a speaker. In 1807 he married Hannah Gurney, sister of Elizabeth Fry. Short of means, he joined his uncles' brewery in 1808 and soon ran the whole concern.

A speech for the Spitalfields weavers in 1816 brought him notice. In 1818 he printed an able inquiry into prison discipline and was elected to Parliament for Weymouth, a seat he held until 1837. In the Commons he was known as a straight, able speaker given to good causes. The greatest of these, the entry says, was the abolition of slavery in the British colonies.
britannica-1911-cardwell:
Cardwell is a town of Queensland, in Australia. It stands on Rockingham Bay, on the north-east coast. It lies about 800 miles north-west by north of Brisbane. Its town and district held 3435 people in 1901. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives its harbour and products. It has one of the best harbours in the state. Ships can enter it easily in all weathers. Its depth ranges from 4 to 10 fathoms.

Gold and tin are among the district's minerals. Various other minerals exist there as well. Preserve and sauce factories operate in the town. Works for meat extract and tinning also run. The dugong fishery is carried on from the port. Oil is extracted from the dugong catch. Large timber forests stand in the district behind. Much cedar is exported from the harbour. The whole notice is brief, and it rests on the port's value.
britannica-1911-cardwell-edward-cardwell:
Edward Cardwell (1813–1886) was an English statesman. He later became Viscount Cardwell. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his career. He was born at Liverpool on 24 July 1813. His father was a merchant of that city. At Oxford he gained a brilliant double first-class degree. In 1842 he entered parliament as member for Clitheroe. In 1845 he became secretary to the treasury.

Cardwell supported Sir Robert Peel's free-trade policy. He went out of office with Peel. In 1847 he was elected for Liverpool, his native city. He lost that seat in 1852 over the navigation laws. Oxford city soon returned him to parliament instead. Under Lord Aberdeen he became president of the Board of Trade. In 1854 he carried a great act on shipping law. It consolidated all the existing shipping laws of the country. In 1855 he resigned with his Peelite colleagues. The article follows his later offices from there.
britannica-1911-cell:
Cell is a word article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Latin cella, a small room. In its earliest use it named a small detached house for monks. Such a cell belonged to a great abbey but stood apart from it, often in the country.

The entry explains what these outposts were for. Monks went there for a change of air and rest. Others lived there to watch over the abbey's lands and tenants. Tynemouth was a cell of St Albans, and Ashwell belonged to Westminster Abbey. The word also named the small sleeping rooms of monks within a house. Hermits and anchorites used cells of their own. The piece notes that the prison cell of later times grew from the same word. Readers watch one small word spread from cloister to gaol and beyond.
britannica-1911-chigwell:
Chigwell is a parish and residential district in Essex, England, 12 miles north-east from London, served by two branches of the Great Eastern railway. Its people numbered 2,508 in 1901, and the village lies in a branch of the Roding valley. The old church of St Mary is mainly Perpendicular and keeps a Norman south door. Fragments of Hainault Forest lie to the south and east, by the village of Chigwell Row.

Pleasant scenery draws many visitors and residents from London, and Dickens described the neighbourhood in Barnaby Rudge. The King's Head Inn, his Maypole in that novel, still stands in the village. An old grammar school founded by Archbishop Samuel Harsnett has become a minor modern public school. William Penn attended school at Chigwell from his home at Wanstead, the entry notes in closing.
britannica-1911-churchill:
Churchill, also called Missinnippi or English, is a river of Saskatchewan and Keewatin in Canada, flowing to Hudson's Bay. It rises in La Loche lake at 1,577 feet above the sea, at 56 degrees 30 minutes north and 109 degrees 30 minutes west. From there it runs east-north-east through a number of lake expansions. Its length is given as 925 miles, and Fort Churchill at its mouth is the best harbour in the southern part of Hudson's Bay.

Chief tributaries are the Beaver, 350 miles long, the Sandy and the Reindeer rivers, the last draining Reindeer Lake and Wollaston Lake. Between Frog and Methy portages the river formed part of the old voyageur route to the Peace, Athabasca and Mackenzie country. Canoes still navigate it, though many rapids break the course. The La Loche portage, twelve and a half miles long, links its head waters to the Clearwater and the Arctic drainage.
britannica-1911-clerkenwell:
Clerkenwell is a district on the north side of the city of London, within the metropolitan borough of Finsbury, named from a well of the parish clerks. Miracle plays were performed by those clerks near that spring, which existed until the middle of the 19th century. A priory founded in 1100 here grew to great wealth as the principal English house of the Knights Hospitallers of St John. Its gateway of 1504 in St John's Square survives.

That gatehouse housed the birth of the Gentleman's Magazine in 1731 and Johnson's work for it, and it now heads the St John's Ambulance Association. St Mary's nunnery stood adjoining, and the Cock Lane Ghost deception was exposed by the neighbouring church. In the 17th century Clerkenwell became a fashionable residence district. Watch making and jeweller's industries, long established here, centre the modern district the entry describes.
britannica-1911-cobb-howell:
Cobb, Howell (1815–1868) was an American political leader, born at Cherry Hill, Jefferson county, Georgia, on 7 September 1815, graduating from Franklin College in 1834. Admitted to the bar in 1836, he served as solicitor-general, then in the National House of Representatives from 1843 to 1851 and again from 1855. He was Democratic leader in the House from 1847 and speaker from 1849 to 1851. Governor of Georgia followed from 1851 to 1853, then secretary of the treasury under Buchanan.

He sided with Jackson on nullification, supported Polk in the Mexican War and ardently advocated slavery extension into the Territories, yet became a staunch Union Democrat behind the Compromise of 1850. In 1860 he ceased to be a Unionist and led in the secession movement, presiding over the convention that drafted the Confederate constitution. Made colonel in 1861 and major-general two years later, he opposed the Reconstruction Acts after the war until his death.
britannica-1911-cogers-hall:
Cogers Hall was a London tavern society built for debate. It began in 1755 at the White Bear Inn in Fleet Street. About 1850 it moved to Discussion Hall in Shoe Lane. In 1871 it settled at the Barley Mow Inn in Salisbury Square. The name is often spelled wrong. Its true root, the entry says, lies in Descartes and his Cogito, ergo sum.

That root gives the sense of a society of thinkers. Its aims joined free speech with loyalty to law. It stood for liberty of the subject and freedom of the press. It also backed the rights of mankind and sound conduct in public and private life. John Wilkes was an early president. Curran spent hours there in 1773. Dickens later ranked among its noted members.
britannica-1911-coll:
Coll, an island of the Inner Hebrides in Argyllshire in Scotland, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It held 432 people in 1901. The island lies about seven miles west of Caliach Point in Mull. It runs twelve miles from north east to south west, with a breadth that shifts from under a mile to four miles.

The rock is gneiss, and the land lies mostly flat. In the west Ben Hogh rises to 339 feet above the sea. Lakes dot the ground at points across the isle. Pasture is good and the soil yields fairly well for crops. Much dairy goods go out for sale, besides sheep and cattle. Old stone circles, duns, and the ruins of Breachacha Castle mark its past. A steamer from Oban calls at Arinagour on a set run.
britannica-1911-creighton-mandell:
Mandell Creighton, an English historian who lived from 1843 to 1901, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He later became bishop of London. Born at Carlisle, the son of a well off upholsterer, he studied at Durham and at Merton College, Oxford. He gained a fellowship at Merton in 1866.

Creighton was ordained priest in 1873 and wed a writers daughter the year before. College duties left him little time to write at first. In 1875 he took a parish on the Northumberland coast and stayed near ten years. There he planned his chief work, a history of the papacy, and wrote its first two volumes. That work won him a new chair in church history at Cambridge in 1884. At Cambridge he reshaped the history school at once. In 1886 he helped found the English Historical Review and edited it for five years.
britannica-1911-cresswell-sir-cresswell:
Cresswell, Sir Cresswell is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English judge. Born at Newcastle in 1794, of an old Northumberland family, he was educated at Charterhouse and at Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He read law at the Middle Temple and was called to the bar in 1819. On the northern circuit he soon won a leading place among his fellow lawyers.

The article follows his judicial career. When a new court for probate and divorce was set up in 1858, he was asked to be its first judge. Though rich and entitled to retire, he accepted and organized the new court. The article records a striking fact: of the very many judgments he gave, only one was ever reversed. He died suddenly in July 1863 while recovering from a knee injury.
britannica-1911-crickhowell:
Crickhowell is a market town in Wales, set on the left bank of the River Usk. The 1911 Britannica entry calls its site fine, with the river parting it from the next village. Its town count at the turn of the age was just over one thousand souls. Rail stops lay a few miles off, and a canal passed close by.

The entry says farm work is near the sole trade of the district. It takes the town name from an old British fort on a flat topped hill near by, called Table Mountain. Of the old castle, one tower stands. The town was once thought a borough by old custom, yet no record shows it held town rule, and its church mixes old styles of building.
britannica-1911-crossbill:
Crossbill is the name of a genus of finches, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains the strange bill that gives the group its name. No other birds have the horny sheaths of the bill crossing each other at a slant. The group's Latin name, Loxia, given by Gesner and kept by Linnaeus, comes from a Greek word for oblique. At first sight the bent bill looks like a deformity.

In fact, the entry argues, the bill is a tool finely fitted to the bird's life. With it the crossbill pulls seeds, its almost unchanging food, out of fir cones and fleshy fruits with the greatest ease. Townson first described how the bird uses the bill, though only in part. Yarrell in 1829 gave the full account of how the jaws and muscles force cones apart.
britannica-1911-eulenspiegel-till:
Till Eulenspiegel is a hero of German folk tales, and this 1911 Britannica entry treats both the man of legend and the chapbook that bears his name. The oldest German text still in hand was printed at Strassburg in 1515, with a second printing in 1519. It is in High German, though the first form of the tales was Low Saxon.

Till himself, a peasant's son, was said to be born at Kneitlingen in Brunswick at the turn of the fourteenth century. By tradition he died at Mölln near Lübeck in 1350. His jests and tricks were gathered, one old print claims, in 1483, and the 1515 book was not even the first High German printing. He belongs to the Low German country between Magdeburg and Hanover, cast there as the wily peasant of the tales.
britannica-1911-femerell: Femerell, properly Fumerell, is an old English term in building, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. It names the lantern in the ridge of a hall roof. Its use was to let out the smoke of the fire kindled on a central hearth below. The word comes from old French fumeraille, from the Latin fumus, meaning smoke. Short as the notice is, it fixes the term, its true spelling, its source, and the part it played in halls that had no chimney in the modern sense.
britannica-1911-football:
Football is a game between two opposing sides, played with a large inflated ball. The ball is driven either by the feet alone or by feet and hands together, according to the code being played. Games of the kind were known to many nations of antiquity. Their presence among peoples as far apart as the Maoris, Faroe Islanders, Polynesians and Eskimos points, the entry says, to how primitive and natural the pastime is. In Greece the game called episkuros resembled the modern one.

The huge article that follows traces football from folk games to fixed codes. It covers the making of the Football Association, the laws of Association football, Rugby football with its own union handbook, and American football across the Atlantic. Laws, tactics and famous matches all find a place. The hosted file opens with other articles before reaching Football.
britannica-1911-foote-andrew-hull:
Andrew Hull Foote (1806-1863), American admiral, was born at New Haven, Connecticut, on 12 September 1806. His father, Samuel Augustus Foote, was a leading lawyer and Whig politician. As a senator he moved the famous resolutions on public lands that drew Webster's reply to Hayne. The son entered the United States navy in 1822 and was commissioned lieutenant in 1830. He cruised round the world in the John Adams in 1837-1840, then served at the Philadelphia Naval Asylum and the Boston Navy Yard.

In 1849 Foote took command of the Perry and spent two years suppressing the slave trade on the African coast. In 1856, commanding the Portsmouth on the East India station, he captured the Barrier Forts near Canton. The entry follows him from October 1858 to the Civil War, and into his river campaigns of that war, where his gunboats made his name. His father's speeches and his own sea service open the story.
britannica-1911-fraser-alexander-campbel:
