Alexander Campbell Fraser (1819- ), Scottish philosopher, was born at Ardchattan in Argyllshire on 3 September 1819. He studied at Glasgow and Edinburgh, taught logic at New College from 1846 to 1856, and edited the North British Review for much of that span. In 1856 he followed Sir William Hamilton in the chair of logic and metaphysics at Edinburgh.

Fraser devoted himself to the English philosophers, above all Berkeley. He issued a collected edition of Berkeley works in 1871, enlarged in 1901, a life of Berkeley, an annotated Locke Essay, a life of Thomas Reid, and the Philosophy of Theism. His own path led from the scepticism of Hume toward faith in a spiritual will as the cause of all things. His 1904 autobiography, Biographia philosophica, traces that growth and pictures university life of his youth.
britannica-1911-gill:
Gill is a word with three chief senses, set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. First, it names the breathing organs of fishes and other water animals. The word is also used for like organs in some worms and arachnids. By likeness it is used for the wattles of a fowl and for the thin plates under fungi. Its origin is obscure, with kin words in Danish and Swedish.

Second, a gill is a liquid measure holding one fourth of a pint. That word comes through old French from a late Latin word for a wine measure. It is linked with gallon, and its first letter is soft in speech. Third, Gill is a short form of the female name Gillian, also spelled Jill.
britannica-1911-golden-bull:
Golden Bull is the general name for any charter decorated with a golden seal, or bulla. The 1911 Britannica entry explains that the honour marked the weight of the contents or the rank of giver or receiver. The custom is said to be of Byzantine origin.

In Germany a golden bull is mentioned under Henry I the Fowler, and the oldest German example, if genuine, dates from 983. The entry describes how the seal changed: first made like a solid coin, later built of two thin gold plates with a filling. From the general term the article moves to the famous particular bulls of medieval history. Chief among them is the imperial Golden Bull that fixed the election of emperors. It is a piece of diplomatics, the study of official documents, as much as of history.
britannica-1911-grinnell:
Grinnell is a city in Poweshiek county, Iowa. It stands 55 miles east by north of Des Moines. Two railways serve it, the Rock Island and the Iowa Central. Its population grew from 3,860 in 1900 to 5,036 in 1910. Carriages and gloves were among its manufactures.

The city is best known as the seat of Iowa College. That co-educational school was founded in 1847. Its founders were the Iowa Band of Congregational missionaries. The college opened at Davenport in 1848. It moved to Grinnell in 1859 and absorbed Grinnell University. The town was settled in 1854. It was chartered as a city in 1882. It took its name from founder Josiah Bushnell Grinnell. He was a clergyman and former congressman. A severe cyclone struck in 1882.
britannica-1911-herries-john-maxwell:
John Maxwell, fourth Lord Herries (about 1512-1583), was a Scottish politician, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his shifting loyalties. He was the second son of Robert Maxwell, Lord Maxwell, and in 1547 he married Agnes Herries, heir to another lordship. In 1567 he gained the title of Lord Herries himself. Early in his public life he stood with the religious reformers and was jailed by the regent, Mary of Lorraine.

From March 1566 he swung firmly to the side of Mary, queen of Scots, joining her at Dunbar after the murder of Rizzio. He led her horse at the battle of Langside and rode with her into England in May 1568. He served as one of her chief envoys at the meetings at York. Back in Scotland he kept working for her cause and was jailed by the regent Murray.
britannica-1911-hill-ambrose-powell:
Ambrose Powell Hill (1825–1865) was an American Confederate soldier, born in Culpeper county, Virginia, in 1825. He graduated from West Point in 1847, served in the Mexican and Seminole wars, and resigned in March 1861. When Virginia seceded he became colonel of a Virginian regiment.

Hill won promotion on the field of Bull Run and rose to major-general in the Peninsular campaign. He was among Lee's most successful divisional commanders, at the Seven Days, Antietam and Fredericksburg. Badly wounded at Chancellorsville in 1863, he then took command of the 3rd corps after Jackson's death. He led it at Gettysburg and before Petersburg, where he was killed on the 2nd of April 1865. Lee and Jackson, dying, both called for A. P. Hill.
britannica-1911-horne-thomas-hartwell:
Thomas Hartwell Horne (1780–1862) was an English theologian and bibliographer, born in London on the 20th of October 1780. He was schooled at Christ's Hospital, where Coleridge was an elder schoolfellow. Leaving school, he became clerk to a barrister, but his taste ran to authorship. As early as 1800 he published A Brief View of the Necessity and Truth of the Christian Revelation, followed by minor works on varied subjects.

In 1814 Horne became librarian of the Surrey Institution and issued his Introduction to the Study of Bibliography. In 1818 came the work he had long matured, the Introduction to the Critical Study of the Holy Scriptures. It won quick popularity, wide fame and an honorary degree from Aberdeen. Ordained in 1819, he held two smaller livings before becoming rector of St Edmund the King and St Nicolas Acons in London.
britannica-1911-invercargill:
Invercargill is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Invercargill is the chief town of Southland county, on the South Island of New Zealand. It lies on a deep estuary of the south coast called New River Harbour. Streams noted for trout fishing run into that harbour.

The entry presents the town as the centre of a wide grazing and farming district. Its factories included breweries, foundries, woollen mills, and timber works. The town was laid out on a rectangular plan with wide streets and a fine open reserve. Most trade, though, passed through Bluff Harbour, some seventeen miles south. From there steamers sailed for Melbourne and Hobart. Wool, preserved meat, and timber were the chief exports named.
britannica-1911-inverell: Inverell is a town of Gough county in New South Wales, Australia, on the Macintyre river, three hundred forty one miles north of Sydney. Its people numbered three thousand two hundred ninety three in nineteen o one. The town is the centre of a rich farming district growing wheat and maize. Vines are also grown, and fine wine is made. Silver, tin, and diamond mines are worked near the town. Inverell became a municipality in eighteen seventy two.
britannica-1911-james-john-angell:
John Angell James lived from 1785 to 1859 and was an English preacher of the free church kind. The 1911 Britannica life begins with his birth at Blandford in Dorset. He first served as a draper's boy at Poole for seven years. A strong call to preach then sent him to train at Gosport in 1802.

A visit to Birmingham changed the course of his life. The flock at Carr's Lane chapel asked him to stay and lead them. He settled there in 1805 and was ordained the next year. Fame came slowly at first, then crowds grew large after 1814. His books, such as The Anxious Inquirer, were read far and wide.
britannica-1911-kemble-john-mitchell:
John Mitchell Kemble (1807–1857) was an English scholar and historian, the eldest son of Charles Kemble the actor. He was born in 1807 and was schooled in part by Dr Richardson, author of a dictionary of English, and in part at the grammar school of Bury St Edmunds. In 1826 he won an exhibition to Trinity College, Cambridge, where his essays on history gained him a high name.

The bent of his studies turned to the Anglo Saxon age under the sway of the brothers Grimm, with whom he studied at Göttingen in 1831. His deep knowledge of the Teutonic tongues and his critical power showed in his Beowulf, issued from 1833 to 1837. In 1836 he published a study of the West Saxon pedigree table. His Codex Diplomaticus Aevi Saxonici, a gathering of Saxon charters, followed from 1839 to 1848. The entry presents him as the scholar who carried the new German rigour into English early history.
britannica-1911-kirkwall:
Kirkwall is a royal, municipal, and police burgh, seaport, and capital of the Orkney Islands, in the county of Orkney, Scotland. It held 3711 people in 1901. It stands at the head of a bay of the same name on the east of the island of Pomona, or Mainland. Leith lies 247 miles south and Wick 54 miles south, both by steamer.

Much of the town looks quaint and old fashioned. Its main street, nearly a mile long, is in parts so narrow that two vehicles cannot pass each other. The newer quarters are built with great regularity, and the suburbs hold several solid villas set in gardens. Kirkwall has very few manufactures. The linen trade brought in during the mid 18th century is gone, and the kelp and straw plaiting trades have met the same fate. Distilling, though, thrives.
britannica-1911-lanman-charles-rockwell:
Charles Rockwell Lanman (born 1850) was an American scholar of Sanskrit. He was born in Norwich, Connecticut, on 8 July 1850. Yale gave him his degree in 1871. He studied there under Hadley and Whitney. Germany followed from 1873 to 1876. Sanskrit and language science were his subjects there. Chairs at Johns Hopkins and Harvard came next.

A trip to India in 1889 stocked Harvard well. Sanskrit and Prakrit books and manuscripts filled the shelves. A bequest from Fitzedward Hall later enriched the store. That store made the Harvard Oriental Series possible. Lanman edited the series. His own work held a Sanskrit Reader in two volumes. A rendered Prakrit drama came in 1900. A revised Whitney version of the Atharva-Veda followed in 1905.
britannica-1911-larkhall:
Larkhall is a mining and factory town in Lanarkshire, Scotland, near the Clyde. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands by the Caledonian railway, close to the left bank of the river. Counts from nineteen o one put its people at just under twelve thousand.

The highest bridge in Scotland spans the river Avon close by the town. Brick making goes on at several coal pits that adjoin the town. Other trades cover bleach work, silk weaving, and fire clay goods. Enamel works and a health ware factory add to its trade base. The town keeps a public hall and public baths for its people.
britannica-1911-lewis-henry-carvill:
Henry Carvill Lewis, an American earth scholar born in eighteen fifty three, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Philadelphia, he took his higher degree at the town university in eighteen seventy six. He joined the earth survey of Pennsylvania in eighteen seventy nine as a free hand for three years.

That work lit his love for the study of ice age marks. He taught the lore of stones at the Philadelphia school of natural study. He then took the chair of earth study at Haverford College. He spent cold months in Heidelberg learning rock craft under a famed master. Warm months he spent tracing ice marks in north Europe and the British Isles. His report on the end ridge of the great ice sheet in two states won wide use. He died young, with his British work still raw.
britannica-1911-lewis-sir-george-cornewa:
Sir George Cornewall Lewis (1806-1863) was an English statesman and man of letters, and this 1911 Britannica entry covers his rise. He was born in London, the son of Thomas Lewis of Harpton Court, who became a poor-law commissioner and a baronet. The young Lewis was schooled at Eton and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he took a first in classics in 1828. He was called to the bar in 1831.

His first public work came in 1833, on a commission looking into the plight of poor Irish people living in the United Kingdom. A year later he joined a commission on church property and church affairs in Ireland. Out of that work came his books on local troubles in Ireland and on the Irish church question, printed in 1836. In them he attacked the tie between church and state and argued for state support of the Catholic clergy.
britannica-1911-loudoun-john-campbell:
John Campbell, first Earl of Loudoun, a Scots statesman who lived from 1598 to 1663, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Sir James Campbell of Lawers. He became Baron Loudoun through his wife Margaret, heir of the first baron. He was made an earl in May 1633, but the grant was held back for his stand against King Charles the First.

Loudoun fought the plan to force the English prayer book on Scotland in 1637. He helped frame the Covenant and took a lead part in the Glasgow assembly of 1638. He served as a Scots envoy to London more than once. A letter to the French king, found in his name, sent him to the Tower for a time. He was freed in June and soon came south again with the Scots army that crossed into England.
britannica-1911-lovell-francis-lovell:
Francis Lovell is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a viscount who backed King Richard the Third. He lived from 1454 to 1487 in England. He was the son of a baron of his house. As a young man he served in a drive to Scotland. That drive in 1480 was led by Richard of Gloucester. After Edward the Fourth died he backed Richard hard.

He was made a viscount in January 1483. Richard, still Protector, made him Chief Butler then. As king, Richard raised him to Lord Chamberlain. He helped crush a revolt led by Buckingham. A mocking rhyme of the day jailed him with two peers. He led a fleet meant to bar a Tudor landing. He fought for Richard at Bosworth and fled to refuge. A last stand at Stoke in 1487 ends his known tale.
britannica-1911-mackenzie-sir-alexander-:
Alexander Campbell Mackenzie is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mackenzie was a British composer born in Edinburgh in 1847. His father was a noted violin player and band leader. The boy was sent to Germany for music study from 1857 to 1861. He then played violin in a ducal band.

The article follows his return home and his win of a top music scholarship. He taught piano in Edinburgh and led choral groups there. Heavy work wore him out, so he moved to Florence to compose. His works there include cantatas and his first opera, given with great success in 1883. Later operas and a famed sacred work followed. Readers get a full view of a leading British composer of his day.
britannica-1911-mackenzie-sir-morell:
Sir Morell Mackenzie (1837-1892) was a British doctor born at Leytonstone in Essex on 7 July 1837. His father was a surgeon who died in 1851. The son trained at the London Hospital and gained his surgical licence in 1858. He then studied in Paris, Vienna, and Pesth. At Pesth he learned to use the new laryngoscope from J. N. Czermak.

Back in London in 1862, Mackenzie won the Jacksonian prize in 1863 for an essay on the throat. He helped found the Throat Hospital in Golden Square that same year. His skill soon made him known across Europe as a top name in throat care. In 1887 he was called to treat the crown prince of Germany.
britannica-1911-mallock-william-hurrell:
William Hurrell Mallock is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1849 at Cockington Court in Devonshire, he was an English author. He was taught at home and at Balliol College, Oxford, where he won a famed verse prize in 1872.

The article centres on the stir made by his first big book. That tale of 1877 mocked living men of note in thin disguise. His sharp logic won him a wide hearing in later years. In books on faith he held that firm dogma must ground all religion. He held that faith cannot rest on the facts of science alone. In books on wealth he struck at the plans of radicals and socialists. More tales and a book of poems round out the list of his works.
britannica-1911-maple-sir-john-blundell:
John Blundell Maple, an English business magnate who lived from 1845 to 1903, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in March 1845, he was the son of a man with a small furniture shop in Tottenham Court Road, London. The business began to grow about the time the son entered it. Practical control soon passed to the younger Maple.

Under him the firm reached vast size and became a limited company in 1890, with Maple as chairman. He entered Parliament in 1887 as a Conservative for Dulwich. He was knighted in 1892 and made a baronet in 1897. He owned a large stud of race horses and won many key races. His gifts included a hospital and the rebuilding of a London hospital at great cost.
britannica-1911-mariazell:
Mariazell is a village of Austria in Styria, north of Graz city. Its shrine entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits in the Salza valley amid the north Styrian Alps range. Counts from nineteen hundred put its people at just under fifteen hundred.

The village fame rests wholly on its shrine, the most sought in Austria. About two hundred thousand pilgrims visit the shrine each year in faith. A wonder working image of the Virgin, carved in lime wood, draws them. That image, eighteen inches high, was given to the place in eleven fifty seven. A chapel rich with silver gifts now holds the famed image.
britannica-1911-mason-lowell:
Lowell Mason (1792–1872) was an American musician, born at Medfield, Massachusetts. For some years he led a life of trade, but he kept up the study of music all the while. In 1821 the Handel and Haydn Society at Boston put out a set of church music that he had formed. As a fruit of that work, he moved to Boston in 1827. There he became head of that society and then set up the Boston Academy of Music in 1832.

Mason put out school books on music that sold well. He was a first mover in the teaching of music in the public schools, a plan taken up in 1838. In 1855 New York University gave him the degree of doctor of music. He died at Orange, New Jersey, on 11 August 1872.
britannica-1911-mccook-alexander-mcdowel:
Alexander McDowell McCook, who lived from 1831 to 1903, was an American soldier in a 1911 Britannica life. He was born in Ohio and finished at the national military academy in 1852. Frontier service against Apache and Ute groups in New Mexico came next. He then taught infantry tactics at the academy before the Civil War.

In 1861 he led the First Ohio Volunteers and fought at the first Bull Run. Commands in Kentucky, Tennessee, and Mississippi followed in quick order. He rose to major general of volunteers by July 1862. After Chickamauga he saw no more front service in the war, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-mccormick-cyrus-hall:
Cyrus Hall McCormick, American maker of grain harvesting machines, was born at Walnut Grove on 15 February 1809 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father was a farmer who built many labour saving tools. That father tried and failed for years to make a good grain cutting machine. Cyrus took up the task at age twenty two.

His machine worked in the late harvest of 1831 and gained a patent in 1834. More gains made the McCormick reaper a full success. In 1847 he moved to Chicago and built large works for his farm machines. Prizes and medals poured in for the reaper. France made him a member of its Academy of Sciences for his service to farming.
britannica-1911-merrill:
Merrill, a city in Wisconsin, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the seat of Lincoln county, on both banks of the Wisconsin river. The entry gives it 8,689 people in the census of 1910. It stands about 1,270 feet above the sea and has a fresh, bracing climate.

Trout and game, deer among them, abound in the woods nearby. Grandfather Falls and the Delles of the Prairie river give both beauty and water power. The chief public buildings named are the county court house, a free library, a high school, and a hospital. Merrill is a big market for hardwood lumber, and its mills make lumber, paper, and pulp. It was settled in 1875 and chartered as a city in 1883.
britannica-1911-motherwell:
Motherwell, a town in Lanarkshire, Scotland, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It stands near the right bank of the Clyde. The Caledonian railway links it to Glasgow, to the south-east. It takes its name from an old well dedicated to the Virgin. Its people grew from 900 in 1851 to 30,418 in 1901.

That swift growth came from the coal and iron mines nearby. The town has large iron and steel works. Bridge-building is a special trade there. Boilers, steam-cranes, and ironmongers' ware are also made. Brick, tile, and fireclay works add to the list. The public buildings include a town hall, a theatre, and a hospital. A park was given to mark Queen Victoria's Jubilee. The article shows a small place turned, in fifty years, into an iron town.
britannica-1911-o-donnell:
O'Donnell was the name of a great Irish family, lords of Tyrconnel in early times. Their story fills an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The family were the chief rivals of the O'Neills in Ulster. Both houses traced their line back to Niall of the Nine Hostages, king of Ireland in the early fifth century.

Tyrconnel, the land named for their clan, took in most of the modern county of Donegal. Since it lay next to the lands of the O'Neills of Tyrone, the family tale is mostly one of tribal war. The first chief of note was Goffraidh, made head of the clan in 1248. He beat Brian O'Neill in 1252 and drove the English from north Connaught in 1257, though he was hurt in single combat.
britannica-1911-o-neill:
O'Neill is the name of a great Irish family, traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The line claims descent from Niall, a king of Ireland of the fifth century. Tales call him Niall of the Nine Hostages and credit him with raids on Britain and Gaul. Those tales come from books penned long after his time.

Niall had fourteen sons, and the later O'Neills spring from one of them, Eoghan. His kin spread over Ireland and split into north and south branches. Near all the high kings of Ireland from the fifth to the twelfth century came from those two branches. A grandson of Eoghan is said to have been the first Christian king of the land. The entry tells how he gave the Stone of Destiny to the king of Dalriada in Scotland.
britannica-1911-pall:
Pall, a cloth word of church and grave, is unfolded in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. All its senses trace to the Latin pallium, a piece of cloth. Such cloth could serve as a garb or as a cover. As a garb the word lives in church dress and in crowning robes. The shield bearing called a pall takes a Y shape from that garb.

As a cover the word names more things of daily rite. It can be an altar front cloth or a chalice veil. Most know it as the dark drape laid on a coffin. London guilds kept rich state palls for the funerals of members. A verb to pall, meaning to go stale, comes from a far root.
britannica-1911-pall-mall:
Pall-Mall is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on an old English game from France. The French name joins their words for ball and mallet. King James the First praised it as fit sport for Prince Henry. It came into England in the reign of Charles the First, or a bit before.

An old gloss from 1670 tells how the game was played. A round bowl was struck with a mallet through a high iron arch. The arch stood at each end of a long alley. The man who did it in the fewest blows won the game. The alley by St James ran some 800 yards. A mallet and balls found in 1845 are now in the British Museum.
britannica-1911-peekskill:
Peekskill is a village of Westchester county in New York, on the east bank of the Hudson. It lies about forty one miles north of New York City. Its people numbered fifteen thousand two hundred forty five in nineteen ten. Rail lines and Hudson steamboats, for freight and travellers, serve the village. Many New York business men make their homes in Peekskill.

The village holds a military academy founded in eighteen thirty three. A girls school, a public library, a hospital, and rest homes also stand there. Near the village lies the state military camp for the national guard. Peekskill has many factories, whose output rose sharply in five years. The site was settled early in the eighteenth century by Dutch traders. In the War of Independence it was a key outpost of the American army.
britannica-1911-phillips-wendell:
Wendell Phillips (1811–1884) was an American orator and reformer, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his father. He was born in Boston on the twenty ninth of November 1811. His father, John Phillips, was a man of wealth and standing. The father became the first mayor of Boston in 1822.

Phillips attended the public Latin school of Boston as a boy. He entered Harvard College before he was sixteen years old. He graduated in 1831, in the same class as the historian Motley. He took his law degree at Harvard in 1834 and joined the Boston bar. Soon after, he came under the sway of the anti slavery movement. In 1835 he saw a mob attack William Lloyd Garrison in the streets of Boston.
britannica-1911-poll:
Poll is a word article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a term whose first sense is the head. From that sense of one head, or one unit, flow most of its uses. A poll tax counts heads, and a challenge to the polls counts jurors. The best-known uses are tied to voting at elections.

To poll is to vote, or to win a set number of votes. The poll can mean the voting, the count of votes, or the time when voting runs. The verb also means to clip or cut back the top of a thing. Hence polled cattle have no horns, and a deed poll has smooth edges. A tree cut back to force short, bushy growth is a pollard. At Cambridge, a pass degree is called a poll degree.
britannica-1911-quill:
Quill is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a word with many uses. At its core, a quill is the bare hard tube of a feather. The word also names the large flight feathers of a bird. Goose, swan, and crow feathers of that kind made quill pens. The root of the word is not clear. Like words in German and French give some hints.

The term spread well past pens and feathers. Old stringed instruments were plucked with a bit of quill. Keys in the harpsichord and spinet struck strings the same way. To quill cloth is to fold it in narrow pleats. Such pleated work is called quilling. A sword's cross guard arms also took a form of the name. The entry shows how one word grew by shape and use.
britannica-1911-ralph-of-coggeshall:
Ralph of Coggeshall, an English chronicler who died after 1227, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was first a monk, then the sixth abbot of Coggeshall. That Essex house belonged to the Cistercian order. He held the abbacy from 1207 to 1218.

Ralph himself tells us these facts, the article notes. His giving up of the abbacy went against the wishes of the brethren. Poor health was the cause. He took up and carried on a Chronicon Anglicanum owned by his house. The old work began at 1066, and his own share began at 1187. He hoped to reach the year 1227. His own copy in his hand breaks off three years short of that mark. The text says he made no claim to be a literary artist. Where a written source lay before him, he copied even its wording.
britannica-1911-rawtenstall: Rawtenstall, a municipal borough in Lancashire, England, is noted in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. In nineteen oh one it had over thirty one thousand folk. The town is a modern creation of the cotton industry. At the start of the last century it was a secluded village in a wild hilly district. Cotton and wool works now employ most of its folk. Stone quarries lie in the area nearby. The town was incorporated in eighteen ninety one, run by a mayor and council.
britannica-1911-rives-william-cabell:
William Cabell Rives, an American political leader who lived from 1793 to 1868, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in Nelson County, Virginia, on May 4, 1793. He went to two colleges, was called to the bar, and practiced law in Virginia. He served in the state house and then in the federal House.

From 1829 to 1832 Rives was minister to France, and he served two spans in the Senate. He was sent to France once more from 1849 to 1853. In 1861 he went to the Peace Conference and fought secession, yet stood by his state when it left. His chief book was a life of James Madison in three volumes, left unfinished at his death.
britannica-1911-rock-hill:
Rock Hill is a city of York county, South Carolina, and this 1911 Britannica entry records its quick growth and its trades. It lies about 670 feet above the sea, north of Columbia, and is served by two lines of the Southern railway. Its people grew from 2,744 in 1890 to 5,485 in 1900 and 7,216 in 1910. Among its buildings are a federal building and a Carnegie library.

The city also holds the Winthrop Normal and Industrial College, a state school for white girls opened in 1894. Cotton is the chief product of the country round it. The Catawba river, five miles away, gives water power, and a large plant turns it into electricity for the city's factories. Rock Hill was incorporated as a village in 1870 and chartered as a city in 1892.
britannica-1911-roll:
Roll, a word for a thing wound up in a round form, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It comes through Old French from a Latin word for a small wheel. At first it named a sheet of parchment or paper rolled up for safe keeping. From that use it came to mean any formal record, list, or register kept in that form.

The entry traces that sense into English law and public life. The Rolls was the house where the records of the Chancery Court were kept. Its keeper, the Master of the Rolls, became a high judge. A roll of solicitors lists those fit to practise, and to strike a name off means removal by the court. The word also fits cloth, tobacco, a small loaf, and a scroll shaped moulding in building.
britannica-1911-rolling-mill:
Rolling-mill is the subject of a trade article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term covers several kinds of machines that make the shaped bars of wrought iron and steel. Boiler makers, platers, bridge builders, and builders in general need those shapes for their work. The entry sets the two metals side by side at the start.

The article says the making of wrought iron had shrunk for many years while the making of steel grew. The plant for both rests on the same basic plan, but steel changed the practice by the sheer size of its sections. Iron sections are small and often built up by piling small bits of worked metal. Steel sections, however large, are rolled from solid cast blocks. The work starts near a white heat and goes on until the metal cools to a low red.
britannica-1911-scafell:
Scafell, a mount of Cumberland in England in the Lake District, is mapped in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name is used in strict use for the south point of a range. That point stands three thousand one hundred and sixty two feet high. Scafell Pike stands apart from it by a steep tight ridge.

The Pike is the top point in all England at three thousand two hundred and ten feet. The ridge runs north east to a third peak. That peak drops sheer to a flat shelf where a small lake lies. A path for walkers crosses that shelf between two passes. West of the Pike a lesser height juts out like a fort wall. The steep flank is scored with a deep gill and sweeps down to Wasdale.
britannica-1911-scott-william-bell:
William Bell Scott (1811-1890) was a British poet and artist, and his career is told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Edinburgh, son of the engraver Robert Scott and brother of the painter David Scott, he studied art and helped his father. In 1837 he went to London.

The entry notes his post from 1844 as master of the government school of design at Newcastle, held for twenty years, where he did good work in art teaching. It praises his wall paintings at Wallington Hall, eight large scenes of Border history, and a like series for Penhill Castle. His verse, it says, recalls Blake and Shelley and bears the mark of his friend Rossetti.
britannica-1911-scull:
Scull is a boating article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A scull is a light oar, its blade more hollowed than a common racing oar. Its shaft is shorter, so a rower can hold one in each hand. Sculling is the art of driving a boat with a pair of these oars.

The word also covers a second method. A single scull worked over the stern can drive a boat on its own. The blade sweeps from side to side, turning at each stroke, while the sculler stands. The entry notes that paired sculling follows the same rules as rowing. It then turns to racing and names the great prizes. The Wingfield Sculls, the English amateur championship, began in 1830. The Diamond Challenge Sculls at Henley followed in 1844. Readers get both the technique and the trophies of the sport.
britannica-1911-sheathbill:
Sheathbill, a bird of the far south seas, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Pennant gave it the name in 1781, from the horny case that sheathes the base of its bill. It first came to notice on New Year Island, off Staten Land. Captain Cook anchored there on New Year's Eve in 1774 and met the bird on rocky shores.

Days later Cook found it again at South Georgia, and in 1776 at the Kerguelen islands. For long, the Kerguelen bird was thought to be the same kind as that of the western ocean. Later study split them as distinct kinds. Naturalists placed the bird in a new genus, and Forster in 1788 named it Chionis, for its snowy plumage. It is about the size of a pigeon, pure white, with a bill yellow at the base and pale pink at the tip.
britannica-1911-smell:
Smell is a science article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on the sense of smell. The sense is stirred when matter in a fine state touches the smelling region of the nose. It is spread wide through the animal kingdom. Low animals, above all those that breathe in water, learn of scented matter near them with no touch, sight or hearing. For them smell has been well named taste at a distance. Scented bits drift through the water to the sense organ, much as food bits touch the tongue.

In higher animals that breathe air, the two senses part ways. The article weighs whether smell starts from a chemical or a physical act, and leaves the question open. The strength of a smell turns on how much of that skin is touched. No sound sorting of smells into classes can yet be made.
britannica-1911-southwell:
Southwell is a cathedral city in Nottinghamshire in England. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it 16 miles north east of Nottingham by rail. Its count in 1901 was 3,161 souls in the town. The minster church of St Mary became a cathedral in 1884. That year a new see was founded with its seat at Southwell.

The see takes in most of Nottinghamshire and of Derbyshire too. Small parts of three more counties fall under its rule as well. The first church there is laid to Paulinus in the 600s. A new church rose in 960 after Northmen had laid waste the old. Work on the present church began in the reign of Henry the First.
britannica-1911-squall:
Squall is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a term from the study of winds. It names any sudden rise of wind to gale force strength. A squall is most times short, but not as brief as a gust. A gust may pass in less than a minute's span.

A squall may hold a string of gusts with lulls between them. It lasts with shifting force for some minutes at the least. The entry sets the two apart by the trace of a wind gauge. That trace forms a ribbon whose breadth shows the wind's mean force. A wide ribbon means a gusty wind at that place. Work by Doctor Simpson at Scilly and Holyhead is cited for its laws.
britannica-1911-squill:
Squill is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a bulb used as a drug. The plant's root bulb comes from lands by the Mediterranean Sea. It is kin to the lily, and garden kinds share the name. The bulbs are round, large, and can weigh more than four pounds.

Men pick the bulbs in August, when the plant has no leaves. The dry outer skins are stripped off, and the flesh is cut and dried in the sun. Most of the drug came to Britain from Malta, the entry says. Greek doctors of old used it with vinegar and honey. The text also names its chief harsh parts, first well studied by Merck in 1878.
britannica-1911-st-austell:
Saint Austell, a market town in Cornwall, England, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It lies north east of Truro on the Great Western line. In nineteen oh one its urban district had over three thousand folk. The town sits on a steep slope two miles inland from its bay.

High ground to the north tops a thousand feet at Hensbarrow Downs. The church of the Holy Trinity has rich ornament, rare in the county. The town is the hub of a china clay district. About four hundred thousand tons are shipped each year to potteries and cloth works. Clay became a big trade about seventeen sixty three. Tin and copper mines came first in some pits.
britannica-1911-still: Still is a word with two roots, set out in a brief word entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The first sense means motionless or noiseless. Used of wines, it means they have little or no fizz. The second sense comes from a clipped form of distil. In that sense a still is gear for heating a liquid and catching its vapour.
britannica-1911-stuart-john-m-douall:
John M'Douall Stuart, a South Australian explorer who lived from 1818 to 1866, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Dysart, in Fifeshire, Scotland. He reached the colony about 1839. He went with Captain Sturt's expedition of 1844 to 1845 as draughtsman.

Between 1858 and 1862 he made six expeditions into the interior. The last of them brought him to the Indian Ocean at Van Diemen's Gulf. He reached that shore in July 1862, at the mouth of the Adelaide River. The article is careful with the honour of the first crossing. That, it says, belongs to Burke and Wills. They reached the Gulf of Carpentaria in February 1861. Stuart came home to Adelaide worn out and broken in health. He never recovered from the hardships of the great trek.
britannica-1911-sturgis-russell:
Russell Sturgis (1836–1909) was an American architect and art critic, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his works. He was born in Baltimore county, Maryland, on the sixteenth of October 1836. He graduated from the Free Academy in New York in 1856. He studied architecture under Leopold Eidlitz, then for two years in Munich.

Sturgis came back to the United States in 1862 and began to build. He designed the Yale University chapel and two Yale dormitories. The Flower Hospital and a bank at Albany also came from his hand. After 1880 he did fairly little work as an architect. He spent four years in Europe, then served for a time in New York city government. He also led a body of architects, as the entry goes on to note.
britannica-1911-tait-archibald-campbell:
Archibald Campbell Tait is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tait was an Anglican churchman who became archbishop of Canterbury. He was born at Edinburgh in 1811 to Presbyterian parents. Early on he turned toward the Scottish Episcopal Church.

He entered Balliol College, Oxford, in 1830 and was confirmed in his first year. He won a scholarship and took a first-class degree in 1833. He became a fellow and tutor of Balliol and was ordained priest in 1838. At twenty-six he was the senior and most trusted of the college tutors. That hard school of experience served him later on the first Oxford University Commission. The entry also notes that he never shared the aims of the Tractarian movement. Readers meet a future primate formed by tutoring and reform.
britannica-1911-terrell:
Terrell is a city in Kaufman county, Texas, some thirty-two miles east of Dallas. Its people grew from 2,988 in 1890 to 6,330 in 1900 and 7,050 in 1910. Two rail lines serve the city, the Texas and Pacific and the Texas Midland. The Texas Midland has its shops and main offices there. The city lies in a rich farming region.

Terrell is the seat of Wesley College, a school of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South. The North Texas Hospital for the Insane, opened in 1885, also stands there. The city has a Carnegie library. It runs a cotton press and cotton gins, along with varied small works. The city was founded in 1872 and chartered in 1874. It was named in honour of Robert A. Terrell, an early settler.
britannica-1911-tortoiseshell:
Tortoiseshell is the shell material of the hawksbill turtle, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It consists of the outer plates that cover the bony shell of that turtle, the smallest of the sea turtles. The plates of the back are 13 in number in the shell. Five of them hold the centre, flanked by four on each side in rows.

Those plates overlap each other by one third of their whole size as they lie. Hence they grow to a large size, up to 8 by 13 inches and 9 ounces in weight. The plates are of horny matter, but harder, more brittle, and less fibrous than common horn. Their value rests on their rich mottled colours, a warm clear yellow dashed with rich brown, and on the high polish they take and keep.
britannica-1911-tread-mill:
Tread mill is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a penal device brought in by William Cubitt in 1818. Cubitt meant it as a means of employing prisoners usefully. It was a large hollow wooden cylinder on an iron frame. Round its surface ran a series of steps, set a short space apart.

The prisoner, holding hand rails on both sides, trod on the steps in turn. His weight made the mill revolve, forcing him to keep stepping. In a harsher use, weights supplied the resistance and the toil was useless. Later the mill was put to grinding corn, pumping water, and other prison work. A brake set its speed. Prisoners worked six hours a day in spells, climbing a vast height in the course of the day.
britannica-1911-twill:
Twill is a woven cloth known by its diagonal lines, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains the weave in a short entry. The name links to the word two. In twill, the weft thread does not pass in plain turn as in plain weaving. It goes over one thread and under two or more, by the kind of twill.

That path of the weft sets up a run of diagonal lines across the cloth. In the normal type the diagonal crosses from selvage to selvage at an angle of forty five degrees. Wide variation is still possible. The diagonal may run from left to right or the other way. Twills can be stout and hard wearing cloths. They are made in silk, woollen, and cotton goods alike.
britannica-1911-vill:
Vill is an old law word for a village or township. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ties it to the Latin villa. In Latin records it stood for the Anglo-Saxon tun. Stubbs called the township the unit of the state's machinery. Vill and township came to be used as the same term in English law. That use lasted until parishes took on civil work under the poor laws.

The word's path runs through many shifts of sense. In classic Latin, villa meant a country house or farm. In late Latin it came to mean a village. A law writer of Edward the First's time split it off from a lone house and from a manor. A manor might hold one vill or more. In Frankish lands the word named royal seats too. From villa came the French ville, and the English words villein and village.
britannica-1911-walsall:
Walsall, a market town in Staffordshire, England, on the north edge of the Black Country, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stood on a small stream of the Tame, served by two rail lines and by canals. Its people grew from about seventy one thousand in 1891 to about eighty six thousand in 1901.

Though old in root, the town looked modern, the entry says. Its core stands high on a ridge, topped by Saint Matthew's church, part of which dates from the fourteen hundreds. A new council house and town hall were finished in 1905. The town also had two theatres, a free library and museum, and a school of science and art. Queen Mary's Schools, founded in 1554, are noted for two famed old boys, Bishop John Hough and Lord Chancellor Somers.
britannica-1911-well:
Well is a 1911 Britannica article on an artificial boring in the earth through which water is drawn. Two classes of well are set apart. Shallow, or ordinary, wells are sunk through a water-bearing stratum. They go down until a stratum that bars water is reached.

Deep and Artesian wells form the second class. They are named from Artois in France. They pass through a barring stratum into a water-bearing one below. Ordinary wells supply water very cheaply. But impurities readily reach them, so the risk of contamination is great. The same does not apply to deep wells. Their water is usually free from organic impurities. In both kinds, water requires pumping to the surface. Health and water readers get a plain split between cheap risk and safer depth.
britannica-1911-whistler-james-abbott-mc:
James Abbott McNeill Whistler (1834-1903) was an American artist, born at Lowell, Massachusetts, on the 10th of July 1834. This 1911 Britannica article first notes him in Europe in 1857, when he had been a student in Paris in the studio of Gleyre. His first etchings, known as the French Set, brought him to the notice of art lovers.

Whistler came to London in 1859 and turned to the Thames below bridge, with its old riverside houses and craft. His set of sixteen Thames etchings, made chiefly in that year, showed a new view of the river. The article praises his sure drawing and lively line in rendering barges, clippers, warehouses, and wharves. It also notes that prints from each plate were few, so their reach was always less than their fame.
britannica-1911-windmill:
Windmill, a machine that puts the energy of the wind to useful work, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Windmills were in use by the twelfth century at the latest, the entry says. They are still widely used in Holland to drain the polders and grind trass. In America they serve for pumping and for driving farm machinery.

Against stronger and more tractable motors, windmills stay serviceable where fuel is scarce and work can wait. A windmill is never a very powerful or efficient motor, and its work is variable. In a good position it will run on average eight hours out of twenty four, the entry finds. For small scale pumping the uneven action matters least, since a tank stores the water. For driving dynamos it is least suited, because its speed varies so much from hour to hour.
bylow-hill:
George Washington Cable wrote a novel of Bylow Hill, put out by Scribner in 1902. F. C. Yohn drew the plates. Ruth and Godfrey open the chapter list. Isabel comes next, then Arthur and Leonard. A tally of shares — and bring down the rest — gives the fourth its odd name.

Sky and pool, the public eye, and the hour's strike fill the mid-run. Five short minutes, a young year's smile, and a storm that gathers again turn the tale. Has it come to this, a snuffed lantern, and a baby mark the dark heart. Thin ice breaks in the fifteenth chapter. A still hunt doubled, a return doubled, and eve close the heads in view. Hill homes, kin strife, and love's tests form the stock the heads lay out.
camp-david-accords-1978-full:
Egypt and Israel signed the Camp David Accords in 1978 after talks at the American presidential retreat in Maryland. President Anwar Sadat of Egypt and Prime Minister Menachem Begin of Israel reached the deal with President Jimmy Carter mediating. The hosted text gives the two framework agreements in full, with their preamble on peace in the Middle East.

One framework sets a basis for settling the wider Arab-Israeli conflict, resting on United Nations Security Council Resolution 242. It sketches self-rule steps for the West Bank and Gaza. The second framework lays out a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel, with Israel leaving the Sinai. That treaty followed in 1979, the first between Israel and an Arab state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-st-g:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Gall describes one of Europe's chief Benedictine abbeys, in the Swiss canton of St. Gall, thirty miles south-east of Constance. Founded about 613 and named for Gallus, an Irishman and disciple of St. Columbanus, it grew from the cell where Gallus remained in Switzerland after his master went to Italy.

A chapel rose over Gallus' cell, and Charles Martel placed the priest Othmar there as custodian of the relics. Under Othmar a monastery was built, favoured by Charles Martel and Pepin, his son, who count with Othmar as chief founders. Othmar replaced Columbanus' rule with Benedict's and founded St. Gall's famous schools, where arts, letters and sciences flourished and manuscript copying built the great library.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-knoll:
Albert Knoll was a Capuchin dogmatic theologian, a teacher of the Church's formal doctrines, born at Bruneck in northern Tyrol in 1796 and dead at Bozen in 1863. Ordained a priest in November 1818, he taught dogmatic theology at the Capuchin house in Meran for twenty-four years. Elected to the senior office of definitor general in 1847, he went to Rome and returned to Bozen in 1853 when his term ended.

While at Rome, Knoll wrote his General and Fundamental Dogmatic Theology, published at Innsbruck in 1852, and followed it with a six-volume Theoretical Dogmatic and Polemical Theology, completed in 1859. The entry praises his brief, exact accounts of ancient and modern heresies and his apt quotations from the Church Fathers. It also praises his handling of grace, free will, and original sin. A two-volume abridgement appeared at Turin in 1868.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-mac:
Alexander Macdonell was the first Bishop of Kingston in Ontario, Canada, born at Inchlaggan in Glengarry, Scotland, in July 1760 and dead at Dumfries in January 1840. Educated at Bourblach and at the Scots Colleges in Paris and Valladolid, he was ordained a priest at Valladolid in February 1787. After five years ministering in the Braes of Lochaber, he saw his people evicted in 1792 as their lands became sheep farms.

Macdonell boldly offered to raise his clansmen as a Catholic regiment. The Glengarry Fencible Regiment was formed in 1794, with Macdonell as its chaplain, the first Catholic chaplain in the British Army since the Reformation. He then spent two years negotiating his people's emigration to Canada against powerful opposition, and triumphed. In 1819 he was appointed vicar apostolic of Upper Canada and consecrated Bishop of Rhosina, later becoming the first Bishop of Kingston.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-bell:
The altar bell sits on the credence or elsewhere on the epistle side. The rubrics ring it only at the Sanctus and the elevation of both Species, inviting adoration. This holds even in private chapels. It may also ring at the Domine non sum dignus, before Communion, and at other times by local custom.

When the Blessed Sacrament is exposed, the bell may or may not ring at high Mass. The same holds for a low Mass replacing high Mass at exposition. It does not ring at low Masses in such a church. A low sacristy-door bell signal may sound before Mass. It does not ring at high Mass at another altar than the exposition altar. Nor does it ring at low Masses during a public celebration or choir office nearby. From Maundy Thursday's Gloria to Holy Saturday's Gloria it does not ring. The clapper, or crotalus, signals instead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelus-bell:
The Angelus bell accompanied the triple Hail Mary recited in the evening, the origin of the modern Angelus. This bell seemingly belonged to Complin, said at sundown in theory, though in practice it followed Vespers closely. In all but a few cases, the Ave bell was distinct from curfew: the former sounded at the end of Complin, the latter signalled day's close and bed-time.

In places in England and France the curfew bell is still rung, prolonged for a hundred strokes or more. Many bells bear Ave inscriptions: Ave Maria, or, on a Helfta bell of 1234, the full Ave Maria, gratia plena, Dominus tecum. In England Angelus bells were very often dedicated to Saint Gabriel. Early rules show the triple pattern. Wells statutes of 1331 direct three strokes struck three times shortly before curfew. At Lerida in 1308 the bishop directed three peals with intervals after Complin as night fell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arthur-bell:
Arthur Bell, alias Francis, a Franciscan friar and English martyr, was born at Temple-Broughton near Worcester on 13 January 1590 and died at London on 11 December 1643. At eight he lost his father, and his mother entrusted him to her brother Francis Daniel, a wealthy, learned, and pious man. He sent Bell at twenty-four to the English school at St. Omer, whence he went to Spain to finish his studies.

Ordained priest, he took the Franciscan habit at Segovia on 8 August 1618, and after his novitiate was called from Spain to help restore the English province. He was among the earliest members of the Franciscan house at Douai, where he served as guardian and professor of Hebrew. In 1632 he went to Scotland as provincial of the Franciscan province there, but restoration failed, and in 1637 he returned to England, labouring until his arrest in November 1643.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-edwar:
Blessed Edward Powell, priest and martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Wales about 1478, he took his M.A. at Oxford, became Fellow of Oriel in 1495, and doctor of divinity in 1506, styled a most learned man by the university. Rector of Bleadon and holder of many prebends, he was a court preacher in Henry VIII's favour until ordered to answer Luther.

Favour faded when he denounced Henry's marriage to Anne Boleyn and disparaged Latimer at Bristol. Discharged from Salisbury's proctorship in 1534, he was attainted with John Fisher for refusing the oath of succession and jailed in the Tower. Sentence waited until 30 July 1540, when he was hanged, drawn, and quartered at Smithfield beside Protestants burned as heretics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bulla-aurea-g:
The Golden Bull, a basic law of the Holy Roman Empire, takes its name from the golden case holding its seal. Emperor Charles IV signed it at Nuremberg in January 1356 and revised it at Metz that November. It fixed the empire's electoral constitution, ordaining that each emperor be chosen by election, with votes vested in seven electoral princes.

Three church electors, the Archbishops of Mainz, Trier, and Cologne, stood beside four secular electors: Bohemia's king, the Rhine's Count Palatine, Saxony's duke, and Brandenburg's margrave. The Bull defined the electors' joint and separate powers in vacancy and in reign, granting them sovereign rights once reserved to the king. That transfer slowly freed them from the imperial head. It also guarded the empire's peace and curbed the rising free cities, confirming rights already grown by custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-corde:
Charles Cordell was an English missionary priest born in 1720 and dead at Newcastle-on-Tyne in 1791. His parents, Charles Cordell and Hannah Darrell, came of the Scotney Castle and Calehill families in Kent. He was schooled at Dame Alice's School, Fernyhalgh, then at Douai, where he began philosophy in 1739. Ordained a priest, he left college for England in June 1748. He served missions at Arundel, in Yorkshire at Rounday, on the Isle of Man, and finally at Newcastle from 1765 until his death.

In 1778 Saint-Omer's English college offered him its presidency, but he would not accept it. Scholarly and fond of books, he preached with some distinction. He stayed a staunch Jacobite in politics. He published many translations, from the Divine Office for the Laity to lives and letters of Clement XIV. He also wrote one original pamphlet answering a candid sketch of that pope's life and government.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-russe:
An entry on Charles Russell, Baron Russell of Killowen, the Irish lawyer who became the first Catholic Lord Chief Justice of England for centuries. Born at Newry in 1832, he qualified as a solicitor in 1854, then as a barrister in London in 1859, and built a practice famed for cross-examination, business sense, and honesty. His fees rose from thousands a year in the 1860s to 150,000 dollars in his last year of practice.

Russell entered Parliament as a Liberal, served as attorney-general under Gladstone, and championed Home Rule, self-government for Ireland. At the Parnell Commission trial of 1888 he exposed the Times forgeries and gave an eight-day speech for the defence. Knighted after the Bering Sea arbitration of 1893, he became a Lord of Appeal and then Lord Chief Justice in 1894. He died in London in 1900, widely mourned across parties and faiths.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-willi:
An entry on Charles William Russell, the Irish priest and scholar who presided over Maynooth College for over twenty years. Born at Killough, County Down, in 1812, he entered Maynooth in 1826, was ordained in 1835, and taught humanities there. In 1842 Gregory XVI chose him for the Ceylon vicariate apostolic, but he refused that dignity, as he refused later bishoprics.

Russell returned to Maynooth as professor of Church history, translated Leibniz's System of Theology in 1850, and published a Life of Cardinal Mezzofanti in 1858. He became president of Maynooth in 1857. He served on the Historical Manuscripts Commission from 1869, jointly editing the Carte manuscripts' eight-volume report and the Calendar of Irish State Papers under James I. A steady writer for the Dublin Review, he was a close friend of Wiseman and Newman. He died at Dublin in 1880.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Edmond Obrecht's entry follows the Missionaries of Mariannhill, a Trappist-rooted missionary body in Natal. Mariannhill sits near Pinetown, fifteen miles from Durban and fifty-six from Pietermaritzburg. In 1882 Francis Pfanner, then prior of Bosnia's Mariastern monastery, answered Bishop Ricards' invitation and the general chapter's consent. He volunteered to plant a monastery in Cape Colony adapting Trappist rule to missionary life. He had landed at Port Elizabeth with thirty-one companions in July 1880, settling at Dunbrody, named for an old Irish monastery.

Dunbrody failed, and in 1882 Bishop Jolivet's solicitation moved the community to Mariannhill. Pfanner's energy won such success that by 1885 the work outgrew its bounds. Within a few years he founded seven mission stations scattered across Natal, from Transvaal's Ratschitz onward. The general chapter at Cîteaux later regularized the new congregation's standing, separating its missionary Trappists from the older observance while keeping the Mariannhill name and Natal center.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert-tuns:
A biographical entry follows Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of London and later of Durham, born at Hackforth in 1474 and dead at Lambeth in 1559. A scholar in theology, law, Greek, and Hebrew, he graduated in law at Padua and won Archbishop Warham's friendship, becoming his chancellor in 1511. Embassies followed, including Brussels with Thomas More, where he lodged with Erasmus.

Made Bishop of London in 1522 and keeper of the privy seal in 1523, he visited Worms and saw the dangers of Lutheran books. In Henry VIII's divorce case he counselled Queen Katherine but urged her not to appeal to Rome. Translated to Durham in 1530, he held quasi-regal power there. Through troubled years he kept Catholic doctrine, though without the constancy of Fisher and More, and died deprived under Elizabeth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-carrol:
A biographical entry presents Daniel Carroll, brother of Archbishop John Carroll, born at Upper Marlboro, Maryland, in 1733 and dead at Washington in 1829. Overshadowed by his illustrious brother, he was in his time one of Maryland's most influential men. Educated abroad like his brother, he lived as a country gentleman until the Revolution, when Catholic men schooled overseas stood out among neighbours of narrow local schooling.

Carroll served Maryland in the old Colonial Congress from 1780 to 1784, then sat in the Philadelphia convention that framed the United States Constitution in 1787. He and Thomas Fitz-Simons of Pennsylvania were the convention's only Catholics. Back in Maryland his efforts helped secure the Constitution's ratification, and he later served in Congress and as a commissioner for the new federal capital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-o-conn:
A biographical entry traces Daniel O'Connell, Ireland's Liberator, born near Cahirciveen in 1775 and dead at Genoa in 1847. His Kerry family, once great, had suffered under the penal laws, and an uncle in France paid for his schooling at Liege, Saint Omer, and Douai. Called to the Irish Bar in 1798, he saw Catholics still barred from Parliament and high office.

Detesting violence and the French Revolution alike, he built the Catholic Association into a mass movement for emancipation, won in 1829. Later he fought the Union, defended tenant rights, and led the repeal campaign, dying on pilgrimage to Rome. The entry follows his legal skill, his oratory, and his conviction that Catholics who paid taxes should share in making the laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-willia:
A biographical entry follows Daniel William Cahill, lecturer and controversialist, born in Queen's County, Ireland, in 1796 and dead at Boston in 1864. Third son of a civil engineer, he studied at Carlow and Maynooth, excelled in natural philosophy and languages, and was ordained after the Dunboyne course. He taught natural philosophy at Carlow, then ran a school at Seapoint from 1835 to 1841.

Meanwhile he wrote for the press, edited the Dublin Telegraph for a time, and became a famed preacher whose attacks on government and the Established Church spread his name widely. Visiting America in December 1859, he lectured on astronomy and preached across the United States and Canada, raising large sums for Catholic causes. Six feet five inches tall and strikingly handsome, he was buried at Glasnevin after exhumation from Boston.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-o-donn:
Edmund O'Donnell was the first Jesuit put to death by the English government in Ireland, born at Limerick in 1542 and executed at Cork in 1575. His family had held high civic office in Limerick for centuries. He joined the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1561, but ill health sent him to Flanders, and in 1564 he came back to teach in a Limerick school.

Troops broke up the school in 1565, and after a spell at Kilmallock the teachers returned, only to face a royal search in 1568. Ordered out on pain of death, O'Donnell withdrew to Lisbon, then risked a return in 1574 and was seized on landing. Tried for coming back, denying the queen's supremacy, and carrying letters, he was hanged, drawn, and quartered. His name also appears in records as Daniell and Donnelly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-caswal:
Edward Caswall was an Oratorian priest and hymn writer, born at Yately in 1814 and dead at the Birmingham Oratory in 1878. Schooled at Marlborough and Brasenose College, Oxford, he first won notice with a witty student satire, The Art of Pluck, signed Scriblerus Redivivus. Ordained in the Church of England in 1839, he served as curate of Stratford-sub-Castle.

Drawn by Newman and the Tracts for the Times, he resigned and was received into the Catholic Church at Rome in January 1847. His wife, also a Catholic, died of cholera in 1849, and he joined the Oratory in 1850. His Lyra Catholica put all the Breviary and Missal hymns into English verse, and his own poems in The Masque of Mary drew a poem in reply from Newman.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-free-will:
Free will, the question of moral liberty, ranks among the three or four greatest problems in philosophy. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry frames it plainly: can a person truly choose, shaping thoughts and character, or are all acts fixed in advance by past events beyond control? How one answers decides the meaning of duty, merit, remorse, and justice.

The article works through the question in stages, from ancient thought and Christian teaching to Thomist and Molinist theories, the Reformers, and modern philosophy. It weighs proofs and objections, then maps the issue across ethics, theology, metaphysics, and psychology. Readers get a full tour of why free choice still troubles every field that touches human action.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-funeral-pall:
The Funeral Pall is the black cloth spread over a coffin during the burial rites, most often marked with a white cross from end to end. The Roman Ritual does not order it for every priest or lay burial, but it does require it for absolution after a requiem when the body is absent. Church law also assumes the pall, barring clerics in vestments from bearing it.

Custom once made pall-bearing an honor, with guests invited to carry the cloth or touch its edge in procession. Costly palls later became sacred vestments, and popes were once buried under altar coverings until abuses ended the practice. English funerals show the splendor well: gold cloths for kings, and three red heraldic palls offered at a Durham bishop's burial in 1316.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-dowdal:
George Dowdall, Archbishop of Armagh, crossed from schism to Rome and back to his own see. Born at Drogheda in 1487, he joined the Crutched Friars and was last prior of Ardee, pensioned at twenty pounds a year when Henry VIII suppressed the house in 1539. The king named him to Armagh in 1543, but the pope withheld recognition, and Dowdall owned Henry as supreme head while denouncing the true primate.

Yet under Edward VI Dowdall led Ireland's Catholic party against Protestantism, and, failing, withdrew in disgust to the Continent. After renouncing the schism he was appointed by the pope in 1553 to the very see he had held schismatically. Through Mary's reign he repaired religion's ravages and held a Drogheda synod in 1554 against priests who had presumed to marry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gustav-bickel:
Cassel Orientalist Gustav Bickell, born in 1838, became one of the leading Semitic scholars of his generation and a Catholic convert through his own research. Teaching Semitic and Indo-Germanic languages at Marburg and Giessen, he found a clear witness to the Immaculate Conception in St. Ephraem's hymns while copying them in London and entered the Church in November 1865.

Ordained at Fulda weeks later, he taught at Münster, defended papal infallibility, and held chairs at Innsbruck from 1874 and Vienna from 1891. His books range from Syriac metre and a Hebrew grammar to editions of Ephraem and Isaac of Antioch. They include a study of the Mass and Passover, a rendering of Kalilag and Damnag, and a late work on Job.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harrowing-of-:
Harrowing of Hell is the Old and Middle English name for Christ's triumphant descent into Hades between Crucifixion and Resurrection, when he freed souls held captive since the world's beginning. The word itself first appears in Aelfric's homilies about the year 1000. The descent already filled poems linked to Caedmon and Cynewulf and the prose homilies and saints' lives of Old England.

Medieval English literature gives the theme its fullest dramatic life. The earliest surviving English religious play treats it, and each of the four great mystery cycles devotes it a scene, with Cornish plays beside them. Details in these versions come largely from the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus, known in England from early times and paraphrased in the long poem Cursor Mundi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hell:
Hell, a word kin to hole and hollow from a verb meaning to hide, is treated here under eight heads. They run from its name and place to the eternity and character of its pains. Theologians split the term four ways: hell proper for the damned, the limbo of infants, the limbo of the Fathers closed at Christ's Ascension, and purgatory. This entry covers only hell in the strict sense.

Latin infernus, Greek Hades, and Hebrew sheol all point below the earth. Gehenna, from Jerusalem's valley of Hinnom defiled by Moloch worship, became the New Testament's commonest name for the damned's abode, beside pool of fire, outer darkness, and second death. Scripture's abyss language, the entry argues, favours a real place within the earth over a hell everywhere, with fire and loss of God as its twin pains.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-conwell:
Henry Conwell, second Bishop of Philadelphia, was born at Moneymore, County Derry, in 1745. He was consecrated in London in 1820 at seventy-four, after two other clergy had declined a see troubled by lay trustees at St. Mary's Church. Trained at the Irish College in Paris, he arrived that December to find the brilliant but unruly Reverend William Hogan stationed at St. Mary's without credentials. When Conwell revoked Hogan's faculties, a schism followed that lasted for years.

Seeking peace, Conwell made two errors the account records plainly. He recalled the dismissed Dominican William Vincent Harold as vicar-general, and capitulated to the trustees in 1826 by yielding them control of salaries and a veto over appointments. Rome, displeased at that surrender of episcopal rights, appointed an administrator and forbade his return to the see. Francis Patrick Kenrick arrived as coadjutor in 1830. Conwell lived his last years in seclusion and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-weedall:
Henry Weedall, born in London in 1788 and orphaned young, was educated at Sedgley Park and Oscott and ordained priest at Wolverhampton in 1814. Already a junior master at Oscott, he continued teaching classics there. He became prefect of studies in 1816 and, in effect, president from 1821, taking the office in name when Bishop Walsh left in 1826. Under his rule Oscott progressed notably, and the present college building, two miles from the old, rose between 1826 and 1838.

Appointed Vicar Apostolic of the Northern District in 1840, Weedall went to Rome and got leave to decline the vicariate. He spent years in humbler posts until Bishop Ullathorne made him vicar-general, cathedral dean, and temporal administrator in 1848. In 1852 he became first provost of the new Birmingham Chapter. In 1853 he went back to Oscott in its troubled hour to renew its spirit of piety and discipline, succeeding despite almost continuous ill health until his death in 1859.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holywell:
Holywell is a town in North Wales on a hillside above a valley, where a broad stream from St. Winefride's Well joins the River Dee two miles away. Lead and copper mines once made it flourish, but mining decayed and its commercial glory fled. Today the only draw for visitors is St. Winefride's miraculous well.

For over a thousand years pilgrims have sought the well. Two twelfth-century documents in the British Museum record its history and earliest cures, covering dropsy, paralysis, gout, melancholia, sciatica, cancer, and many other ills, plus deliverance from evil spirits. Pilgrims still came in the sixteenth-century persecutions, and Bishop Goldwell won papal confirmation of indulgences granted by Martin V.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-maccaghw:
Hugh MacCaghwell, also called Cavellus, was an Irish archbishop and theologian, born at Saul in County Down in 1571 and dead in 1626. Schooled first at home and then at a famous school in the Isle of Man, he returned to Ireland and became tutor to the sons of Hugh, Prince of Tyrone. The prince sent him as special messenger to the Spanish court seeking aid for Ulster forces.

At Salamanca, where the court then sat, MacCaghwell frequented the university schools and took doctorates in divinity. Soon after, he gave up worldly greatness for the Franciscan order. His commentaries on Duns Scotus won high repute, and his holiness and learning made him, one writer says, the miracle of his time. Largely through his influence at the Spanish court, the Irish Franciscan College of St. Anthony arose at Louvain, where he later taught.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-o-neill:
Hugh O'Neill, earl of Tyrone, was born in 1550 and died at Rome in 1616. Mathew's youngest son, his parentage doubtful, yet Conn, first earl of Tyrone, recognized him as heir, he was ennobled as Baron of Dungannon. Shane O'Neill contested the arrangement, and in the petty wars that followed both Mathew and his eldest son were killed. Hugh became Baron of Dungannon in 1562.

His youth passed partly in Ireland, partly among English courtiers, where he picked up English ways and grew more English noble than Irish chief in manner. Camden praised his industry, large mind, military knowledge, and profound, dissembling heart, judging him born for great good or ill to his country. The entry follows his shifting alliances, his peerage under Perrot, and his later career as Tyrone's earl.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-tootell:
Hugh Tootell, commonly known as Charles Dodd, was an English historian, born in Lancashire in 1671 or 1672 and dead at Harvington Hall in 1743. He studied at the English College, Douay, and at St. Gregory's Seminary, Paris. Ordained, he came back to England in 1698 as the Molyneux family's chaplain at Mosborough Hall.

In 1711 he returned to the Continent, reportedly witnessing the siege of Douay as a regimental chaplain, and wrote a short history of the English College there, attacking the Jesuits. Father Hunter's reply drew Dodd's Secret Policy of the English Society of Jesus in 1715. From 1718 he gathered material at Douay for his great Church History of England from 1500 to 1688, twenty years in the making at Harvington Hall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-bell:
Priest and martyr James Bell was born at Warrington, Lancashire, probably about 1520. He died on 20 April 1584. What little is known comes from Bridgewater's Concertatio of 1588, drawn from a Douay manuscript later kept in Westminster archives. Challoner added details, as did state papers. Bell studied at Oxford and was ordained priest in Mary's reign. Under Elizabeth he unfortunately conformed to the established Church.

By the Douay account he ministered its bare sacraments for about twenty years in diverse English places. At last conscience deterred him from the cure of souls, and destitution reduced him to seeking a small readership for bare subsistence. To obtain it he approached a patron's wife, a Catholic lady, whose influence turned him back toward the old faith. The entry follows a conforming priest's return to Catholic ministry and martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-campbel:
James Campbell was born at Philadelphia on 1 September 1812 and died there on 27 January 1893. His father was Anthony Campbell, and his grandfather George Campbell came from Fintona, County Tyrone. James was educated at Geraldus Stockdale's private school. He studied law with Robert D. Ingraham and was admitted to the bar on 14 September 1833. The next day he became commissioner of Southwark district. He served until appointed to the board of education.

On 16 April 1840 he offered the resolution that founded Philadelphia's Girls' High School. He served on the education board until 1840, when Governor Porter named him judge of common pleas, orphans' court, and oyer and terminer courts. He held those posts until 1 January 1851, when Pennsylvania judgeships became elective. Nominated for supreme court judge during Know-Nothing and anti-Catholic agitation, he faced a hostile climate. The entry follows a Catholic jurist of Philadelphia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-dowdall:
Martyr James Dowdall, birth date unknown, was executed for his faith at Exeter, England, on 20 September 1600. By Rothe's account he was a Drogheda merchant, trading with England and the Continent. Some authorities, including Challoner, call him a Wexford native. Further confusion comes from another James Dowdall who died a confessor.

In summer 1598, returning from France, his ship was driven by weather onto Devon's coast, where William Bourchier, Earl of Bath, arrested and examined him. Dowdall publicly avowed that he rejected the queen's supremacy and recognized only the Roman pontiff's. The earl sent the examination to Sir Robert Cecil and committed Dowdall to Exeter jail. In prison he was tortured and racked, yet stayed unchanged in his fidelity. The entry presents a merchant whose storm-driven landing led to martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-ryder-r:
Journalist and poet James Ryder Randall was born at Baltimore, Maryland, on 1 January 1839. He died at Augusta, Georgia, on 15 January 1908. As author of Maryland, my Maryland, the Confederacy's famous war song, he is often styled poet laureate of the Lost Cause. He was educated at Georgetown University but did not graduate. He traveled in South America and the West Indies. Returning to America, he took the English literature chair at Poydras College, Pointe-Coupée, Louisiana.

Hearing of the 21 April 1861 attack on federal troops in Baltimore, in which a classmate was wounded, his Southern sympathies flared. During that night, by candlelight, he composed America's most martial poem, as it is often called. It first appeared in the New Orleans Sunday Delta on 26 April 1861. Reaching Baltimore, it was set to the music of Lauriger Horatius. The entry presents a teacher whose overnight verses became a Confederate anthem.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-adam-s:
Johann Adam Schall von Bell, a leading Jesuit missionary to China, was born at Cologne in 1591 and died at Peking in 1666. He studied at Rome, joined the Society in 1611, and sailed from Lisbon for China in April 1618, reaching Macao the next year amid a mandarin's persecution.

Penetrating inland only in 1622, Schall worked at Xi'an until Peking summoned him in 1630 to reform the Chinese calendar in place of the late Father Terrentius. Calendar-making, a high affair of state run by a two-hundred-member Board of Mathematics, became the mission's lifeline. Schall's science won the court standing his preaching alone could not.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-baptist-:
John Baptist Purcell was the Irish-born Archbishop of Cincinnati who built the Church across Ohio in the nineteenth century. Born at Mallow in 1800, he was barred from Irish colleges by the penal laws and sailed to America, taught at Baltimore, and entered Mount St. Mary's Seminary at Emmitsburg in 1820. Ordained at Paris in 1826, he returned to teach at Mount St. Mary's and became its president.

Consecrated Bishop of Cincinnati in 1833, he attended the Third Provincial Council of Baltimore the same day. He spent fifty years guiding a diocese that grew from a frontier mission into a great archdiocese. The entry follows his long episcopate through the building of churches, schools, and seminaries, and his care for immigrants. It covers the financial troubles that clouded his final years, ending with his death in Ohio in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-carroll:
John Carroll was the first bishop of the Catholic hierarchy in the United States and first Archbishop of Baltimore.
