Born at Upper Marlboro, Maryland, in 1735 to an Irish merchant father and a mother educated in France, he studied at the Jesuits' school at Bohemia, then at St. Omer's in French Flanders, and joined the Society of Jesus in 1753, being ordained at Liege in 1769.

When Clement XIV suppressed the Jesuits in 1773, Carroll wrote a vindication of the order and returned to Maryland, where penal laws left no public Catholic church. He built a small frame chapel on his mother's estate and began missionary life in Maryland and Virginia, saying Mass in her house on weekdays. From those modest beginnings he rose to lead an American Church that had to organize itself anew after the Revolution, and he died at Baltimore in 1815.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-caryll:
John Caryll was an English Catholic poet, dramatist, and diplomatist of the Stuart age. Born at West Harting in Sussex in 1625, head of an old Catholic and royalist family, he was educated at the English colleges of St. Omer and Rome. Under Charles II he produced plays and poems above the average in merit, including a translation of Ovid's letter of Briseis to Achilles.

His tragedy The English Princess, or the Death of Richard III, seen by Pepys in 1667 and judged no more than pretty good, played at the Duke of York's Theatre. So did his comedy Sir Solomon Single, modeled on Moliere's School for Wives. Imprisoned in the Tower during the Popish Plot scare of 1679, he later served James II as agent to Pope Innocent XI. He was secretary to Queen Mary of Modena, following the exiled court to Saint-Germain and losing his estate by attainder in 1696.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-martiall:
John Martiall was an English Catholic exile who helped found the English College at Douai. Born in Worcestershire in 1534, he was educated at Winchester and New College, Oxford, graduating in civil law in 1556. He then taught at Winchester until Elizabeth's accession drove him and his master abroad to Louvain.

Moving to Douai, he graduated in divinity in 1567 and was one of six companions who joined Dr. Allen in founding the English College there in 1568, a foundation of great importance for English Catholic affairs. Leaving over the smallness of his allowance, he later gained a canonry at St. Peter's in Lille, installed in 1579, which he enjoyed eighteen years. His Treatise of the Cross of 1564 defended honor paid to the cross and drew a Calvinist reply he answered in 1566.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-cornw:
John of Cornwall was a twelfth-century theologian known for a single certain work against Abelard's doctrine. Living about 1176, he came from St. German's in Cornwall and studied under Peter Lombard and Robert of Melun at Paris, and became a teacher himself. From Lombard he briefly took the view that Christ's humanity was merely the garment clothing the Logos.

Abandoning that doctrine after its condemnation at Tours in 1163, he defended orthodox teaching in his Eulogium to Pope Alexander III, arguing that Christ is truly a man. The preface's reference to William, formerly of Sens, as Archbishop of Reims dates it after 1176. Other works, including an apology on the Incarnation and a treatise on the Mass, are assigned to him without sufficient grounds, and nothing is known of his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-baron-:
Joseph, Baron von Hammer-Purgstall was an Austrian diplomat and Oriental scholar who lived from 1774 to 1856. Born at Graz, he trained in Eastern languages at Vienna's Oriental academy and served as interpreter at Constantinople and in Egypt during the campaign against the French. He rose to Aulic Councillor and, in 1847, president of the new Academy of Sciences.

His output was huge but uneven, since his grasp of Eastern tongues was broad rather than deep and his translations were often faulty. Still, his ten-volume history of the Ottoman Empire and his version of Hafiz, which inspired Goethe's West-Eastern Divan, left a mark on history and on German letters alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-creswe:
Joseph Creswell was an English Jesuit controversialist of the Elizabethan age. Born in London in 1557, he studied at Reims and the Roman College and joined the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1583. He led the English College at Rome after Father Persons and then acted as vice-prefect for English Jesuit interests in Spain.

His writings answered royal proclamations, defended martyrs such as Henry Walpole, and meditated on the Rosary, often under false names. His handling of seminary disputes in Seville and Valladolid drew severe criticism from later historians. Sent to Belgium in 1614, he became rector of Ghent in 1621 and died about 1623.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juliana-morel:
Juliana Morell was a Spanish Dominican nun famed as a child prodigy of learning. Born at Barcelona in 1594, she began Latin, Greek, and Hebrew at four and wrote her father a Latin letter before seven. Her father fled to Lyons over a murder charge, and at twelve she defended theses in ethics and dialectics with highest praise.

At Avignon in 1608, Juliana publicly maintained law theses before a distinguished audience and earned her doctorate. Lope de Vega called her the fourth Grace and tenth Muse. Spurning wealth and marriage, she entered the Dominican convent of Sainte-Praxède that year, took vows in 1610, and served three terms as prioress before her death in 1653.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-zell:
Karl Zell (1793-1873) spent his working life in the German state of Baden, first as a classical scholar and teacher, then as a politician who fought publicly for Catholic interests. This reference entry follows him from school in Mannheim through university study at Heidelberg, Gottingen, and Breslau to teaching posts at Rastatt, Freiburg, and Heidelberg.

In the Baden diet he pushed a full overhaul of secondary schooling and helped run the new board that oversaw higher study. Later, almost alone among public men, he spoke and wrote for the Church, Christian schools, and religious orders during bitter clashes with liberal governments. He also advised the Freiburg archbishop in the Kulturkampf years. And he set up the St. Michael's Association, which gathered gifts for the pope across the archdiocese. His books ranged over Aristotle, Calderon, Shakespeare, and Baden history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kirkwall:
Kirkwall, from Norse Kirkjuvagr or church-bay, is the chief town of Orkney in northern Scotland and long the home of its Norse earls and bishops. Its first church honoured St. Olaf, and the landward parish still bears his name.

Earl Magnus was murdered by his cousin Haco about 1115. Magnus's nephew Ronald vowed to raise a stone minster for his uncle if he won the islands, and St. Magnus's church, begun in 1137, became cathedral of a see founded in 1102 under Trondhjem. With Glasgow, it is one of two ancient Scottish cathedrals preserved whole, 234 feet long with a 133-foot tower. Its steeple was struck by lightning in 1671, and restorations came in 1805 and 1845.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximilian-he:
Maximilian Hell, a Hungarian astronomer born at Schemnitz in 1720, died at Vienna in 1792. He joined the Society of Jesus at Trentschin in 1738 and studied philosophy at Vienna, where his early bent for science showed. In 1744 he turned to maths and astronomy as assistant to Father Joseph Franz, director of the Vienna observatory. Ordained in 1751, he taught maths at Klausenberg and in 1755 became director of the imperial observatory at Vienna.

His chief work was the yearly Ephemerides astronomicae ad meridianem Vindobonensem, begun in 1757 and packed with observations and data. The King of Denmark invited him to Vardo in Norway to watch the 1769 transit of Venus, which he did with success. He prepared his results at Copenhagen and returned to Vienna in 1770. Slow publication later raised suspicion that he had trimmed his data to match others, a charge the entry examines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-georg:
Michael George Mulhall, a statistician born in Dublin on 29 September 1829, died there on 13 December 1900. He was educated at the Irish College, Rome. Going to Buenos Aires, he founded there in 1861 the Standard, the first English paper published in South America. In 1869 he issued the Handbook of the River Plate, the first English book printed in Argentina.

His later books include the Progress of the World in 1880, the Balance Sheet of the World, 1873-1880, in 1881, and the Dictionary of Statistics in 1883. That dictionary, a standard reference few modern compilations have matched in use, was followed by the History of Prices since 1850 in 1885. In 1896 he travelled widely in Europe gathering material for an English Parliament committee reporting on a proposed Irish agriculture department. The pope decorated him for his literary work, in which his wife Marion McMurrough Mulhall, herself a prolific writer, was his active and practical helper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mother-france:
Mother Frances Mary Teresa Ball, born in Dublin on 9 January 1794, founded the Irish branch of the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary, known as the Sisters of Loreto. She died on 19 May 1861. Daughter of John Ball and Mabel Clare Bennet, she was sent at nine to the convent school at the Bar in York, run by the English Ladies of the Institute.

After her father's death in 1808 she spent time at home. In 1814, under Archbishop Daniel Murray of Dublin, she returned to York, entered the novitiate and professed in 1816 as Mary Teresa. Recalled to Dublin with two novices in 1821, she opened the order's first Irish house at Rathfarnham in 1822. She devoted her great piety and administrative skill to schools and to a sisterhood now spread across many countries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-owen-roe-o-ne:
Owen Roe O'Neill was an Irish soldier born in 1582 and dead near Cavan on 6 November 1649. He was son of Art O'Neill and nephew of Hugh, the great Earl of Tyrone. Too young for his uncle's long war, he went abroad after the peace of 1603 and served the archdukes in Flanders. By 1606 he was a captain at Brussels, and by the Thirty Years War he ranked colonel, high among Spanish commanders for skill, courage, and resource.

Chosen to hold Arras against the French in 1640, he kept the town for nearly two months with only 1,500 men. The force against him grew from 30,000 to three times that number. The French commander who took the place praised him warmly. Back in Ireland, where the flight of the earls, the Ulster plantation, and Strafford's tyranny had left Catholics no safety, O'Neill led the Catholic cause in arms until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pall: A pall is a heavy black cloth laid over the coffin in church at a funeral, or over the catafalque at other services for the departed. A white or red cross usually stands at its centre. It must always be black, though its stuff and trimming may vary. Death signs like skulls and crossbones, banned on altar and vestments, are allowed on palls. The pall is in wide use, though not prescribed, and where no bier stands, absolution needs a black cloth spread on the sanctuary floor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontius-carbo:
Pontius Carbonell was a Catalan Franciscan teacher and confessor whose identity is hard to pin down among many namesakes. He entered the Franciscan Order and lived chiefly at the Barcelona convent, where he taught and served as confessor to Saint Louis, Bishop of Toulouse, during his seven years' captivity. He died about 1320.

He was also confessor to the Infante Juan of Aragon, Archbishop of Saragossa, and probably superior in 1314. That year King James II sent him to his brother Frederick II of Sicily to beg him not to shelter the Fraticelli. He wrote commentaries on both Testaments, quoting the fathers and doctors at length, and some hold that he composed the Catena Aurea on the Gospels usually printed among Saint Thomas's works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-of-co:
Richard of Cornwall, also called Richard Rufus, was a thirteenth-century Franciscan scholar who lectured on theology at Oxford and Paris. His birth and death dates are unknown, though he was still living in 1259. He studied for a time in Paris in 1238, then returned to Oxford, and was sent with Haymo of Faversham to Rome to oppose the minister-general Elias.

By 1250 he taught the Sentences, Peter Lombard's standard theology textbook, at Oxford. Riots drove him back to Paris, where he kept lecturing and earned the title Philosophus Admirabilis, the Wonderful Philosopher. Roger Bacon, however, judged his teaching harmful, blaming it for bad effects over the next forty years. Several commentaries on the Sentences survive in manuscript under his name. A later writer denied that he was Richard Rufus at all, claiming Rufus was born at Cirencester, not Cornwall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-russe:
Richard Russell rose from humble beginnings to become a bishop in Portugal, after a youth spent in service at Lisbon College. Born in Berkshire in 1630, he became a servant at twelve to the college's newly appointed president, Dr Edward Daniel. Using his spare hours for study, he was admitted as a student five years later, then moved to Douai and Paris, where he was ordained.

Back in Lisbon as procurator in 1655, he later served as chaplain to the Portuguese ambassador in London and as secretary to the Queen of Portugal. Hopes that he might return to lead the English clergy came to nothing. Instead he accepted the see of Portalegre in 1671, reformed the diocese over ten years of hard work, and was transferred to Viseu in 1682. He spent his last eleven years there and died in 1693. His portrait survives at the English College, Lisbon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-gradwe:
Robert Gradwell was an English bishop whose career ran from revolutionary France to the rectorship of the English College at Rome. Born at Clifton-in-the-Fylde in 1777, he went to Douai in 1791. The college was suppressed by revolutionaries, and he was held for a time before returning to England in 1795. With other Douai refugees he moved to Crook Hall, Durham, where he was ordained in 1802.

For seven years he taught poetry and rhetoric at Crook Hall and the new Ushaw college. On Lingard's recommendation, Pius VII made him rector of the reopened English College at Rome in 1818, where his prudent rule made the house flourish. He also acted as Roman agent for the English vicars apostolic, and became a doctor of divinity in 1821. Consecrated Bishop of Lydda in 1828 as coadjutor for London, he died of dropsy in 1833 after years of ill health.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-catholi:
The Penal Laws began at Elizabeth's accession in 1558. Under those laws, taking Roman orders and coming to England was high treason, as were reconciliation to Rome and procuring another's. Aiding or sheltering such a priest was capital felony. Papists could not educate their children in their own religion. A home schoolmaster who skipped the parish church and lacked the bishop's licence cost parents ten pounds a month and himself forty shillings a day.

Sending children to overseas seminaries cost parents one hundred pounds and barred the children from inheriting property. Saying Mass cost 200 marks; hearing it, 100. Recusancy fines ran twenty pounds per lunar month of absence from church. In 1593 they were limited to Popish recusants. A convicted Popish recusant, besides the fine, lost office, arms, lawsuits, executorships, guardianships, and presentations. He needed a licence to travel five miles from home, and paid one hundred pounds for coming to court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-gall:
Gall was an Irish monk, one of the twelve who followed Columbanus to Gaul and settled with him at Luxeuil. He went with his master up the Rhine to Bregenz in 610. When Columbanus left for Italy in 612, Gall stayed behind in Swabia and lived as a hermit near the source of the Steinach with several companions. After his death a church rose on the spot, and before the middle of the eighth century it had grown into a monastery under its first abbot, Otmar.

The house belonged to the diocese of Constance until 818. That year Louis the Pious ranked it among the royal monasteries, and in 854 it was freed from nearly all obligation to Constance. Its name honours Gall himself, not a founder abbot. Later Lives of the saint, the oldest from the late eighth century, mix true incidents with legend, including his missionary work and the healing of Fridiburga.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-comgall:
St. Comgall was founder and abbot of the great Irish monastery at Bangor, flourishing in the sixth century. This entry follows a man of uncertain birth year, which the Irish annals place between 510 and 520. His death is put in 602 by the Annals of Tighernach and the Chronicon Scotorum, or in 597 by the Annals of Innisfallen.

He was born in Dalaradia, Ulster, near today's Magheramorne in County Antrim. He apparently served as a soldier first; freed from military service, he is said to have studied at Clonard under St. Finnian, and at Clonmacnoise under St. Ciaran, who died in 549. Next we find him in Ulster, on a Lough Erne island, with a few friends living a very severe form of monastic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ulrich-of-:
Ulrich of Zell, also called of Cluny and of Ratisbon, brought Cluniac observance to the Black Forest. Born at Ratisbon at the beginning of 1029 to the pious and rich Bernhold and Bucca, niece of Bishop Gebhard II, he was probably schooled at St Emmeram. In 1044 he went to the court of his godfather Henry IV as page to Empress Agnes.

Ordained deacon by his uncle Nidger of Freising, he became cathedral archdeacon. After a journey to Rome he gave his possessions to the poor, pilgrimaged to the Holy Land, and entered Cluny in 1061 under Hugh. There he excelled in piety and diligence, was ordained priest, and served as confessor at Marcigny and prior of its men's community. He founded Zell and died there, probably on 10 July 1093.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-and-ar:
Thomas Marshall, a controversial writer born in 1818, moved from Anglican ministry to the Catholic Church and then to public defence of Catholic schools and missions. Educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, he served as vicar of Swallowcliff before the Tractarian movement pushed him to study church government. His own research led him to leave Anglicanism, and he was received into the Catholic Church in 1845.

In 1847 he became the first inspector of Catholic schools, a post he held until a pamphlet on Anglican missions forced his resignation in 1860. After time in America he published his best known work on Christian missions in 1862 and lectured in the United States in 1870 and 1871. He died at Surbiton in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-goldwe:
Thomas Goldwell, Bishop of St. Asaph, was the last survivor of England's ancient hierarchy, dying at Rome in 1585. Born in Kent between 1501 and 1515, he studied at All Souls, Oxford, where he shone in mathematics and astronomy, and stood firm against Henry VIII's religious changes. As chaplain to Cardinal Pole he shared exile and attainder, reaching Rome in 1538.

He joined the Theatines at Naples in 1547, attended the conclave of 1549-50 with Pole, and under Mary returned as Bishop of St. Asaph. At Elizabeth's accession he fled again, refusing an Italian bishopric to work for England's conversion. He was the only English bishop at Trent, where he helped revise the Breviary and Missal and urged Elizabeth's excommunication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ulrich-zell:
Ulrich Zell was a publisher and the first printer of Cologne, born at Hanau-on-the-Main at an unknown date and dead about 1507. He learned printing before 1462 in the shop of Fust and Schöffer at Mainz. Shortly after the sack of Mainz in 1462 he moved to Cologne, whose university promised a market for printed books. He was printing there apparently as early as 1463, though his first dated book comes from 1466.

His work as printer and publisher runs to 1502, with about 120 known publications. Only nine bear his name, but he probably printed many more besides. His six kinds of type closely match the Durandus and Clement types of Fust and Schöffer, and he may even have used some of their matrices. The entry gives a compact life of a pioneer who carried the new art from Mainz to the Rhineland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-wall:
John Wall was a martyr born in Lancashire in 1620 who suffered near Worcester on 22 August 1679. Known at Douai and Rome as John Marsh, he used the mission aliases Francis Johnson, Webb, and Dormore. Son of wealthy and staunch Lancashire Catholics, he was sent very young to Douai College. He entered the Roman College on 5 November 1641, was made priest on 3 December 1645, and was sent on the mission on 12 May 1648.

On 1 January 1651 he assumed St Francis's habit at Douai's St Bonaventure Friary, and a year later professed as Joachim of St Anne. He worked as vicar and novice master at Douai until 1656, when he returned to the mission. He laboured with zeal in Worcestershire for twenty years. Seized in December 1678 at Rushock Court near Bromsgrove, he was tried for his priesthood and suffered at Worcester.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-richard-h:
Richard Hill was an English martyr executed at Durham on 27 May 1590. Very little is known of him and his fellow martyrs John Hogg and Richard Holiday. All three were Yorkshiremen: Holiday reached Reims's English College on 6 September 1584, Hill on 15 May 1587, and Hogg on 15 October 1587. All three were ordained subdeacons at Soissons, deacons and priests at Laon by Bishop Valentine Douglas.

Together with fellow martyr Edmund Duke, they left for the English mission on the following 22 March and were seized in northern England soon after landing. Arraigned, condemned, and executed at Durham under the statute 27 Elizabeth, chapter 2, they suffered with four felons who protested that they died in the same faith. Divers beholders, the entry notes, were moved by their constancy at the scaffold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-tu:
Thomas Tunstall was a northern priest executed at Norwich in July 1616. Descended from the Tunstalls of Thurland in Lancashire, he is listed in the Douai diaries under the alias Helmes and as a native of the old diocese of Carlisle. He took the college oath at Douai in 1607 and left as a priest in 1610.

Almost at once he was seized in England and spent four or five years in various prisons before escaping from Wisbech Castle. Making for a friend's house near Lynn, he was recaptured and committed to Norwich gaol, where he was tried and condemned on 12 July 1616. The holiness of his bearing on the scaffold deeply impressed onlookers. A contemporary portrait at Stonyhurst shows a still-young man with abundant black hair and a dark moustache.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-rob:
Robert Southwell was a Norfolk-born Jesuit poet executed at Tyburn in February 1595. Born at Horsham St Faith's in 1561, grandson of the courtier who had sent the poet Earl of Surrey to the block. He was raised Catholic, studied at Douai under the austere Leonard Lessius, and entered the Jesuits at Rome in 1578. Ordained in 1584, he became prefect of studies at the English College.

Sent to England in 1586 with Henry Garnet, under the name Cotton, he became chaplain to the Countess of Arundel and befriended her imprisoned husband, Philip, Earl of Arundel. His verse began in boyhood laments at his first refusal by the Society. Arrested and tortured, he was hanged at Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-will:
This reference entry treats will as a topic in psychology and Catholic philosophy. Will counts as the rational appetite, set above lower drives, and its full act picks an object by the light of reason from competing aims. Its object is good in general, and its mark is freedom among different forms of good. Modern writers often stretch the word wider, covering any inner drive, even blind instinct, a usage the entry calls an abuse of terms.

Sections follow will through its links with knowledge, feeling, schooling, movement, and laboratory study. Most daily choosing, the entry notes, is swift and unreflecting, working through habit or rule of thumb rather than formal debate. Two Scholastic maxims frame the account: nothing is willed unless first known, and all knowledge starts in the senses. The piece thus maps both deliberate choice and the humbler, half-formed acts of willing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-darre:
William Darrell was an English Jesuit theologian whose Sunday reflections and conduct books reached many readers. Born in Buckinghamshire in 1651, he died at Saint Omer in 1721. From the old Catholic Darrell family of Scotney Castle, he joined the Jesuits in 1671 and made his profession in 1689. His pen defended Saint Ignatius and the Jesuits against Henry Wharton's charges in 1688 and answered Leslie's Case Stated in 1717.

Darrell's best-loved book, Moral Reflections on the Epistles and Gospels of Every Sunday, appeared in 1711 and ran through many printings. The Gentleman Instructed, on a virtuous and happy life, reached a tenth edition by 1732 and spread into Italian and Hungarian. He also issued Theses Theologicae, a treatise on the Real Presence, and a translation of discourses on Pascal's Provincial Letters. Other tracts are ascribed to him by later editors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-maxwe:
William Maxwell, fifth Earl of Nithsdale, was a Jacobite lord saved from the scaffold by his wife's daring escape plot. Born in 1676, he died at Rome in 1744. He succeeded his father at seven, and his Douglas mother raised him in Catholic faith and Stuart loyalty. About twenty-three he visited the French court to honour King James and wooed Lady Winifred Herbert, youngest daughter of the Marquis of Powis, marrying her in March 1699.

The couple lived chiefly at Terregles in Dumfriesshire and raised five children. In 1715 Nithsdale joined the rising for Prince James Stuart, was taken at Preston, and sent to the Tower under sentence of death. Lady Nithsdale begged George I in vain, then smuggled her husband out in disguise on the eve of execution. The pair fled to France and spent their last years in great poverty at Rome, attending their exiled king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-winifred-maxw:
Winifred Maxwell, Countess of Nithsdale, is famed for smuggling her husband out of the Tower on the eve of his execution. Daughter of the exiled Marquis of Powis, she died at Rome in May 1749. Her married life passed chiefly at Terregles, where news reached her of her husband's defeat at Preston. After hiding the family papers, she hurried to London to plead for him.

Winifred warned that a border Catholic with a great following and a family ever loyal to the royals could expect no mercy, and even her personal appeal to George I failed. With courage and ingenuity she then contrived his escape in women's dress on 23 February 1716 and arranged his passage to France. She returned to Scotland for papers vital to her son, endured George's charge that she had done him more mischief than any woman in Christendom, and joined her husband in Roman exile.
cobwebs-from-an-empty-skull:
Cobwebs from an Empty Skull, by Ambrose Bierce, collects the fables and tales he first published in the comic paper Fun. Its contents list runs past two dozen short pieces. Titles include Feodora, Dr. Deadwood, I Presume, Mrs. Dennison's Head, A Fowl Witch, and Jim Beckwourth's Pond.

The preface is a joke at the book's own expense. Homer's Iliad was little prized by Homer's contemporaries, Bierce notes, and Milton got but twenty-five pounds for Paradise Lost. His own pieces, the editor of Fun admitted, were not quite perceived at first. The tales inside keep that dry tone: one follows Johnny, too manly to whimper when the promised Christmas presents fail to appear.
dinosaurs-with-special-reference-to-the-:
Giant reptiles of the past fill W. D. Matthew's guide, written with the American Museum collections in view. Matthew was curator of vertebrate palaeontology there. Eleven chapters run from the age of reptiles to the work of collecting dinosaurs.

Kinds come first: flesh eaters like Allosaurus, the great amphibious Brontosaurus, and the beaked kinds in three chapters. Range across the world, and how and where bones are dug, close the book. From the Trachodonts, Matthew reads a north once far warmer than now. Wyoming and Montana then matched Southern California, he says, and palm leaves like the Florida palmetto lie in the same rocks as the skeletons. The book is a museum man's plain tour of his halls.
divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-hell:
Dante Alighieri's Hell, the Inferno, appears here in the Reverend H F Cary's blank-verse translation, the version that carried Dante to English readers for a century. It opens midway in Dante's life, lost in a gloomy wood, with Virgil offering rescue through the underworld. Thirty-four cantos descend the funnel of hell.

Dante passes the indifferent at the gate, Francesca among the lustful, gluttons, misers, heretics, and suicides turned to trees. Horned demons with great lashes drive the fraudulent along the grisly rock in the middle cantos. At the bottom, traitors lie frozen and Satan chews the worst of them. Cary's Miltonic verse keeps the journey solemn and readable.
doe-osti-2583518-in-silico-design-of-nex:
Futamura USA asked whether cellulose packaging could gain strength and water resistance without losing its biodegradability, and NREL answered in simulation. The CRADA work, closed out in report NREL/TP-2800-94277 dated December 20, 2024, used molecular dynamics to test natural additives inside a cellulose matrix. Peter Ciesielski was the laboratory's contact. Cellophane and its kin rot away in soil and sea, but petroleum films beat them on moisture barriers and strength.

Models blended xylan and lignin, in varied monomer mixes, into the cellulose. Stress-strain simulations measured the mechanical effect, and contact angle simulations measured water repellency. Xylan helped: it tended to raise the mechanical properties, with an optimal loading near twenty-seven percent by weight. Because both additives occur in nature and biodegrade, the gains do not compromise the material's end of life. The study gives packaging designers a screened recipe before anyone books pilot plant time.
doe-osti-3002983-microstructural-evaluat:
Alan F. Jankowski, Andy Gardea, Jeffrey Chames, Ryan Nishimoto, Meghan Rogers, Manuel Lopez Martinez, and Joshua K. Yee examine printed metal in Sandia report SAND2025-13933, printed November 2025. The samples are thin-wall sections of 316L stainless steel made by laser powder-bed fusion. Thin walls cool fast and freeze differently from bulk prints, so their grain structure needs its own check.

The team polished samples through a series of grit steps and imaged them with laser microscopy. They identified phases, measured composition, and tested microhardness across the walls. Elevation maps from interferometry trace height changes across grain boundaries over paths of about 20 micrometers. The evaluation gives process engineers a baseline for how thin printed features form, which matters for small, precise parts in weapons and energy systems.
doe-osti-3010890-a-spline-based-method-t:
Spatially varying viscosity in confined flows is handled with a spline based method in a September 2025 report by Jean Chun, Craig Palmer, and Simon Simonnin of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. The method fits spatially dependent viscosity values directly from non equilibrium molecular dynamics of Couette and Poiseuille flows. The fitted curves then enter Navier Stokes calculations of non uniform viscosity flow.

The molecular dynamics used LAMMPS with SPC/E water and the CLAYFF force field for quartz, talc, and ions. Systems were equilibrated for 500 picoseconds under 300 K and 1 bar, then run 5 nanoseconds in NVT. A constant acceleration drove Poiseuille flow. The report presents the coupling as a route to convective heat and mass transfer models.
doe-osti-3015895-southern-company-servic:
Galen Maclaurin and Anthony Lopez led the National Laboratory of the Rockies side of this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-6A20-96678, with Will Hobbs among the other named contributors. The client was Southern Company Services, a utility support firm. Two studies are bundled here: tall tower wind potential in the Southeast, and offshore wind potential for the same company.

For the land study, the lab assessed system performance, available capacity, transmission distance, and levelized cost of energy for turbines on towers 100 to 160 meters tall inside the service territory. It also assessed utility-scale solar potential there. Siting screens in the work exclude places such as radar setbacks, slopes over 25 percent, and federal lands. Utility planners can use the results to see where taller turbines change the wind map of the Southeast.
doe-osti-3016889-solar-panel-installatio:
Goucher College's research performance progress report for award DE-EE0010813, led by principal investigator Ryan Glaeser with Andrea Marsh as business contact, covers September through December 2025. The project installs solar panels at the college, as the first phase of a wider green campus plan. The college aims to cut energy use, water use, and waste by 2030.

Two separate solar projects are planned first, one of them on the Facility Management Services building. Early tasks cover tearing off the old roof on that building and clearing debris. Workers also check the deck and drainage for faults that could hurt the new roof. A new thermoplastic polyolefin roof follows before panels go on. The quarterly filing shows a campus solar job still in its roof-first groundwork stage.
doe-osti-3027647-validation-of-simulatio:
Christopher Hansen of the University of Washington and Columbia University, with Jeff Levesque as Columbia's institutional investigator, reports award DE-SC0021657 for September 2020 through April 2025. The work validates simulation models of scrape-off layer currents that connect to the wall of the HBT-EP tokamak during magnetic events. Such currents matter in disruptions and resistive wall modes, where plasma and conducting structures trade energy.

Modeling used the NIMROD and PSI-Tet codes for plasma plus three-dimensional conducting structures, including non-axisymmetric resistive wall models shown at the 2024 APS plasma physics meeting. Synthetic test sensors, built with the NIMPY library, mimic the machine's magnetic sensors, poloidal EUV view, and current tiles so simulations can be compared against readings flow by flow. Linear runs of non-disruptive external kink events in HBT-EP are among the cases examined.
doe-osti-3376472-crada-number-nfe-24-104:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory CRADA final report ORNL/TM-2026/4630, by Nicholas Sokol and dated January 2026, closes joint work with Algaeo, LLC on microbe mixes for algae growth. The mix paired two fungi, Laccaria bicolor and Serendipita indica, with Pseudomonas bacteria. On land, such partners help plants grow and shrug off disease. The test asked if the same crew could boost the freshwater alga Chlorella vulgaris in a tank.

Cultures grew side by side under set lab conditions. Staff tracked growth rate, biomass density, and metabolic activity across a standard run. The verdict was plain. The alga kept its own growth path, untouched by the fungi or bacteria at its side. No clear partnership formed, and no growth gain showed. The report logs the null result as the project's answer, with growth curves for two test cultures in the figures.
doe-osti-3409103-analyze-landscape-of-so:
NLR/TP-6A20-100240 is a August 2026 report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies that maps solar panel installs and retirements for Solar Prize Round 7. Hope Wikoff was the lab contact, with Heather Alvis in the evidence record. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-24-30364.

Tables cite state and federal rules that shape panel disposal and reuse. Waste codes, transport rules, and state laws all appear in the legal survey. Old panels are a growing waste stream as early fleets age out. Prize teams and policy staff can see where rules help recycling and where gaps could send panels to landfills.
doe-osti-3799883-evaluation-of-hardware-:
Pacific Northwest report PNNL-39652, dated September 2026, reviews ways to list every part inside digital reactor gear. William Hutton, Jessica Smith, Corinne Roth, and Fleurdeliza de Peralta are the printed authors. New reactors lean on programmable devices packed with chips, code libraries, and vendor parts. Hidden shared parts can fail together, breaking the diversity that safety cases rely on. Hardware and software bills of materials promise a clear view of what sits inside each device.

The team compares the main list formats: CycloneDX, SPDX, and SWID tags. They survey tools that build lists from source code, finished programs, and hardware records. Each route shows gaps, and vendors rarely publish lists, which starves the research. A starter parts list from one vendor's safety filing shows how a system-level list could be framed. The report also probes machine learning help for scanning lists at scale.
doe-osti-3883788-utilizing-telecommunica:
Livermore technical report LLNL-TR-2024498, dated August 31, 2026, explores telecom fibre as a seismic sensor network for nuclear monitoring. Gene Ichinose, lead of the Low Yield Nuclear Monitoring Sensing Venture, is the sole printed author. Distributed acoustic sensing turns ordinary buried cable into thousands of virtual vibration sensors. One desktop-sized interrogator reads light backscatter along the fibre and converts stretch into strain. For explosion monitoring, that density could aid location and yield estimation.

Three work strands fill the report. The first mines the FUSE dataset for signal detections to train learning algorithms. The second compares earthquake records from dark and installed fibres, testing how three burial styles change ground-to-cable coupling. The third supports a tunnel-road sensing deployment. Findings stress variability: slack loops in vaults and mixed burial methods make coupling uneven along a line. Even so, existing telecom fibre beats newly ploughed lines.
doe-osti-3895872-general-motors-llc-auto:
NLR report NLR/TP-5900-99326, dated September 2026, closes a long cooperative project with General Motors on car fuel cells. The final report is dated January 12, 2026, and the citation lists thirteen laboratory contacts, led by Ademola Odusanya, Adam Phillips, and Bhushan Sopori. The shared aim was cutting fuel cell stack cost so hydrogen cars can compete. Work split into four strands: electrode materials, diagnostics, contamination studies, and manufacturing methods.

Catalyst work compared platinum on varied carbon supports in membrane assemblies. Supports with accessible inner pores cut transport resistance and lifted performance. Diagnostics sharpened test methods for kinetics and mass transfer. The contamination strand hunted chemicals leaching from plastics and sealants, then measured their harm. Manufacturing work built on-line coating checks, ending in a thermal scanning system that runs at line speed. The report is the agreement's closeout record.
dorothy-vernon-of-haddon-hall:
Charles Major, author of When Knighthood Was in Flower, tells of Dorothy Vernon of Haddon Hall in Elizabethan Derbyshire. The hosted copy is the Mary Pickford edition of 1908, with scenes from the photoplay. A wizard's prologue summons the past out of a boiling caldron, and then John Manners rides down to Haddon in the first chapter.

Dorothy, heiress of the hall, loves John, a younger son of Rutland, against her father's will. Chapter heads promise a golden heart, a dangerous trip to Derby town, a tryst at the Bowling Green gate, and Mary Stuart herself. At the gate John waits and frets while Dorothy feigns not to see him. The tale rests on the old legend of the elopement down the hall's famed steps. Major writes rich costume romance: proud days, hard fathers, and love that finds a way out by night.
farewell:
Farewell, by Honore de Balzac and translated by Ellen Marriage, opens with hunters joking across a stubble field. Balzac dedicates the tale to Prince Friedrich von Schwarzenberg. In the Forest of Isle-Adam, a stout marquis puffs over the furrows. His friend teases him to jump like a stag. September heat, panting dogs, and the dinner hour all feel safely ordinary.

The ordinariness is a trap. The hunt leads toward a country house. A woman lives there lost in madness, her reason gone. The narrative turns back to Napoleon's retreat from Moscow. It reaches the crossing of the Berezina river, where her mind broke. Cold, hunger, and bereavement did the work there. An old love recognizes the countess. He tries to call her back by restaging the past, scene by scene. Balzac's Adieu, as the tale is also known, studies war's aftermath. It is among his shortest and cruelest pieces.
fifteen-years-in-hell:
Benson tells the truth about drink in Fifteen Years in Hell, his autobiography of 1885. Luther Benson writes as a man who lived the curse he names. His contents map the road: an unmerciful enemy, homes blighted, and a slavery he calls utter. He holds his tale to be a true one, and warns that drink stings like an adder.

The sampled pages find him in Bluffton, Indiana, where he had come to practice law. The saloons, which he calls the devil's recruiting offices, took him the first night. A bout of delirium tremens followed. Broke and near bare of clothes, he walked more than a hundred miles home to his father. Benson's book is a temperance testimony, set down by a man who fell and rose more than once.
foe-farrell:
Quiller-Couch tells a tale of hate in Foe-Farrell. Arthur Quiller-Couch dedicates the book to anyone who supposes he has a worse enemy than himself. The story is told in nights, across four books: Ingredients, The Chase, The Retrieve, and The Counterchase. John Foe meets Farrell at the baths on the second night, and the hunt is up by the ninth.

The sampled pages are a doctor's letter from America. He and Farrell had spent five days in New York. He means, he writes, to ease the chain: his visits to his patient will grow rarer, for a new and harder course of treatment calls for holidays. Farrell, he notes, can bear any heat so long as it comes without noise. Noise and heat together drive him crazy. The tale joins a vendetta to a case study, told by the man who holds the chain.
from-the-ball-room-to-hell:
Faulkner wrote this tract as a convert against his old trade. He had run the Los Angeles Dancing Academy. He also led the Pacific Coast dancing masters' group. In plain words he now calls dancing a path to ruin. The preface warns parents most of all. He says young girls face grave danger in the ball-room.

His case rests on his years inside the business. He began dancing at twelve and taught for six years. He claims most fallen women took a man's arm first at a dance. Stories and quoted authorities support his charge. The book urges readers to quit the dance floor for a Christian life. It is a fierce piece of moral reform writing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DurhamBill_Durh:
Bill Durham wrote to Harold Weisberg on May 27, 1975 about a small object with large meaning: Lee Harvey Oswald's notebook. The letter discusses names found in it, including FBI agent James Hosty and a Gandy. A notebook page naming the agent who knew Oswald before the shooting was evidence worth arguing over.

Durham also takes up J. Edgar Hoover's notification of Robert Kennedy and claims made by former FBI agent Joseph Schott. The letter moves the way researcher mail did, lead by lead, through the open questions of the case. It preserves that exchange between two men still working the file in 1975.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MillerBill_Mill: William P. Miller filed this document in court himself, without a lawyer. He titled it 'We the People — Represent the Spirit of John F. Kennedy,' and it carries case number 112263-2000. Citizens have long filed such papers in assassination cases, asking courts to act on claims no agency would take up. The file gives Miller's title and the case number, but not the relief he asked the court to grant.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MoyersBill_Moye:
A Washington Post magazine page presents Bill Moyers in his own words and in pictures. Moyers had been President Johnson's press secretary and a central aide. One line from the page is quoted in the file: 'We won the civil rights battles of the '60s, but lost the political war.' A photograph shows Moyers with Johnson in 1964.

Moyers left the White House and became a publisher and then a television journalist. The page belongs to his years of looking back at the Johnson era he served. His quoted judgment is bleak about politics and proud about civil rights at once. The feature preserves both the man's summary of his decade and the image of him at the president's side.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RaysAll_Rays_Al:
James Earl Ray signed this application for a pardon on October 6, 1980. He filed it with the Tennessee Board of Paroles. Ray was prisoner number 65477 at Brushy Mountain Prison. He was serving his sentence for the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., to which he had pleaded guilty in 1969.

Ray spent the rest of his life trying to undo that plea. He claimed he was a patsy in a larger plot and asked courts and boards, again and again, for a trial or a pardon. This application is one formal round of that campaign. It preserves his prisoner number, his prison, and his request in his own filing, twelve years after the murder.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SartorBill_Sart:
An FBI memorandum records Robert Patrick Lyons's account of meeting Bill Sartor. Lyons met Sartor through a woman named Marie Geisandorf. The meeting happened after the death of Martin Luther King Jr. Sartor was a figure whose name drew agents' attention in the King case's wide net.

Memos like this one log introductions: who met whom, through whom, and when. In a case built on possible conspiracies, introductions were evidence, the joints where a plot would have to connect. Lyons's account gives the bureau one such joint, dated after the assassination. The memorandum preserves it in the standard form, a small link kept because no one could yet say which links mattered.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Windowsill_Wind: Only a fragment of an article on the James Earl Ray case survives here. It touches on Ray's guilty plea and his later escape. The scan is garbled, and optical character reading recovers little of the text. Damaged as it is, the fragment was kept, because Ray's plea and escape stayed central to doubts about the King case long after 1968.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va: Cybersecurity: When Hackers Went to the Hill - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture revisiting the hackers' account before Congress. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Federal_Judg: On October 4, 2019, a federal judge ordered the White House to preserve records of the president's calls with foreign heads of state. A National Security Archive news post reported that order, which landed days after the Trump-Ukraine call became the center of an impeachment inquiry and raised fears that call records might vanish. Preservation orders are the emergency brake of records law: they change nothing about release, but they stop destruction while courts decide. The posting captures the moment archivists and lawyers moved to lock the record room door.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_The_Capitol_:
Donald Trump's official call log for January 6, 2021 has a gap of more than seven hours while the Capitol was under attack. In June 2022, the House January 6 committee opened televised hearings. The National Security Archive then published this account of its chronology work, and of the questions raised by that missing stretch of the president's day.

One puzzle anchors the posting. A phone call absent from the official log still showed up in the end-of-day diary. So how did it get there, and what else is missing? Call records matter because they can show who a president spoke with while events unfolded. Readers get a focused look at a documentary gap, the evidence around its edges, and why archivists treat a blank space in the record as a finding in itself.
greek-in-a-nutshell:
James Strong, professor at Drew Theological Seminary and famed for his concordance of the Bible, made this small manual in 1876 for beginners in Greek. Its full title calls it an outline of Greek grammar with brief reading lessons, designed for beginners in the New Testament. Strong first prepared it for a journal's normal class, and for the Sunday-school assembly held each year at Chautauqua. Its form, twelve series of two pages each, comes from that start.

The simplest elements of the language are packed into the narrow limits, with reading lessons full enough for later study. Strong tells the learner plainly that only the basics can fit such a compass. Sunday-school teachers with no college Greek were the book's first market. It is a neat sample of the Chautauqua movement, which carried study to the whole people.
headlong-hall:
Thomas Love Peacock published Headlong Hall in 1816, the first of his talk novels. A preface added in 1837, for this and the three novels printed with it, says the little books first appeared without prefaces and were left to speak for themselves. The contents map a country-house party: the mail, the squire, the breakfast, the arrivals, the grounds, the dinner, and the evening. A walk, a tower, a sexton, and a skull follow, then a lecture, a ball, and proposals.

At Squire Headlong's table, guests who each ride one idea argue them all to absurdity: the perfectibilian, the deteriorationist, and the statu-quo man among them. Peacock mocks the systems of his day in talk that sparkles and stings. Almost nothing happens, and everything is said. The book invented a kind of novel that England has loved since: clever people, good wine, and philosophy as sport.
how-to-tell-stories-to-children-and-some:
Sara Cone Bryant wrote How to Tell Stories to Children as a practical manual for teachers and parents, first in a series of books for storytellers. Early chapters explain the purpose of storytelling in school, how to choose tales, and why telling beats reading aloud. She studies what qualities children like and what a spoken tale needs.

The second half supplies stories ready to tell, including The Three Bears, The Three Little Pigs, and fables such as the lion and the mouse retold in the text. Bryant gives delivery advice alongside each example. Her book helped launch the storytelling movement in American schools and libraries, and its guidance on voice, pacing, and selection still reads sensibly.
ireland-since-parnell:
Captain D. D. Sheehan, barrister and late member for Mid-Cork, wrote Ireland Since Parnell in London in 1921. A leader appears is his first chapter. Sheehan defends Parnell's greatness against those who credit his lieutenants. No mediocrity, he argues, could have overawed the House of Commons so.

Ireland under Parnell rose from a corpse on the dissecting table, in Sheehan's phrase. Later chapters fight over a Home Rule bill and clerical feeling. A banquet for Mr. Birrell in London is recalled with bitterness. The book is a party man's history of the years after the fall.
jack-and-jill:
Louisa May Alcott inscribed this village story to the schoolmates of Ellsworth Devens in 1880 and called it a tale of her young neighbours. It begins with a catastrophe: Jack and his friend Jill come down a hill on one sled, crash, and are laid up with injuries that take a winter to mend. The chapters that follow are titled for their recovery: Two Penitents comes second.

Alcott keeps the two invalids at the centre of village life while they heal. Jack's broken leg and Jill's hurt back become lessons in patience for two children who were never still. Schoolmates, mothers, and a round of small adventures and scrapes fill the months of getting well. It is a quieter book than Little Women, built on friendship tested by a long enforced rest.
jimmy-lucy-and-all:
Jimmy, Lucy, and All is a children's story book by Sophie May, issued in Boston in 1900. It belongs to her Little Prudy's Children set, alongside the Little Prudy, Dotty Dimple, and Flaxie Frizzle series. The title page lists Lee and Shepard as publishers. Fourteen chapters follow the children through small adventures at home and away.

Chapter titles promise a tallyho ride, a first dinner, and Lucy's gold mine. A zebra kitten, a stolen chimney, and a thief found keep the fun moving. One chapter turns on begging pardon, and another on the little schoolma'am's earthquake. Nate's cave and Jimmy's good luck close the book. It is gentle family fiction of the kind May wrote for young readers.
larry-dexter-s-great-search-or-the-hunt-:
Howard R. Garis published Larry Dexter's Great Search in New York in 1909. Its subtitle is The Hunt for the Missing Millionaire. Garis also wrote the Dick Hamilton books for boys.

Larry Dexter works as a young reporter in this series. A missing millionaire gives him a case to chase. The frontispiece shows Larry crying out that he has found something. Clues, travel, and rival hunters keep the pace quick. Garis wrote for boys who liked newsroom adventure mixed with mystery. Garis fills the hunt with newspaper work and quick travel. Boys of 1909 met a hero whose tools were questions and shoe leather.
lemorne-versus-huell:
Elizabeth Stoddard published Lemorne Versus Huell in Harper's Magazine in 1863. The narrator spends two months at Newport with her Aunt Eliza Huell. Those months, she says, created all that is dramatic in her destiny.

Aunt Eliza came to the seaside for her health. She was also caught in a lawsuit, which made her troublesome company. The niece serves her from duty more than affection. A legal fight gives the tale its very title. Stoddard's sharp eye turns a family visit into quiet drama. Newport's shore setting cools a story of family friction. Stoddard's narrator watches more than she speaks, to sharp effect.
love-conquers-all:
Love Conquers All is a book of comic essays by Robert Benchley, printed in 1922. Gluyas Williams drew the pictures that go with the jokes. Contents promise family life in America and rules for watching auction bridge. Benchley also tells how to watch a chess match and a baseball game.

He asks whether insects think, and what to do while the family is away. Every piece takes a small, dull subject and makes it absurd. Benchley's mock-serious voice is the real show in each essay. He was one of America's best-loved humorists between the wars. These short pieces still raise laughs a century later.
ma-pettengill:
Ma Pettengill is a book of comic Western tales by Harry Leon Wilson. Wilson, who wrote Ruggles of Red Gap, published it in 1919. The narrator strolls up from the Arrowhead corrals on a Sunday afternoon. His hostess, Mrs. Lysander John Pettengill, sits knitting on the ranch piazza.

Ma runs her ranch and her neighbors with a firm, funny hand. Stories here tell of a love affair, a vendetta, and a porch wren. Red Gap's big-league pretensions get their share of teasing. Wilson writes in a dry, drawling, very American voice. Ma Pettengill stands among his best-loved comic creations. The book is pure pleasure for lovers of Western humor.
maastricht-treaty-1992-full:
The Maastricht Treaty is the 1992 agreement that founded the European Union. Its full text runs from a preamble through seven titles and many protocols. Title I states common provisions for the member states. Later titles amend the treaties of the European Communities.

The treaty creates a common foreign and security policy. It also joins the states in justice and home affairs work. Protocols set rules for the future European Central Bank. Others fix deficit limits and the tests for joining the euro. Denmark's property rights get a protocol of their own. Few documents have reshaped modern Europe more deeply. This is the complete legal text, article by article.
milly-darrell:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon, the Victorian novelist of Lady Audley's Secret, wrote Milly Darrell as a serial story. It ran in the magazine Belgravia from November 1870 to January 1871. This Paris printing of 1873, in Asher's Collection of English Authors, joins it with other stories. The edition was copyrighted for foreign circulation only.

Braddon was among the most popular English novelists of her era. Her sensation fiction turned on secrets, strong feeling, and threatened reputations. Milly Darrell belongs to the shorter tales she supplied to the magazines. Continental editions like this one carried her work to English readers traveling and living abroad.
miss-minerva-and-william-green-hill:
Frances Boyd Calhoun opens this Southern children's tale at a small-town gate at night. Little William Green Hill arrives by bus, riding up front beside the driver, Sam Lamb. His Aunt Minerva waits on the porch, scandalized that he would not ride inside. The boy wipes her kiss and claims he is only rubbing it in.

Billy, as he insists on being called, has run wild on a plantation until now. Miss Minerva intends to raise him by her strict rules. Calhoun tells the clash in rich dialect and gentle comedy. A Major's name makes the spinster blush, hinting at romance for her as well.
mr-hogarth-s-will:
Catherine Helen Spence wrote this novel about a death, a will, and two young women left in doubt. Mr. Hogarth of Cross Hall, in rural Scotland, dies suddenly in the early 1850s. He had raised two orphan nieces as his own daughters. The opening chapter gathers mourners to hear what his will will do.

Hogarth was known as odd and strict, yet fond of his nieces. He trusted women in theory but ruled the girls with many limits. Their schooling was shaped to fit his own views. The will sets the story's test of character, money, and freedom. Spence uses one household to probe how women could live and choose.
mr-meeson-s-will:
H. Rider Haggard's novel turns on a will, a shipwreck, and a fight in court. The contents name Augusta, her publisher Meeson's, and young Eustace. Eustace is cut off early, and Augusta sails on the Kangaroo. A wreck strands the party on Kerguelen Land.

Back in England the tale becomes a legal battle. Chapter titles promise lawyers, flight, and a case called Meeson v. Addison. Augusta holds the key to who gets the fortune. Haggard mixes sea adventure with courtroom drama. The odd will at the center tests greed, loyalty, and love under hard pressure.
nasa-tm-19660011811-prime-minitrack-and-:
Hans G Hertz at Goddard compared two ways of tracking the Vanguard II satellite in this report. One way is Prime Minitrack, which listens to the satellite's radio transmitter. The other is the Baker-Nunn camera, which photographs the satellite against the stars. Data cover twenty-six days while the transmitter still worked, in 1959. In all, hundreds of observations from both systems are presented.

Only readings made at the same time by both systems are used for the comparison. That pairing gives a fair test of accuracy. Tracking accuracy decides how well an orbit is known. Hertz's study helped judges weigh radio tracking against camera tracking, at the dawn of the satellite age.
nasa-tm-19680018321-nasa-lrc-program-to-:
Langley Research Center staff outline a program to define Earth's infrared horizon by direct experiment. Infrared horizon sensors steer spacecraft by watching the edge of Earth glow in heat light. To design such sensors well, engineers first need flight measurements of that horizon's true brightness pattern, called its radiance signature.

Flights on the X-15 research aircraft gathered data in three bands of the infrared spectrum. A second effort, Project Scanner, measured the horizon in two spectral bands. The report also weighs a larger flight program to widen coverage beyond both efforts. Its stated goal is sensor accuracy near one hundredth of a degree in judging vertical direction.
nasa-tm-19700025113-spectral-responses-o:
Henry W. Brandhorst Jr. and Russell E. Hart Jr. of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 solar cell conference in Seattle. It measures how silicon solar cells respond to light at low temperatures. Cells on deep-space craft can grow very cold.

The team measured responses for cells that did well in the cold and cells that did poorly. Poor cells showed a faulty rear contact or a flat spot in their output curve, they report. Their current also fell fast as the temperature dropped. Good cells lost output in a slow, even way. The authors hope the contrast points to better cold-weather cells.
nasa-tm-19720004062-flight-investigation:
Richard R Burley of the Lewis Research Center flew this nozzle study in November 1971, as NASA TM X-2396. An auxiliary inlet ejector nozzle sat on an engine nacelle under a wing. Burley warned that air reaching a mounted nozzle differs from clean tunnel flow. A podded engine near the wing's lower rear surface was the case of general interest. Flight tests could show what the mounting really did to performance.

Nozzle behavior alone in a tunnel can mislead designers. The wing, nacelle, and passing airflow all reshape the stream the nozzle breathes. Burley's flights measured the installed case directly. Programs building ejector nozzles for supersonic cruise aircraft needed such data. The report belongs to a wider Lewis effort on these nozzles.
nightfall:
Anthony Pryde opens Nightfall in a dark manor house called Wanhope, on a June afternoon. Laura Clowes comes in from the garden to tell Bernard that tea is ready. It is five o'clock, yet the hall is so dark she must grope her way through it.

Wanhope has a plain brick front and a great gateway of weathered stone. The family arms and motto, Fortis et Fidelis, are carved there. Inside, Spanish chestnut wood lines floor, stairs, walls, and ceiling. Flemish glass dims the light still more. A wall of old weapons, armour, and blades from many lands gives the hall its one glint.
oslo-accords-1993-full:
Signed on September 13, 1993, the Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government Arrangements is the founding text of the Oslo Accords between the Government of Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization. Its opening declares an end to decades of confrontation and a mutual recognition of legitimate and political rights, with a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace as the stated goal.

The articles provide for free elections to a Palestinian council under international observation, with Palestinian police keeping public order in the West Bank and Gaza Strip. A five-year transitional period begins with withdrawal from Gaza and Jericho. Permanent status talks, covering Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, security, and borders, must start by the third year. The document framed Middle East diplomacy for a generation.
project-gutenberg-complete-works-of-wins:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, is gathered here in a full set of his books, with a note making clear he is not the British statesman of the same name. The list runs from early romances to later novels of American public life.

Named works include Richard Carvel, The Crisis, Coniston, The Inside of the Cup, Mr. Crewe's Career, and A Far Country, plus a play and an essay on democracy. The set opens with The Crossing, a tale of the old border country. Readers get the whole shelf of a once-famous writer in one place.
puck-of-pook-s-hill:
Rudyard Kipling wrote a set of linked tales for children in which Puck, the old spirit of England, calls up figures from the land's past. Stories and songs alternate, each tale tied to the Sussex hill country where two children act out a play.

The contents run from Weland's Sword and Sir Richard's Norman knights to a Roman centurion on the Great Wall, Pictish raiders, a smuggler's tale, and a final story of treasure and law. Songs by Puck, the Danes, and the children thread the book. Readers get English history told as magic, memory, and adventure.
purcell:
Purcell, by John F. Runciman, is a short life of the composer Henry Purcell in Bell's Miniature Series of Musicians, published in London by George Bell and Sons in 1909. Five chapters and a list of works make up the book, with portraits by Kneller and Clostermann and a page of Purcell's own score among the pictures.

Runciman opens with a lost golden age: England once had a glorious school of composers, and it closed with Purcell, with the freshness of early morning still on its last music. The book traces that final figure of the school through his life and his works.
sejanus-his-fall:
Ben Jonson wrote this tragedy on Sejanus, the Roman courtier whose rise and fall shook the court of Tiberius. Jonson packed the play with learning, adding hundreds of notes drawn from Latin and Greek sources. A modern editor's opening essay ranks Jonson just below Shakespeare among English stage writers.

The essay traces Jonson's poor start in Westminster, his lost father, and his rise by sheer force of mind. The play itself follows Sejanus through five acts of plotting and ruin. Readers meet both a stern Roman tale and the strong, learned poet who chose to tell it in full classical dress.
sophocles-seven-plays-campbell:
Sophocles of Athens wrote the seven tragedies that survive complete from his large output. Lewis Campbell translated all seven into English verse. Oedipus Rex, Antigone, and Electra lead a set that defined tragedy itself.

Oedipus hunts the killer who polluted Thebes and finds himself. Antigone buries her brother against the king's decree and accepts death. Ajax, the Trachiniae, Philoctetes, and Oedipus at Colonus complete the surviving plays. Sophocles balances irony, character, and fate with unmatched control. Campbell's dignified verse served English readers for generations. No shelf of Greek drama feels complete without these seven plays.
st-george-s-cross-or-england-above-all:
H. G. Keene wrote St. George's Cross; or, England Above All. The sub-title calls it an episode of Channel Island history. Frederick Clarke printed it at Guernsey in 1887. W. H. Allen and Co. printed it at London. Keene tells the reader the tale is mixed. It is neither pure made-up story nor strict truth. It shows Channel Island life of two centuries back. Dr. S. E. Hoskins supplied its ground.

The prologue opens on a bright September day in 1649. Mr. William Prynne sits at his window in the Strand. Thames water at high tide laps his lawn. Prynne was a barred member of Parliament. Cavaliers had pilloried and jailed him. They had maimed and fined him as well. His university cast him out. His inn of court did the same. Roundheads in turn dealt hard with him, the tale goes on to say.
the-art-of-iugling-or-legerdemaine-where: A title page dated 1612 and a verse dedication are present for The Art of Iugling or Legerdemaine, signed only S. R. The title promises to lay open all the conveyances of juggling and sleight of hand, how they are done and where they lie. It also pledges warnings against cheating at cards and dice, the exposure of the beggarly art of alchemy, and the folly of charming charms, all tending to mirth. The dedication offers the work to the writer's father, William Bubb, as first fruits of their time together.
the-bronze-bell: Louis Joseph Vance wrote The Bronze Bell, dated 1909. Vance gave the book to F. E. Z., chatelaine of Juniper Lodge, in thanks for hospitality transplanted from its Kentucky home. A plate caption shows Amber watching a man who does not look back, himself split between amusement, annoyance, and astonishment. The chapters start with Destiny and the Babu, then The Girl and the Token. Marooned, The Man Perdu, and The Goblin Night come next. The Maharana of Khandawar, The Tonga, and The Long Day close the heads shown.
the-camp-fire-girls-at-sunrise-hill:
Margaret Vandercook wrote The Camp Fire Girls at Sunrise Hill, first of a series. Its chapters start with The Voice and Methinks You Are My Glass. Work, Health and Love, Meg, and Their First Meeting come next. The Law of the Camp Fire, White Clouds, and Other Girls lead to The Guardian. The End of the Summer Camp closes the list.

Chapter I opens on Betty Ashton, alone with a book. She sighs till the leaves quiver, then flings it face down on the floor. She wishes some one would invent something new for girls. All girls do nowadays, she exclaims to the empty room, is imitate boys: their games, their old books, even their work. All the time girls are really wanting girl things. She agrees with King Solomon that there is no new thing under the sun, at least not for girls.
the-case-of-richard-meynell:
The Case of Richard Meynell, by Mrs. Humphry Ward, was published in 1911 and dedicated to the memory of a beloved child. Its foreword addresses American readers directly. It asks those not intimate with English rural and religious life to remember one factor. On that factor the whole story depends: the existence of the State Church.

That church, she explains, is the direct heir of the pre-Reformation Church. It owns the cathedrals and parish churches. It crowns, marries, and buries the kings of England. It holds half the elementary schools. Through the great public schools it shapes the ruling class. Against it stands half the nation in the non-conformist bodies, in perpetual warfare of opinion and social jealousy, while new movements of thought gather in both camps. The foreword lays out the battlefield before the novel begins.
the-coming-of-bill:
P. G. Wodehouse published this novel in 1920, divided into two books. The contents promise a pawn of fate, troubled waters, a widening gap, outcasts, and a sixty-first street cyclone. Chapter I of Book One opens on Mrs. Lora Delane Porter and her automobile.

Mrs. Porter dismisses the hired man who brought her car round from the garage and seats herself at the wheel. Driving herself, readers learn, is her habit for refreshing her mind and improving her health. Other chapter titles name Ruth, who states her intentions, Steve, who suffers a misadventure and later comes to a rescue, and Mr. Penway, who ends up on the grill. Mrs. Porter's Waterloo closes the second book, just before a final chapter on the White-Hope link. Wodehouse builds a light romance of strong wills, money, and rescue, driven by daily habits like that morning drive.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-james-rus:
James Russell Lowell's complete poetical works appear here in a Cabinet Edition from Houghton, Mifflin and Company of Boston and New York, printed at the Riverside Press, Cambridge. A publishers' note explains the line of editions behind it. Lowell himself, the year before he died, edited a definitive Riverside edition of his works.

After his death his literary executor, Mr. C. E. Norton, brought out a last gathering of the poems, and the Cambridge edition followed. That Cambridge set held all the poems in the Riverside edition plus those Norton had edited. The Cabinet edition holds all the poems in the Cambridge edition, made from new plates. For the student's convenience, the longer poems have their lines numbered. Indexes of titles and first lines are also added.
the-courtship-of-susan-bell:
Drawn from the 1864 Chapman and Hall Tales of All Countries edition, with a frontispiece by Marcus Stone, The Courtship of Susan Bell opens on a widowed household. John Munroe Bell, a lawyer in Albany, New York, thrived for twelve years of marriage. Then he died, leaving his wife Henrietta and two daughters, a second Hetta and Susan, the heroine.

Bell left only a few thousand dollars, but he had built a small, well-furnished house at Saratoga Springs, part investment and part health retreat for his girls. There the widow has lived ten years with her daughters, taking in a few steady boarders each summer when heat drives New Yorkers out of the city. Saratoga in July, August, and September, the tale notes, is a gay place for girls with trunks of muslin and a carriage at hand.
the-dawn-of-all:
Printed at the Mayflower Press in Plymouth and headed Rome, Lent 1911, The Dawn of All opens with a prologue of waking. Memory and awareness creep back into a man lying in bed. They build step by step, like the theses he learned twenty years before in his seminary. First comes the sheet below his chin. Then a red coverlet, first seen as a blood-colored landscape, and a ceiling remote as the vault of heaven.

The roar in his ears sinks to a murmur like a tide at the foot of cliffs, then to street sounds. He first thinks he lies in his own lodgings in Bloomsbury, but the ceiling is too far away. Then the room rushes back into view, large and airy, with a doctor in white and a nurse watching him. Memory springs farther back, into a forgotten childhood, up to a blank stretch of days.
the-divine-comedy-volume-1-hell:
Charles Eliot Norton's prose rendering of Dante's Divine Comedy fills three volumes, and this first one holds Hell. A note dated at Cambridge, Massachusetts, in October 1891, ties the book to James Russell Lowell, who read its proofs in the last year of his life. Short prose summaries head each canto, from the dark wood and the three beasts onward.

Norton aims for close, plain English over rhyme. His summaries tell what each canto holds before the text begins. Readers get the full descent, circle by circle, with a steady guide to names, places, and sins.
the-downfall: The Downfall, also titled La Débâcle or The Smash-up, is a novel by Émile Zola in E. P. Robins's English rendering. Its contents divide the book into three parts of eight chapters each. No chapter bears a name. Only the title page and that bare list are present here. No story text appears, so the plot cannot be drawn from what is shown.
the-ear-in-the-wall:
Arthur B. Reeve's The Ear in the Wall lines up eighteen Craig Kennedy cases in its contents. First heads name The Vanisher, The Black Book, and a safe robbery; then come an anonymous letter, a suffragette secretary, and a woman detective. Later heads promise a jury fixer, a typewriter clue, and the portrait parlé method.

Kennedy fights graft with science: hidden mics, prints, and lab tests. Reeve's cases draw on real New York scandals of graft and gangs. Will Foster drew the frontispiece, as in the rest of the series.
the-high-school-left-end-or-dick-co-gril:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The High School Left End, subtitled Dick & Co. Grilling on the Football Gridiron. Chapter titles include Sulking in the Football Camp, The Start of the Dodge Mystery, The Soreheads in Conclave, Dick, Like Caesar, Refuses the Crown, and The Thanksgiving Day Game. Chapter one opens with Dave Darrin muttering in camp.

Dave calls football all at sixes and sevens this year. Tom Reade adds a darker hint: two members of the Athletics Committee have told Coach Morton they would rather see football passed by this year. Dick Prescott listens with rare attention, since Reade seldom uses that tone. A season under threat, a mystery around Dodge, and hard practice fill the football tale.
the-history-of-john-bull:
John Arbuthnot, M.D., wrote The History of John Bull. Henry Morley wrote an introduction for this edition. Morley calls the book the work that fixed a national figure. John Bull stands as ruddy and plump, with trumpeter's cheeks. He is an honest tradesman, simple and straightforward. He is easily cheated, Morley says, until he takes charge himself.

Morley dates the start of the book to 1712. It ran in four groups of chapters. The chapters dealt playfully with public affairs from the Tory side. Their subject was the road to the Peace of Utrecht. Later chapters treat feuds between Church and Dissent. They also treat the union of England and Scotland. John Bull then receives his Sister Peg into his house.
the-journal-of-a-tour-to-the-hebrides-wi:
James Boswell dedicated this journal to Edmond Malone. The letter is dated London, September 20, 1785. Truth in narrative matters most, he begins. He appeals to Johnson's friends to judge. Internal evidence will show whether the talks are rightly told. The talks form the book's most valued part. Malone had read the manuscript itself. He could vouch for the printed text's strict fidelity.

Boswell stacks his reasons for the choice. Malone knew Johnson well. His work editing Shakespeare links them too. Above all, Boswell wants the world to know their friendship. He recalls inscribing a former work to General Paoli. Paoli was the Corsican patriot honored in Britain. He had failed to preserve his country's freedom. The dedication shows Boswell's gratitude and self-display at once. Both habits make his journals live.
the-late-mrs-null:
Frank R. Stockton published his comic novel in 1886. Chapter one describes Midbranch, a Virginia family mansion set in a farm of nine hundred fifty acres. Its wide front gate almost never opens, since carriage wheels would ruin lawn grass said to date from statehood days.

Visitors instead climb broad wooden steps over the fence in front of the porch. Wood carts reach the back by a roundabout track among trees and deep chip soil. Stockton lingers on these odd arrangements with dry patience, letting a house entrance explain a family proud of habit and slow to change.
the-little-princess-of-tower-hill: L. T. Meade wrote The Little Princess of Tower Hill, dated 1889 and published in New York by A. L. Burt with six page illustrations. Only the title page, a transcriber's note, and part of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. Chapter titles shown include Her Very Young Days, Father's Short Visitor, Snubbed, The Stable Clock, and The Empty Hutch. The transcriber's note adds that the volume holds three stories: Tom, Pepper, and Trusty; Billy Anderson and his Troubles; and The Old Organ-Man.
the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-intere: Julian Hawthorne edited The Most Interesting Stories of All Nations for The Lock and Key Library, and this record shows the American section. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the stories themselves do not appear. The contents open with Hawthorne's introduction, called "Riddle Stories." First come F. Marion Crawford's By the Waters of Paradise and Mary E. Wilkins Freeman's The Shadows on the Wall. Melville D. Post's The Corpus Delicti follows, with tales by Ambrose Bierce, Poe, Washington Irving, and Charles Brockden Brown.
the-moorland-cottage-by-elizabeth-clegho:
Elizabeth Cleghorn Gaskell's The Moorland Cottage, dated 1850 in the record heading and shown in a New York printing of 1851, begins with a guided walk. Chapter I leads from the gate of Combehurst Church over a brook bridge and up a mounting field path. Sheep graze the short upland turf while the town and its church spire fall away below.

Beyond lies a common coloured with golden gorse and purple heather, where a lark drops suddenly into her hidden nest. The path then falls into a grassy hollow holding a house-sized dwelling. Mrs. Browne, widow of the late curate of Combehurst, lived there with her servant Nancy and her children Edward and Maggie. A sibling record of the same New York printing opens identically but names no author.
the-napoleon-of-notting-hill:
G. K. Chesterton's The Napoleon of Notting Hill came out in 1904. John Lane, The Bodley Head, published it in London and New York.
